title: VCS
text:
VCS
Architectures, Platforms, Operations, and GitOps
A practical path from your first commit to running a forge and shipping with GitOps. You start as a Git user, then you install and compare hosting platforms, then you operate them, then you let Git drive the cluster.
The sidebar is the full TOC (chapters 1–66 plus appendices). Every chapter starts with Theory (invariants, a diagram, what can break). Parts I–II have prose for the original pages and for chapter 7 (reset, restore, and checkout). The other newer core sub-pages are still stubs. Later parts are stubs until a writing pass fills them, except chapter 25 (Gitea and Forgejo), which is prose. The overall map lives in content/_planning/SYLLABUS.md, and the hosting/operations track is specified in content/_planning/SYLLABUS-ARCHITECTURES-PLATFORMS-AND-OPERATIONS-FOR-INDEPENDENT-CODE-HOSTING.md.

title: VCS
text:
Who this book is for
Software engineers, DevOps, platform, and SRE readers on Linux. You can start with no Git. Terms are defined on first use. Depth ramps: user → installer → admin → operator → GitOps practitioner.
Commands, paths, and package names assume a POSIX shell on Linux (bash is fine). Examples use /home/…, ~/.gitconfig, and distro packages (pacman, apt, dnf). The Git commands themselves are the same on other Unix systems; this book does not walk macOS or Windows.

title: VCS
text:
What you will master

Git’s object model, everyday commands, and recovery
How a Git hosting platform is built, and how GitLab, Forgejo, Bitbucket, Gerrit, SourceHut, and GitHub differ
Identity, CI, packages, supply-chain controls, backups, and air-gap
GitHub Actions as one CI product
GitOps with Flux and Argo CD, then progressive delivery with Argo Rollouts

title: VCS
section: How to read this so it sticks
text:
How to read this so it sticks
Work front to back in Part I. Type every command in a throwaway directory. Later parts assume you can commit, branch, and push. Platform labs reuse the same three desk repositories: desk-web, desk-api, desk-infra.

title: VCS
text:
The companion kit
Required for Parts I–II: Git 2.45 or newer on Linux (examples checked against 2.55), a terminal, and a text editor (nvim is the default in config examples).
Required from the GitOps parts onward: Docker, kind or K3s, kubectl, and Helm. Install those when you reach Part VII. You do not need a cluster to finish Git foundations.

title: VCS
text:
Conventions
Commands are complete. Run them from the directory the page names. Output is representative; hashes and timestamps on your machine will differ.
Heredocs create files without opening an editor:
cat > README.md <<'EOF'
# desk-api
EOF
The quoted 'EOF' keeps $variables and backticks literal. Drop the quotes only when you want the shell to expand them.
A repository (repo) is a directory Git is tracking. A forge is a Git hosting platform: the website and services around repositories (issues, pull requests, CI, packages). A remote is another copy of a repository you fetch from and push to.

title: VCS
text:
Acknowledgements
K19G. Built as part of the books library.

title: Theory
text:
Theory: Snapshots, Names, and a Graph
This chapter is the model the rest of the book assumes. Commands later only add objects and move names.

title: Theory
text:
Invariants

A commit names a complete tree, not a patch. Unchanged files reuse blob hashes.
History is a DAG: each commit points at parent(s). Nothing in the object store is rewritten in place.
A branch is a movable name for one commit. HEAD is a name for “where I am,” usually a pointer to a branch name.
Everyday work uses three trees: working directory, index, HEAD. Status is the report of how they differ.
Distribution means every clone is a repository. A forge is extra software around that fact.

  names (refs)                         objects (content-addressed)
  HEAD → main → C                      C  commit  → tree T → blobs
                ↑                      B  commit
                B ← A                  A  commit
If the name moves and the objects stay, you have not lost history; you have lost a pointer. Reflog (chapter 17) is the local journal of pointer motion.

title: Theory
text:
Why this model
Centralized systems made the server the only full history. Git inverts that: the laptop is complete. Cheap branches follow from “a branch is a file containing a hash.” Integrity follows from hashing content. Hosting platforms, CI, and GitOps cannot escape these invariants; they only add names, ACLs, and jobs.

title: Theory
text:
What can break

Treating Git like a file-sync tool (last write wins, no merge).
Treating GitHub as Git (issues, Actions, and PRs are forge objects).
Committing on a detached HEAD and switching away without a branch name.
Assuming git pull is a primitive; it is fetch plus integrate.

title: Theory
text:
How to read this chapter
Landscape is why a VCS. DAG, three trees, objects, refs, and distribution are how Git thinks. Detached HEAD and revision ranges are the first notations you will type. Install and the first repository apply this model on Linux.

title: The Version Control Landscape
text:
The Version Control Landscape
After this page you can say what version control is for, why Git is the usual tool, and what a forge is.

title: The Version Control Landscape
text:
Why you need a history
Without version control, a desk project grows copies:
desk-api/
├── app.py
├── app_backup.py
├── app_final.py
├── app_final_v2.py
└── app_really_final_fixed.py
You lose which file is current, who changed the login line, and any way to undo Tuesday without also undoing Wednesday. Two people editing app.py overwrite each other.
A version control system (VCS) keeps one tree of files, a history of snapshots, and a way to merge parallel work.

title: The Version Control Landscape
text:
Three generations








Generation
Idea
Examples




Local
History on one disk
SCCS, RCS


Centralized
One server is the repository
CVS, Subversion, Perforce


Distributed
Every clone is a full repository
Git, Mercurial



Local tools recorded deltas next to the files. Fine for one person on one machine.
Centralized tools put the real history on a server. You check out a working copy. Committing needs the network. If the server dies, history you do not have locally is gone.
Distributed tools give every clone the whole history. git commit is a local operation. A remote is another copy you push to when you choose. That is why Git works on a train, and why rewriting commits you already shared is a people problem.

title: The Version Control Landscape
text:
Why Git
Git won the ecosystem. The properties that matter for this book:

A commit is a snapshot of the whole tree, not a pile of patches as the primary model.
A branch is a cheap name for one commit. Merging and rebasing are graph operations.
Object names are hashes of content. Bit flips show up as missing or mismatched objects.
Log, diff, commit, branch, and merge all work without a network.
Hosting platforms speak Git remotes. Learning Git is not loyalty to one website.

Git vs Subversion, the comparison that still comes up:




Git
Subversion




Architecture
Distributed
Centralized


Offline commit
Yes
No


Branch
A name on a commit
A copy in the tree


Typical remote
Any number
One canonical server



Mercurial is also distributed. Git is what forges, CI systems, and GitOps engines speak.

title: The Version Control Landscape
text:
What a forge is
A repository is a directory Git is tracking (the .git folder plus your files).
A forge is a Git hosting platform: the website and services around repositories. Issues, pull requests, CI, packages, and user accounts live on the forge. GitHub, GitLab, Forgejo, Bitbucket, Gerrit, and SourceHut are forges. This book treats Git first, then the platforms.
Git is the tool. The forge is the product you log into. GitOps (later) is the idea that the same Git history should drive what runs in production.

title: The Version Control Landscape
text:
What Git is not

Not a backup by itself. A single laptop clone can die; you still need remotes and backups.
Not a file-sync tool. Dropbox overwrites. Git records snapshots and asks you to merge.
Not GitHub. You can use Git for years with a forge you run yourself, or with no forge at all.

title: The Version Control Landscape
text:
Next
The next pages are how Git thinks: a graph of commits, three trees on disk, four object types, names for those objects, and what “distributed” means for a server.

title: The Directed Acyclic Graph
text:
The Directed Acyclic Graph
After this page you can draw a tiny Git history as a graph and say what a branch is.

title: The Directed Acyclic Graph
text:
Snapshots with parents
A commit is a snapshot of the whole project at one instant, plus metadata (author, message, time) and a pointer to the commit that came before it — its parent.
Two commits in a row:
A  ←  B
B’s parent is A. Time flows left to right in this book’s diagrams; the parent pointer points backward, toward history.
A chain of commits is a directed acyclic graph (DAG): directed because each commit points at parents, acyclic because a commit cannot be its own ancestor.

title: The Directed Acyclic Graph
text:
A branch is a name
A branch is a movable name for one commit. main is a file that contains a hash. When you commit, Git writes a new snapshot whose parent is the current tip, then slides the name forward.
A  ←  B  ←  C     main
main now names C. A and B are still there. Nothing was overwritten.

title: The Directed Acyclic Graph
text:
A second line of work
Start a branch named feature while main is at C, then add two commits:
A  ←  B  ←  C          main
            ↑
            D  ←  E    feature
C has two children. Git is fine with that. A merge commit has two parents:
A  ←  B  ←  C  ←  M     main
            ↑     ↑
            D  ←  E     feature
M ties the two lines together. Rebase (chapter 9) copies D and E onto a new parent instead. New hashes, similar diffs. You will do that after first-repository muscle memory is in place.

title: The Directed Acyclic Graph
text:
HEAD
HEAD is “where I am.” Most of the time it points at a branch name, and the branch name points at a commit:
HEAD → refs/heads/main → C
Commands that “move HEAD” are moving that name, or (when HEAD is detached) pointing HEAD at a raw commit hash. Detached HEAD shows up when you check out a tag or a hash. New commits on a detached HEAD are easy to lose when you switch away. Create a branch before you leave, or find them later with the reflog (chapter 17).
git log --oneline --graph --all
git rev-parse HEAD main
git status
git status says HEAD detached at … when it is.

title: The Directed Acyclic Graph
text:
Look at the graph
Once you have a repository (next chapter’s neighbor, chapter 3):
git log --oneline --graph --decorate --all
--decorate prints the names (main, HEAD, tags) next to the commits they point at. The graph is the truth. Commands add objects and move names. If you hold the graph, reset, rebase, and reflog stop feeling like magic.

title: The Three-Tree Model
text:
The Three-Tree Model
After this page you can name Git’s three snapshots of the same project and say which command copies between them.

title: The Three-Tree Model
text:
Three snapshots, one project
Everyday Git is three versions of the same tree:








Name
On disk
Role




Working directory
your files
What you edit


Index (staging area)
.git/index
What the next commit will contain


HEAD commit
an object in .git/objects
Last committed snapshot on this branch



working directory  --git add-->  index  --git commit-->  HEAD
                 <--git restore--      <--git restore --staged / git reset--

 ~/desk/desk-api/              .git/index                 .git/objects
 README.md, src/…              next commit                last commit (HEAD)

git add copies working-tree bytes into the index (and writes blob objects).
git commit writes a tree from the index, then a commit pointing at that tree and at the current HEAD, then slides the branch name forward.
git restore <file> copies from the index (or a commit) onto the working tree.
git restore --staged <file> copies from HEAD into the index, leaving your working-tree edit in place.

There is no fourth “GitHub tree.” A remote is another repository’s names plus objects you have fetched.

title: The Three-Tree Model
text:
Why the index exists
The index lets the next commit be a chosen subset of what is on disk. You can edit five files and commit two.
echo "ok" >> README.md
echo "wip" >> notes.txt
git add README.md
git status
# README.md is staged; notes.txt is not
git commit -a copies already tracked files from the working tree into the index and commits. New files still need git add. Prefer explicit git add until that distinction is boring.

title: The Three-Tree Model
text:
status is the three-tree report
git status
Git compares:

working tree vs index → “Changes not staged for commit”
index vs HEAD → “Changes to be committed”
untracked files → paths the index does not know

When all three match, status is clean. That is the happy state after a commit.

title: The Three-Tree Model
text:
reset in one sentence
git reset moves HEAD and optionally the index and working tree. Soft / mixed / hard are which of the three trees follow. Chapter 7 (reset) and chapter 17 (reflog) use this on purpose. For now, prefer git restore to throw away an unstaged edit, and git restore --staged to unstage.

title: The Three-Tree Model
text:
Check it
git status
git diff              # working tree vs index
git diff --staged     # index vs HEAD
If git diff is empty and git diff --staged is not, the next commit already contains the change. If both are empty and status still lists a file, it is untracked — git add it.

title: Object Types
text:
Object Types
After this page you can name Git’s four object types and say what a hash is identifying.

title: Object Types
text:
Content-addressed storage
Git stores objects in .git/objects. The name of an object is a hash of its content. Change one byte of a file → new blob, new tree, new commit. Unchanged files keep the same blob hash across commits, which is why a one-line edit is cheap.
Historically the hash is SHA-1. Repositories can use SHA-256. Commands look the same. This book prints short hashes (a1b2c3d) the way git log --oneline does.

title: Object Types
text:
Four types



Type
Payload




blob
file bytes (no filename)


tree
name → object (a blob or a nested tree)


commit
a tree + parent commit(s) + author + message


tag
annotated pointer + message + optional signature



Filenames live in trees, not in blobs. Rename a file: new tree, same blob.
commit C
  tree T
    README.md  → blob B1
    src/       → tree T2
      main.py  → blob B2
  parent → commit B
  author Ada Desk <ada@example.com>
  message "Add ping"
A lightweight tag is only a name (a ref). An annotated tag is a real tag object. Chapter 12 covers tagging in daily use.

title: Object Types
text:
Packfiles are compression
Git also stores packfiles: many objects packed together with deltas, for disk. That is compression, not the data model. You still think in snapshots. Chapter 16 opens the object store with git cat-file. You can peek now:
git cat-file -t HEAD          # usually "commit"
git cat-file -p HEAD          # the commit payload
git rev-parse HEAD^{tree}     # the tree that commit names
-p pretty-prints. -t prints the type.

title: Object Types
text:
Integrity
Because names are hashes, a silent bit flip in a blob does not match the name the tree recorded. git fsck (chapter 21) walks the graph and reports missing or malformed objects. Forges and GitOps engines rely on this: the commit you pulled is the tree the author hashed.

title: Object Types
text:
What this buys a server
A Git hosting platform is, at minimum, a store of these objects plus names (branches, tags) plus auth. Chapter 23 is that architecture. The object model you just learned is the constraint the server cannot wish away: clones fetch objects and update names.

title: References: Branches, Tags, and HEAD
text:
References: Branches, Tags, and HEAD
After this page you can say what a ref is, where it lives, and how HEAD relates to a branch.

title: References: Branches, Tags, and HEAD
section: A ref is a name for a hash
text:
A ref is a name for a hash
A ref (reference) is a name that points at a commit (or, for annotated tags, at a tag object). Git stores them as files under .git/refs/ and, when there are many, in .git/packed-refs.








Ref
Typical path
Meaning




Branch
.git/refs/heads/main
Movable name for a line of work


Tag
.git/refs/tags/v1.0
Name meant to stay put


Remote-tracking
.git/refs/remotes/origin/main
Last-seen tip of a branch on a remote


HEAD
.git/HEAD
Where you are



git rev-parse main
git rev-parse HEAD
cat .git/HEAD
# ref: refs/heads/main
git rev-parse turns a name into a hash. Use it when a diagram and the disk disagree in your head.

title: References: Branches, Tags, and HEAD
section: Branches move, tags mostly do not
text:
Branches move, tags mostly do not
git branch                  # local branches
git branch feature          # new name at current HEAD
git switch feature          # HEAD now points at feature
git switch -c hotfix        # create and switch
git switch is the modern command for changing branches (git checkout still works; this book uses switch for branches and restore for files).
A tag is a bookmark:
git tag v0.1                # lightweight: a name at HEAD
git tag -a v0.1 -m "first"  # annotated: a tag object
Moving a published tag surprises people who already fetched it. Moving a branch is normal.

title: References: Branches, Tags, and HEAD
section: HEAD is usually a pointer to a pointer
text:
HEAD is usually a pointer to a pointer
.git/HEAD          →  ref: refs/heads/main
.git/refs/heads/main →  a1b2c3d4….
Commit while on main: Git writes a new commit whose parent is a1b2c3d4…, then overwrites refs/heads/main with the new hash. HEAD did not change its text; the branch it names did.
Detached HEAD: .git/HEAD contains a raw hash instead of ref: refs/heads/…. You get there with git switch --detach, or by checking out a tag. To keep work from a detached HEAD:
git switch -c keep-this
That creates a branch at the current commit and attaches HEAD to it.

title: References: Branches, Tags, and HEAD
text:
Remote-tracking names
After you add a remote named origin and fetch (chapter 11):
refs/remotes/origin/main
That is your last photograph of main on that remote. It updates on fetch. You do not commit onto it. Your local main is a separate name you push.

title: References: Branches, Tags, and HEAD
text:
Plumbing vs porcelain
git branch, git switch, git tag are porcelain (human commands). git update-ref and git symbolic-ref are plumbing (the same operations, no sugar). This book stays on porcelain until internals (chapter 16). Knowing refs are files is enough to understand why creating a branch is cheap: Git writes a 41-byte file.

title: The Distributed Model
text:
The Distributed Model
After this page you can explain why every clone is a repository, and what that implies for a hosting server.

title: The Distributed Model
section: Every clone is a full copy
text:
Every clone is a full copy
When you git clone, you get:

every commit reachable from the branches and tags you fetched
a working tree checked out at one branch (usually main)
a remote named origin pointing at the URL you cloned

There is no “thin client.” git log, git diff, git commit, git branch, and git merge talk to .git/ on your disk. The network is for fetch (download objects and update remote-tracking names) and push (upload objects and ask the other side to move a name).
your laptop                         a forge
┌─────────────────┐                ┌─────────────────┐
│ .git/objects    │   fetch/push   │ .git/objects    │
│ refs/heads/main │ ←────────────→ │ refs/heads/main │
│ refs/remotes/   │                │ (plus issues,   │
│   origin/main   │                │  CI, packages)  │
└─────────────────┘                └─────────────────┘
Both sides are Git repositories. The forge adds a website, accounts, and extra services. Git itself does not need them.

title: The Distributed Model
text:
Implications
Offline work is real. You can commit on a plane. Push when you have a network.
Several remotes are normal. origin is a convention, not a law. You can push the same desk-api history to a laptop USB clone, a Forgejo server, and GitHub. Chapter 22 uses that as an independence move.
The server does not own history uniquely. If the forge vanishes, every up-to-date clone still has the Git objects. What you lose are issues, pull-request comments, CI logs, and packages — the forge’s extras. That split is the rest of this book.
Rewriting shared history is a social operation. git commit --amend and rebase change hashes. On your laptop before anyone fetched, that is fine. After others based work on those hashes, you are asking them to reset. Chapter 9 is the skill; this page is the reason it matters.
Fetch is not pull. git fetch updates origin/main on disk. git pull is fetch plus a merge or rebase into your current branch. Chapter 11 separates them. Prefer fetch until pull’s extra step is a choice you can name.

title: The Distributed Model
section: What a hosting platform must speak
text:
What a hosting platform must speak
A Git server has to:

Store objects and refs.
Speak the Git protocol over SSH and/or HTTP (smart protocol: the client and server negotiate which objects to send).
Decide who may move which refs (authorization).
Run hooks on receive (the server-side programs that can reject a push).

Everything else — pull requests, CI, registries, SAML — is forge software on top of that. Chapter 23 draws the boxes. Chapter 3 stays on your laptop: git init, add, commit.

title: Theory
text:
Theory: Identity and Config are Data, Not Login
Git does not have accounts. It has key-value config and author strings baked into commits. A forge later matches those strings to a user.

title: Theory
text:
Invariants

Config is three layers: system (/etc/gitconfig), global (~/.gitconfig), local (.git/config). Later overrides earlier.
user.name and user.email are copied into every commit object. Changing config does not rewrite old commits.
Authentication to a remote (SSH key or HTTPS token) is separate from commit identity.
init.defaultBranch only affects new repositories.

  /etc/gitconfig          machine
  ~/.gitconfig            you
  .git/config             this repo     ← wins

  user.email ──► commit.author     (history)
  SSH key    ──► git@host          (transport)

title: Theory
text:
Why layers
One person, two emails (home and work) is a local or includeIf problem, not a second Git install. One laptop, several forges, is several keys in ~/.ssh/config, not several user.names.

title: Theory
text:
What can break

Commits with $USER@$HOSTNAME because identity was never set (user.useConfigOnly refuses that).
Pushing with HTTPS using an account password; most forges want a token.
Setting core.autocrlf on Linux and fighting LF files.
Assuming core.editor is optional and then hanging in vim on git commit with no -m.

title: Theory
text:
How to read this chapter
Install is PATH and version. Layers are which file won (--show-origin). Identity is what history will say. SSH vs HTTPS is how a remote will know you. Editor, aliases, and updates are the Linux daily driver.

title: Installing Git
text:
Installing Git
After this page you have a current git on your PATH on Linux and can print its version.

title: Installing Git
text:
Check what you already have
git --version
which -a git
This book wants 2.45 or newer on Linux. Examples were checked against 2.55. You need git switch, git restore, and (later) SSH commit signing.
Most desktop distros already ship a new enough Git. If which git prints /usr/bin/git and the version is 2.45+, you are done.

title: Installing Git
text:
Install from the distro
Arch Linux and Omarchy
pacman -Q git
# missing or too old:
sudo pacman -S git
Debian and Ubuntu
sudo apt update
sudo apt install git
Fedora
sudo dnf install git
Enterprise images sometimes freeze Git at 2.25. If git --version is older than 2.45, use your distro’s backports or a current tarball from git-scm.com so switch and restore exist.

title: Installing Git
text:
Line endings and the filesystem
Linux stores LF line endings and executable bits. Leave core.autocrlf unset. Leave core.fileMode at the default (true) so chmod +x is recorded. Those defaults are why hooks and scripts in later chapters work with chmod +x hook.sh.

title: Installing Git
section: What else you need for Parts I–II
text:
What else you need for Parts I–II







Tool
Role




A Linux terminal
Where you run git (bash or another POSIX shell)


A text editor
nvim in this book’s config examples; any editor is fine



Docker, Kubernetes, and a forge account wait until later parts.
Set core.editor once you know which editor you type in (next page). Until then, git commit -m "message" avoids opening one.

title: Installing Git
text:
Confirm
git --version
which git
echo "$HOME"
$HOME should be /home/<you>. Then set identity and the three config layers on the next page.

title: Config Layers
text:
Config Layers
After this page you can say which file a Git setting comes from, and set the handful of keys this book assumes.

title: Config Layers
text:
Three layers



Layer
Flag
Typical file
Who




System
--system
/etc/gitconfig
every user on the machine


Global
--global
~/.gitconfig
you, every repo


Local
--local (default)
.git/config
this repo only



Later keys override earlier ones. Work email in a company repo is a local user.email, not a second global identity you forget to switch.
  wins
    ▲
    │   .git/config          local    this repo
    │   ~/.gitconfig         global   this user
    │   /etc/gitconfig       system   this machine
    │
  reads bottom → top; last value for a key wins
git config --list --show-origin --show-scope
git config --show-origin user.email
--show-origin prints the file that won. --unset removes a key at the layer you name:
git config --global --unset core.editor

title: Config Layers
text:
Set the global layer once
git config --global init.defaultBranch main
git config --global core.editor "nvim"
git config --global pull.ff only
git config --global rerere.enabled true
git config --global diff.algorithm histogram
git config --global merge.conflictstyle zdiff3







Key
Why




init.defaultBranch main
git init creates main, not master


core.editor
git commit without -m opens this editor (code --wait, vim, nvim)


pull.ff only
git pull fast-forwards or fails; you merge or rebase on purpose


rerere.enabled
reuse recorded conflict resolutions


diff.algorithm histogram
better diffs on refactored files


merge.conflictstyle zdiff3
conflict markers include the common ancestor



pull.ff only means a pull that would create a merge commit fails instead. That is safer than the old default. Chapter 11 is remotes; this setting is safe to apply now.
Leave core.fileMode at the default so Git records executable bits. Set it to false only on a filesystem that cannot store those bits.

title: Config Layers
text:
Repo-only overrides
cd desk-api
git config user.email "ada@work.example"
# writes .git/config
Inspect:
git config --local --list --show-origin

title: Config Layers
text:
includeIf for home vs work
# ~/.gitconfig
[user]
    name = Ada Desk
    email = ada@example.com

[includeIf "gitdir:~/work/"]
    path = ~/.gitconfig-work
# ~/.gitconfig-work
[user]
    email = ada@work.example
Any repo under ~/work/ picks up the work email without a per-repo command. Paths in gitdir: should be absolute or start with ~/.

title: Config Layers
text:
See the result
git config --list --show-origin --show-scope | less
Identity (user.name, user.email) is the next page. Those two keys go into every commit.

title: Identity, Email, and Essential Settings
text:
Identity, Email, and Essential Settings
After this page every commit you make records a name and email you chose.

title: Identity, Email, and Essential Settings
section: Identity is metadata, not a login
text:
Identity is metadata, not a login
user.name and user.email are written into every commit. They are not a password and not a forge account. Forges match the email to an account when they display history. A typo produces “unknown author” on the website. git commit still succeeds.
~/.gitconfig
  user.name  = Ada Desk
  user.email = ada@example.com
           │
           ▼
      commit object
        tree    …
        parent  …
        author  Ada Desk <ada@example.com>  1774… +0530
        committer Ada Desk <ada@example.com> …
        message …
git config --global user.name "Ada Desk"
git config --global user.email "ada@example.com"
Use the email the forge should associate with you. For a first laptop, any address you control is fine. For work, the company address, often via includeIf from the previous page.
Refuse to commit if identity is missing, instead of guessing $USER@$HOSTNAME:
git config --global user.useConfigOnly true

title: Identity, Email, and Essential Settings
text:
Check what will be recorded
git config user.name
git config user.email
git config --show-origin user.email
After you have a commit (chapter 3):
git log -1 --format=full
Author: is user.name <user.email> from the time of the commit. Changing ~/.gitconfig later does not rewrite old commits. Chapter 6 is amending; chapter 20 is signing.

title: Identity, Email, and Essential Settings
text:
Signing is later
Signed commits (SSH or GPG) prove the commit came from a key you hold. Set identity here first. Signing is chapter 20.

title: Identity, Email, and Essential Settings
text:
Author vs committer
A commit has two people fields: author (who wrote the patch) and committer (who made the commit object). They match until you cherry-pick, rebase, or apply a patch from someone else. git log shows the author by default. You do not need to set GIT_COMMITTER_NAME for Part I.

title: Identity, Email, and Essential Settings
text:
Essential settings, one list
If you jumped here from install, this is the whole global block this book expects:
git config --global user.name "Ada Desk"
git config --global user.email "ada@example.com"
git config --global user.useConfigOnly true
git config --global init.defaultBranch main
git config --global core.editor "nvim"
git config --global pull.ff only
Replace the name, email, and editor with yours. Then pick SSH or HTTPS on the next page.

title: SSH vs HTTPS
text:
SSH vs HTTPS
After this page you can authenticate to a forge over SSH or HTTPS and know which URL form you are looking at.

title: SSH vs HTTPS
section: Two ways to talk to a remote
text:
Two ways to talk to a remote









SSH
HTTPS




URL
git@host:owner/repo.git
https://host/owner/repo.git


Secret
Private key on disk
Password, personal access token, or credential helper


Typical use
Daily push/fetch on a machine you own
CI, quick clone, hosts that block SSH



Both speak the Git smart protocol. The difference is how the server decides who you are. Part I does not require a forge. Set this up before chapter 11 so the first push is not a scavenger hunt.
  Linux laptop                         forge
 ┌──────────────────┐                 ┌──────────────────┐
 │ ~/.ssh/id_ed25519│  SSH            │ authorized keys  │
 │   (private)      │ ──────────────► │ git@host         │
 │ id_ed25519.pub   │  or HTTPS+token │ + Git objects    │
 └──────────────────┘                 └──────────────────┘
         git push / git fetch

title: SSH vs HTTPS
text:
SSH keys
Generate an ed25519 key if you do not have one:
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "ada@example.com" -f ~/.ssh/id_ed25519
Press Enter for no passphrase, or set one (then ssh-agent remembers it for the session):
eval "$(ssh-agent -s)"
ssh-add ~/.ssh/id_ed25519
Public key (this is what you paste into the forge):
cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub
The private file ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 stays on your machine. Never commit it. Never paste it into a ticket.
On the forge: account settings → SSH keys → paste the .pub line. GitHub, GitLab, and Forgejo all have this screen. The label can be laptop.
Test (GitHub as an example host; use your forge’s hostname):
ssh -T git@github.com
A greeting that includes your username means the key was accepted. A password prompt means the server did not see the key (ssh -v shows which files it tried).
~/.ssh/config for several hosts:
Host github.com
  HostName github.com
  User git
  IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_ed25519

Host forgejo.home
  HostName 192.168.68.200
  User git
  Port 2222
  IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_ed25519
A later Forgejo lab uses a port like 2222. The Host alias lets you write git@forgejo.home:ada/desk-api.git.

title: SSH vs HTTPS
text:
HTTPS and tokens
git clone https://github.com/example/desk-api.git
Pushing over HTTPS asks for a username and a personal access token (not your account password on most forges). Store it in a credential helper:
git config --global credential.helper libsecret   # GNOME Keyring / libsecret, if installed
# memory-only fallback (forgets at reboot or after a timeout):
git config --global credential.helper cache
CI systems often use HTTPS with a job-scoped token. Humans on a laptop usually have an easier time with SSH.

title: SSH vs HTTPS
text:
Pick one default
For this book’s desk repos on a machine you own: SSH. Clone and remote URLs will look like:
git@host:owner/desk-api.git
You can change a remote later (chapter 11):
git remote -v
git remote set-url origin git@host:owner/desk-api.git
Chapter 3 stays local: git init does not need SSH or HTTPS.

title: Theory
text:
Theory: The Add/Commit Cycle is the Product
A repository is useful the moment you can take bytes on disk, choose a subset, and name a snapshot. Everything else (branch, rebase, push) is names and copies of that operation.

title: Theory
text:
Invariants

git init creates .git/ and a symbolic HEAD. The first commit creates refs/heads/main.
git add copies working-tree bytes into the index (and writes blobs). It does not create a commit.
git commit writes a tree from the index, then a commit, then slides the current branch name.
git status is three comparisons: working vs index, index vs HEAD, untracked vs index.
Undo of uncommitted work is restore. Undo of the last unpublished commit is --amend. Undo of published history is revert (later).

  edit  →  add  →  commit
   WD       index    HEAD / main

  status reports which of the three disagree

title: Theory
text:
Why the index exists
Without an index, every commit would be “whatever is on disk.” The index is how you commit two of five edited files, or one hunk of a file (add -p). That is also why .gitignore exists: untracked paths never enter the index unless you force them.

title: Theory
text:
What can break

git add . of .env and secrets (ignore first).
git commit -a on a new file (it only auto-stages tracked paths).
git init in $HOME and then every subdirectory looking like a repo.
Amending after someone else fetched that hash.

title: Theory
text:
How to read this chapter
Init, add/commit, status/log/diff, and undo are the loop. The hands-on page is that loop on desk-api. Ignore, interactive add, rm/mv, and “what not to commit” are the same loop with sharper edges.

title: Initializing a Repository
text:
Initializing a Repository
After this page you have an empty Git repository on main and you know what git init created.

title: Initializing a Repository
text:
A directory becomes a repository
mkdir -p ~/desk/desk-api
cd ~/desk/desk-api
git init
Output looks like:
Initialized empty Git repository in /home/ada/desk/desk-api/.git/
If you set init.defaultBranch main (chapter 2), the empty branch is named main. Confirm:
git status
On branch main

No commits yet

nothing to commit (create/copy files and use "git add" to track)
~/desk/desk-api is the working tree. ~/desk/desk-api/.git/ is the repository (objects, refs, config). You edit files next to .git, not inside it.
~/desk/desk-api/                 working tree (you edit these)
├── README.md
├── src/
└── .git/                        repository
    ├── HEAD                     ref: refs/heads/main
    ├── config
    ├── objects/                 empty until first commit
    └── refs/heads/              main appears after first commit
This book’s recurring desk is three repos: desk-web, desk-api, desk-infra. Part I uses desk-api as the tiny project. Create the other two the same way when a later chapter asks.

title: Initializing a Repository
text:
What git init wrote
ls -a .git
You will see at least config, HEAD, objects/, refs/. HEAD currently says ref: refs/heads/main even though refs/heads/main does not exist yet. The first commit creates that file.
cat .git/HEAD
git rev-parse --git-dir
# .git
--git-dir is useful when you are in a subdirectory later.

title: Initializing a Repository
text:
init vs clone







Command
When




git init
You are starting a project that has no Git history yet


git clone <url>
You are copying an existing repository, including its history



clone is chapter 11. For a brand-new desk project, init is the right verb.

title: Initializing a Repository
text:
Already have files?
git init in a directory that already has source files is fine. Git does not add them until you git add. The next page is that loop.

title: Initializing a Repository
text:
init in the wrong place
If you run git init in your home directory, every git status from a subdirectory without its own .git will try to use ~/.git. Remove a mistaken repo with:
# only if you meant to throw it away and there are no commits you need
rm -rf .git
That deletes Git’s data for that directory, not your files. The first-commit hands-on page builds desk-api from scratch so you can see a clean init.

title: The Add/Commit Cycle
text:
The Add/Commit Cycle
After this page you can take a file from the working tree to a commit on main.

title: The Add/Commit Cycle
text:
The loop
edit files  →  git add  →  git commit  →  git status (clean)
That is the whole product: copy chosen files into the index, snapshot the index, name the snapshot with a message, slide main forward.
 working tree          index             HEAD / main
 ┌──────────┐      ┌──────────┐      ┌──────────┐
 │ README.md│ -add→│ README.md│-commit→│ commit C │
 │ ping.py  │      │          │      │ tree  T  │
 └──────────┘      └──────────┘      └──────────┘
                                          ▲
                                     main ─┘

title: The Add/Commit Cycle
text:
One file, one commit
From an initialized desk-api (previous page):
cd ~/desk/desk-api

cat > README.md <<'EOF'
# desk-api

HTTP API for the desk.
EOF

git add README.md
git status
git commit -m "Add README"
git log --oneline
git add stages README.md. git commit -m writes the commit without opening an editor. git log --oneline prints one line: a short hash and the message.
status is now clean. Working tree, index, and HEAD match.

title: The Add/Commit Cycle
text:
A second commit
mkdir -p src
cat > src/ping.py <<'EOF'
def ping():
    return "ok"
EOF

git add src/ping.py
git commit -m "Add ping"
git log --oneline
Two commits. src/ exists in the tree object because Git stored a tree named src pointing at the ping.py blob. You did not git add the directory separately; adding the file is enough.

title: The Add/Commit Cycle
text:
What -m is doing
Every commit needs a message. -m "Add README" is the short form. Without -m, Git opens core.editor. Multi-paragraph messages:
git commit -m "Add ping" -m "Returns a fixed ok string so the health check has a function to call."
The first -m is the subject. The second is the body. Chapter 6 is Conventional Commits (feat:, fix:). For Part I, a short imperative sentence is enough: Add ping, Fix empty name, Document env vars.

title: The Add/Commit Cycle
text:
git add shapes
git add README.md              # one file
git add src/ping.py src/app.py # several
git add src                    # a directory, recursively
git add .                      # everything from here down, still respects .gitignore
git add -p README.md           # hunk by hunk (interactive)
.gitignore is a file of patterns Git will leave untracked. Create it when you have build output or secrets to skip:
cat > .gitignore <<'EOF'
__pycache__/
.env
EOF
git add .gitignore
git commit -m "Ignore bytecode and env files"
Patterns are matched from the file’s directory downward. /build at the repo root is only build/ at the root; build/ is every directory named build.

title: The Add/Commit Cycle
text:
commit -a
git commit -a -m "Touch tracked files"
Stages already tracked files and commits. New files still need git add. Prefer explicit git add until that is automatic in your head.

title: The Add/Commit Cycle
text:
After the cycle
git status
git log --oneline
Clean status, two or three commits. Next page: how to read what you just did (status, log, diff).

title: status, log, and diff
text:
git status, git log, git diff
After this page you can read the three-tree report, walk history, and see a patch before you commit it.

title: status, log, and diff
text:
git status — where you are
cd ~/desk/desk-api
git status
git status -sb          # short: branch + one letter per file
-sb prints ## main and lines like M README.md (modified) or ?? notes.txt (untracked). Use it when the long form is noise.
git status is the three-tree report from chapter 1: working tree vs index vs HEAD.
 git diff              git diff --staged         git log
 working vs index      index vs HEAD             HEAD chain

 working tree          index                     HEAD
 ┌──────────┐         ┌──────────┐              A ← B ← C  main
 │ extra    │         │ staged   │
 └──────────┘         └──────────┘

title: status, log, and diff
section: git log — the DAG as a list
text:
git log — the DAG as a list
git log
git log --oneline
git log --oneline --graph --decorate --all
git log -3                          # last three
git log --oneline -- README.md      # commits that touched this path
git log -p -1                       # last commit plus its patch
--oneline is the default view in this book. --graph --decorate --all is the view that matches the mental-model diagrams.
Useful format:
git log --format='%h %an %s'
%h short hash, %an author name, %s subject. git help log lists more placeholders. You will use --format in hooks and CI later; for now, --oneline is enough.

title: status, log, and diff
text:
git diff — the patch
git diff                 # working tree vs index (unstaged)
git diff --staged        # index vs HEAD (what the next commit will contain)
git diff HEAD            # working tree vs HEAD (staged and unstaged together)
git diff HEAD~1 HEAD     # last commit vs its parent
git diff main feature    # two branches (once you have them, chapter 8)
Empty git diff and non-empty git diff --staged means everything is already in the index. Empty both, plus an untracked file in status, means you still need git add.

title: status, log, and diff
text:
DiffTool
For a side-by-side view in the terminal:
git config --global diff.tool nvimdiff    # or vimdiff, meld
git difftool README.md
git difftool --staged
difftool opens each changed file in the tool you named. mergetool is the sibling for conflicts (chapter 8). Stay on git diff until you want the split view. The patch is the same data.

title: status, log, and diff
text:
A one-minute drill
echo "note" >> README.md
git status
git diff
git add README.md
git diff                 # empty
git diff --staged        # the note
git restore --staged README.md
git restore README.md    # discard the note
git status               # clean
restore is the next page, on purpose. Here you only need to see the three diffs change as the file moves.

title: Undoing Mistakes
text:
Undoing Mistakes
After this page you can discard an unstaged edit, unstage a file, and rewrite the last commit before anyone else has it.

title: Undoing Mistakes
text:
Three common “undo”s








You did
You want
Command




Edited a tracked file, not staged
Throw the edit away
git restore <file>


git add too soon
Keep the edit, leave it out of the next commit
git restore --staged <file>


Last commit message (or last commit contents) is wrong, not pushed
Replace that commit
git commit --amend



These are safe on a laptop branch nobody has fetched. After git push, amending rewrites a hash other people may have. Chapter 9 and chapter 11 cover that case. Chapter 17 (reflog) is the safety net when you went too far.
 restore <file>              restore --staged           commit --amend
 working ← index             index ← HEAD               A ← B ← C
                                                        A ← B ← C'   (C gone from main)

title: Undoing Mistakes
text:
Discard unstaged work
cd ~/desk/desk-api
echo "oops" >> README.md
git restore README.md
The working-tree file matches the index again. The “oops” line is gone. Git cannot get it back from Git; your editor’s undo might.
Restore one file from HEAD even if it was staged:
git restore --source=HEAD --worktree --staged README.md
That is “make this file look like the last commit, in both index and working tree.”

title: Undoing Mistakes
text:
Unstage, keep the edit
echo "keep me" >> README.md
git add README.md
git restore --staged README.md
git status
The line is still in the file. It is not in the index. The next git commit will not include it until you git add again.
Older docs say git reset HEAD README.md for the same unstage. This book uses git restore --staged.

title: Undoing Mistakes
text:
Amend the last commit
You just committed and noticed a typo in the message:
git commit --amend -m "Add ping helper"
You forgot a file:
git add src/ping.py
git commit --amend --no-edit
--no-edit keeps the old message. --amend replaces the last commit with a new one (new hash) whose parent is the same as before. git log no longer shows the old hash as main. The old commit is still in the reflog for about 30 days (chapter 17).
Amend only when:

it is the latest commit on this branch, and
you have not pushed it, or you are sure no one else built on it.

title: Undoing Mistakes
text:
Revert is a new commit
git revert <hash> adds a commit that undoes a previous one. Use it on history other people already have. Chapter 10 is revert and cherry-pick. For a local last-commit mistake, amend. For an old published mistake, revert.

title: Undoing Mistakes
text:
rm and mv
git rm src/old.py              # stop tracking and delete the file
git rm --cached secrets.env    # stop tracking, keep the file on disk
git mv src/ping.py src/health.py
git status
git commit -m "Rename ping to health"
git mv is mv plus git add of the rename. Git detects renames in diffs even if you mv and add by hand; git mv is the tidy form.

title: Undoing Mistakes
text:
If you are lost
git status
git log --oneline -5
Status tells you which of the three trees disagree. Log tells you where main points. The hands-on page next builds a tiny desk-api from scratch so you can practice the whole loop, including one amend.

title: Hands-On: Build a Tiny Project
text:
Hands-On: Build a Tiny Project
Build desk-api from nothing: init, two commits, a bad edit, a restore, an amend, a clean log.

title: Hands-On: Build a Tiny Project
text:
Setup
Use a throwaway directory. If ~/desk/desk-api already exists from earlier pages, either work there or pick ~/desk/desk-api-lab.
mkdir -p ~/desk/desk-api
cd ~/desk/desk-api
git init
git status
Expect On branch main and No commits yet.

title: Hands-On: Build a Tiny Project
text:
Commit 1 — README
cat > README.md <<'EOF'
# desk-api

HTTP API for the desk.
EOF

git add README.md
git commit -m "Add README"
git log --oneline
One line of history.

title: Hands-On: Build a Tiny Project
text:
Commit 2 — a tiny module
mkdir -p src
cat > src/ping.py <<'EOF'
def ping():
    return "ok"
EOF

cat > .gitignore <<'EOF'
__pycache__/
.env
EOF

git add src/ping.py .gitignore
git status
git commit -m "Add ping and gitignore"

title: Hands-On: Build a Tiny Project
text:
Read it
git status
git log --oneline --graph --decorate
git show --stat HEAD
git show prints the last commit’s metadata and patch. --stat is the short file list.

title: Hands-On: Build a Tiny Project
text:
Break it on purpose
echo "oops" >> README.md
git status
git diff
git restore README.md
git status
Clean again. The “oops” line is gone.

title: Hands-On: Build a Tiny Project
text:
Stage, unstage, restage
echo "Health: GET /ping" >> README.md
git add README.md
git diff --staged
git restore --staged README.md
git diff
git add README.md
git commit -m "Document /ping"

title: Hands-On: Build a Tiny Project
text:
Amend the message
That last message is vague. Replace it (still local, unpushed):
git commit --amend -m "Document the ping endpoint in README"
git log --oneline
Three commits. The amended hash is new. git status is clean.

title: Hands-On: Build a Tiny Project
text:
Ignore a secret-shaped file
echo 'TOKEN=dev' > .env
git status
.env should be untracked (your .gitignore lists it). If it shows as untracked, the ignore pattern is working. If Git wants to add it, the .gitignore commit is missing — add the file and commit.
Leave .env untracked. Do not git add .env.

title: Hands-On: Build a Tiny Project
text:
Done when
git status
git log --oneline

Status: clean, on main
Log: three commits (README, ping, document endpoint)
.env exists on disk and is untracked

You now have the loop this book’s later Git chapters assume: init, add, commit, status, log, diff, restore, amend.
Part II starts with commit anatomy and Conventional Commits. Remotes and forges wait until you can do this drill without looking at the page.

title: Theory
text:
Theory: History is a Query over the DAG
git log is not a file. It is a walk of commit objects from one or more tips, filtered by paths, dates, pickaxe, and ranges. Blame is a walk of lines through that DAG.

title: Theory
text:
Invariants

Reachability: git log B shows commits reachable from B by following parents.
Two-dot A..B = reachable from B, not from A (what a feature branch adds).
Three-dot A...B = reachable from A or B, not from the merge base (symmetric difference). A pull-request diff is often git diff A...B (merge-base to B).
git blame attributes each line of a file to the commit that last touched it; -C also hunts copies.
Pickaxe -S/-G filters commits by whether a string’s count or a regex’s hunk changed.

 A ← B ← C ← G     main
      ↑
      D ← E        feat

 main..feat     =  D, E
 main...feat    =  G, D, E     (both sides since split)

title: Theory
section: Why this matters on a forge
text:
Why this matters on a forge
A PR “files changed” list is this query, computed on the server. Reviewers who can run git log main..HEAD and git diff main...HEAD on Linux are not trapped in the UI.

title: Theory
text:
What can break

Reading A..B as “between A and B inclusive on a line” (it is set difference of reachability).
git blame on a file that was reformatted in one giant commit (whitespace; -w).
--follow only works when you name one path.

title: Theory
text:
How to read this chapter
Log flags, ranges, show, blame, pickaxe, shortlog, then a lab that finds a line’s origin in desk-api. The last page keeps blame useful across mass reformats with .git-blame-ignore-revs, and follows moved code with -C.

title: Blame through reformats: .git-blame-ignore-revs
text:
Blame through reformats: .git-blame-ignore-revs
After this page you can run a mass reformat (a new formatter, a re-indent, a quote-style change) without making git blame useless for the code it touched. You can tell git blame to look through that commit, mark the lines where it had to guess, and share that setting with the whole team through one committed file that GitHub and GitLab read too. You will also know the four ways this setup breaks: a global setting that makes blame fatal in every other repository, a squash merge that quietly changes the hash you listed, an abbreviated hash, and code that moved to another file.

title: Blame through reformats: .git-blame-ignore-revs
text:
Thesis
git blame gives each line to the last commit that changed it. A formatter changes nearly every line, so after a reformat, blame names the formatter, and the question you wanted answered (“who wrote this check, and why?”) is one git log hop further away, for every line, forever.
-w (ignore whitespace) only helps when the formatter changed nothing but whitespace. Formatters usually change more: quotes, trailing commas, wrapped calls.
Git 2.23 (2019) added the real fix. git blame --ignore-rev <commit> assigns blame “as if the change never happened”: lines that commit changed go to the commit that touched them before. --ignore-revs-file <file>, and the config key blame.ignoreRevsFile, read a list of such commits from a file. By convention that file is .git-blame-ignore-revs at the repository root, and the forges read it under that name. Newer releases filled in the edges:

2.50 made --porcelain report the ignored and unblamable lines.
2.52 added the :(optional) prefix for path-valued settings, so a global blame.ignoreRevsFile stops being fatal in repositories that don’t have the file.
2.56 (2026-09-28, current) aligns the hash column only when marks are shown.

What it doesn’t do: it never changes history. The reformat commit is still there for git log and git show. Ignoring is a view setting for blame, and without the setting you get the plain view back.

title: Blame through reformats: .git-blame-ignore-revs
text:
Mental model



How .git-blame-ignore-revs changes blame for pricing.py: the history, who owns each line with and without the ignore file, and where it goes wrong


git blame pricing.py
  for each line: walk back to the last commit that changed it
    commit in the ignore list?  → pretend its diff didn't happen; keep walking
                                  (Git matches the line to the parent's lines nearby;
                                   blame.markIgnoredLines marks it "?")
    the commit only *added* the line (nothing to match)? → it stays on the ignored commit
                                  (blame.markUnblamableLines marks it "*")
  ignore list = blame.ignoreRevsFile files (config order), then --ignore-revs-file, then --ignore-rev








Knob
What it does
Since




git blame --ignore-rev <rev>
Ignore one commit. Repeatable. An unknown revision is fatal
2.23


git blame --ignore-revs-file <file>
Ignore the commits listed in a file. Repeatable; "" clears every list read so far, config files included
2.23


blame.ignoreRevsFile
The same file, from config. Repeatable; an empty value resets. A relative path is taken from the top of the work tree
2.23


:(optional)<path> value
The setting is treated as absent if the file doesn’t exist
2.52


blame.markIgnoredLines
Prefix ? on lines blame passed past an ignored commit
2.23


blame.markUnblamableLines
Prefix * on lines an ignored commit added that blame couldn’t hand back. (The 2.23 manual spelled it blame.markUnblamables; the code has always read markUnblamableLines)
2.23


--porcelain / --line-porcelain
An ignored or unblamable line in the entry’s header
2.50



File format (from git-config(1), blame.ignoreRevsFile): one unabbreviated object name per line; whitespace and # comments are ignored. It is the same format as fsck.skipList. The parser (oidset_parse_file_carefully() in oidset.c) fails on anything that isn’t a full hash, and the blame code silently skips any hash that isn’t a commit it can find. Case 5 shows both.

title: Blame through reformats: .git-blame-ignore-revs
text:
Worked examples (Cases)
Run on Debian 13 (Linux 6.12) with Git 2.56.0, the current release (2026-09-28), built from the release tarball in user space. The box’s distribution Git is 2.47.3, and Case 4 uses it on purpose. Every listing below was run, and every output block is pasted from the run. Commit hashes are reproducible because names and dates are fixed.
Source this file first. It points “global” config at a throwaway file and fixes names and dates per commit:
# env.sh — source this so your hashes match the transcripts (needs git 2.52+)
export GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL=/tmp/blamelab/global.gitconfig GIT_CONFIG_NOSYSTEM=1
export GIT_CONFIG_COUNT=1 GIT_CONFIG_KEY_0=init.defaultBranch GIT_CONFIG_VALUE_0=main
# commit as <name> on <date>: as Ana 2026-01-05 commit -m "..."
as() { local who=$1 day=$2; shift 2
  GIT_AUTHOR_NAME=$who GIT_AUTHOR_EMAIL=$(echo "$who" | tr A-Z a-z)@example.com \
  GIT_COMMITTER_NAME=$who GIT_COMMITTER_EMAIL=$(echo "$who" | tr A-Z a-z)@example.com \
  GIT_AUTHOR_DATE="${day}T09:00:00Z" GIT_COMMITTER_DATE="${day}T09:00:00Z" git "$@"; }
Run the cases in order; they share /tmp/blamelab.

Case 1: A reformat takes over blame
Three people write pricing.py, then a formatter re-indents it from two spaces to four, switches to double quotes, and puts two blank lines between functions.
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# lab-01-history.sh — three people write pricing.py, then a formatter rewrites every line
set -e; . ./env.sh
rm -rf /tmp/blamelab && mkdir -p /tmp/blamelab && cd /tmp/blamelab && : > global.gitconfig
git init -q desk && cd desk

cat > pricing.py <<'PY'
def net_price(gross, vat):
  return round(gross / (1 + vat), 2)

def discount(price, pct):
  if pct > 50:
    raise ValueError('discount too large')
  return price * (1 - pct / 100)
PY
git add pricing.py && as Ana 2026-01-05 commit -qm "pricing: net price and discount"

sed -i "s/pct > 50/pct > 30/; s/'discount too large'/'discount over 30% needs approval'/" pricing.py
git add pricing.py && as Ben 2026-02-10 commit -qm "pricing: cap discounts at 30%"

cat >> pricing.py <<'PY'

def bulk(prices, pct):
  total = sum(discount(p, pct) for p in prices)
  return round(total, 2)
PY
git add pricing.py && as Cara 2026-03-03 commit -qm "pricing: bulk discount total"

# the formatter: 4-space indent, double quotes, two blank lines between functions
python3 - <<'PY'
import re
src = open("pricing.py").read().splitlines()
out = []
for line in src:
    if line.startswith("def ") and out:
        while out and out[-1] == "": out.pop()
        out += ["", ""]
    m = re.match(r"( *)(.*)", line)
    line = " " * (len(m.group(1)) * 2) + m.group(2)
    out.append(line.replace("'", '"'))
open("pricing.py", "w").write("\n".join(out) + "\n")
PY
git add pricing.py && as Fmt 2026-04-01 commit -qm "style: reformat (4-space indent, double quotes)"

git log --format='%h %an %ad %s' --date=short
echo "--- git blame pricing.py"
git blame --date=short pricing.py
echo "--- git blame -w pricing.py"
git blame -w --date=short pricing.py
f2170a2 Fmt 2026-04-01 style: reformat (4-space indent, double quotes)
fcd481d Cara 2026-03-03 pricing: bulk discount total
e226a2a Ben 2026-02-10 pricing: cap discounts at 30%
97c900f Ana 2026-01-05 pricing: net price and discount
--- git blame pricing.py
^97c900f (Ana  2026-01-05  1) def net_price(gross, vat):
f2170a20 (Fmt  2026-04-01  2)     return round(gross / (1 + vat), 2)
f2170a20 (Fmt  2026-04-01  3) 
^97c900f (Ana  2026-01-05  4) 
^97c900f (Ana  2026-01-05  5) def discount(price, pct):
f2170a20 (Fmt  2026-04-01  6)     if pct > 30:
f2170a20 (Fmt  2026-04-01  7)         raise ValueError("discount over 30% needs approval")
f2170a20 (Fmt  2026-04-01  8)     return price * (1 - pct / 100)
f2170a20 (Fmt  2026-04-01  9) 
fcd481d1 (Cara 2026-03-03 10) 
fcd481d1 (Cara 2026-03-03 11) def bulk(prices, pct):
f2170a20 (Fmt  2026-04-01 12)     total = sum(discount(p, pct) for p in prices)
f2170a20 (Fmt  2026-04-01 13)     return round(total, 2)
--- git blame -w pricing.py
^97c900f (Ana  2026-01-05  1) def net_price(gross, vat):
^97c900f (Ana  2026-01-05  2)     return round(gross / (1 + vat), 2)
^97c900f (Ana  2026-01-05  3) 
f2170a20 (Fmt  2026-04-01  4) 
^97c900f (Ana  2026-01-05  5) def discount(price, pct):
e226a2a6 (Ben  2026-02-10  6)     if pct > 30:
f2170a20 (Fmt  2026-04-01  7)         raise ValueError("discount over 30% needs approval")
^97c900f (Ana  2026-01-05  8)     return price * (1 - pct / 100)
fcd481d1 (Cara 2026-03-03  9) 
f2170a20 (Fmt  2026-04-01 10) 
fcd481d1 (Cara 2026-03-03 11) def bulk(prices, pct):
fcd481d1 (Cara 2026-03-03 12)     total = sum(discount(p, pct) for p in prices)
fcd481d1 (Cara 2026-03-03 13)     return round(total, 2)
Plain blame gives 8 of 13 lines to Fmt. -w gets the indentation-only lines back (Ben’s if pct > 30:, Cara’s bulk() body). It can’t help line 7: the quotes changed, so to -w it’s a real change, and Ben’s error message still belongs to the formatter. Most real formatters change more than whitespace.


Case 2: --ignore-rev, and the marks that show the guesses
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# lab-02-ignore-rev.sh — blame "as if the reformat never happened", and mark what that guessed
set -e; . ./env.sh; cd /tmp/blamelab/desk
fmt=$(git rev-parse HEAD)          # the "style: reformat" commit
echo "--- git blame --ignore-rev $fmt"
git blame --date=short --ignore-rev "$fmt" pricing.py
echo "--- the same, with blame.markIgnoredLines and blame.markUnblamableLines"
git -c blame.markIgnoredLines=true -c blame.markUnblamableLines=true \
    blame --date=short --ignore-rev "$fmt" pricing.py
echo "--- porcelain: one 'ignored' or 'unblamable' line per affected entry"
git -c blame.markIgnoredLines=true -c blame.markUnblamableLines=true \
    blame --line-porcelain --ignore-rev "$fmt" pricing.py |
  awk '/^[0-9a-f]{40} /{n=$3} /^author /{a=$2} /^(ignored|unblamable)$/{m=$1}
       /^\t/{printf "%2d %-5s %s\n", n, a, m; m=""}'
--- git blame --ignore-rev f2170a20db04e64e3d4d950c496f0ded431cba9a
^97c900f (Ana  2026-01-05  1) def net_price(gross, vat):
^97c900f (Ana  2026-01-05  2)     return round(gross / (1 + vat), 2)
f2170a20 (Fmt  2026-04-01  3) 
^97c900f (Ana  2026-01-05  4) 
^97c900f (Ana  2026-01-05  5) def discount(price, pct):
e226a2a6 (Ben  2026-02-10  6)     if pct > 30:
e226a2a6 (Ben  2026-02-10  7)         raise ValueError("discount over 30% needs approval")
^97c900f (Ana  2026-01-05  8)     return price * (1 - pct / 100)
f2170a20 (Fmt  2026-04-01  9) 
fcd481d1 (Cara 2026-03-03 10) 
fcd481d1 (Cara 2026-03-03 11) def bulk(prices, pct):
fcd481d1 (Cara 2026-03-03 12)     total = sum(discount(p, pct) for p in prices)
fcd481d1 (Cara 2026-03-03 13)     return round(total, 2)
--- the same, with blame.markIgnoredLines and blame.markUnblamableLines
^97c900fc (Ana  2026-01-05  1) def net_price(gross, vat):
^?97c900f (Ana  2026-01-05  2)     return round(gross / (1 + vat), 2)
*f2170a20 (Fmt  2026-04-01  3) 
^97c900fc (Ana  2026-01-05  4) 
^97c900fc (Ana  2026-01-05  5) def discount(price, pct):
?e226a2a6 (Ben  2026-02-10  6)     if pct > 30:
?e226a2a6 (Ben  2026-02-10  7)         raise ValueError("discount over 30% needs approval")
^?97c900f (Ana  2026-01-05  8)     return price * (1 - pct / 100)
*f2170a20 (Fmt  2026-04-01  9) 
fcd481d10 (Cara 2026-03-03 10) 
fcd481d10 (Cara 2026-03-03 11) def bulk(prices, pct):
?fcd481d1 (Cara 2026-03-03 12)     total = sum(discount(p, pct) for p in prices)
?fcd481d1 (Cara 2026-03-03 13)     return round(total, 2)
--- porcelain: one 'ignored' or 'unblamable' line per affected entry
 1 Ana   
 2 Ana   ignored
 3 Fmt   unblamable
 4 Ana   
 5 Ana   
 6 Ben   ignored
 7 Ben   ignored
 8 Ana   ignored
 9 Fmt   unblamable
10 Cara  
11 Cara  
12 Cara  ignored
13 Cara  ignored
Every line of real code is back with the person who wrote it. Line 7 is Ben’s again, and line 8 is Ana’s, because Ben never touched it. The marks say how sure blame is:

? means the ignored commit changed this line, and blame matched it to a line in the parent. Here every match is right. In general it’s a heuristic: a line the formatter rewrote beyond recognition can be matched to the wrong neighbour.
* means the ignored commit added this line, and there was nothing to match it to. These are the formatter’s extra blank lines (3 and 9). They stay on Fmt, which is the honest answer.

The default, unmarked output is shorter but hides which lines are guesses. Turn the marks on in any repository that ignores commits. The porcelain format (used by editors and scripts) has carried the same information since 2.50.
Notice the hash column. Here a line can carry two marks (^ for the boundary commit, plus ?), so Git widens the column to 9 characters and extends unmarked hashes to match. Git 2.56 reserves room for marks only when the output actually shows them. Case 3’s -L6,7 listing has no marks and prints plain 7-character hashes, while Git 2.47.3 prints 8 (e226a2a6) for the same two lines.


Case 3: Share it: .git-blame-ignore-revs and blame.ignoreRevsFile
Passing --ignore-rev by hand doesn’t scale. The convention is to commit a file at the root listing the mechanical commits, and have each clone opt in once.
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# lab-03-ignore-file.sh — commit .git-blame-ignore-revs, opt in once with blame.ignoreRevsFile
set -e; . ./env.sh; cd /tmp/blamelab/desk
fmt=$(git log -1 --format=%H --grep='^style: reformat')
cat > .git-blame-ignore-revs <<IGN
# .git-blame-ignore-revs — mechanical commits that blame should look through.
# Full 40-hex hashes only; add one line per commit, with a comment saying what it was.

# style: reformat (4-space indent, double quotes), 2026-04-01
$fmt
IGN
mkdir -p docs && echo "# Pricing rules" > docs/pricing.md
git add .git-blame-ignore-revs docs && as Dev 2026-04-02 commit -qm "blame: ignore the reformat commit"

who() { git blame --line-porcelain "$@" | sed -n 's/^author //p' | sort | uniq -c; }
echo "--- who owns pricing.py, before opting in"
who pricing.py
git config blame.ignoreRevsFile .git-blame-ignore-revs
echo "--- after: git config blame.ignoreRevsFile .git-blame-ignore-revs"
who pricing.py
echo "--- the relative path is read from the top of the work tree, so a subdirectory works too"
(cd docs && git blame --date=short -L6,7 ../pricing.py)
echo "--- one-off: see the formatter again"
git blame --date=short --ignore-revs-file="" -L6,7 pricing.py
--- who owns pricing.py, before opting in
      3 Ana
      2 Cara
      8 Fmt
--- after: git config blame.ignoreRevsFile .git-blame-ignore-revs
      5 Ana
      2 Ben
      4 Cara
      2 Fmt
--- the relative path is read from the top of the work tree, so a subdirectory works too
e226a2a (Ben 2026-02-10 6)     if pct > 30:
e226a2a (Ben 2026-02-10 7)         raise ValueError("discount over 30% needs approval")
--- one-off: see the formatter again
f2170a2 (Fmt 2026-04-01 6)     if pct > 30:
f2170a2 (Fmt 2026-04-01 7)         raise ValueError("discount over 30% needs approval")
Three details that matter in practice:

The file is added in a later commit. A commit can’t contain its own hash, so the reformat lands first and its hash is added afterwards. Nothing breaks in between; blame just isn’t fixed yet.
The relative path works from anywhere in the work tree. git blame runs from the top of the work tree, so .git-blame-ignore-revs is found from docs/ too.
--ignore-revs-file="" clears the list for one run. That’s how to answer “what did the formatter actually change?”, which git show <fmt> answers better anyway.

The opt-in is per clone: blame.ignoreRevsFile lives in .git/config, which isn’t cloned. GitHub’s blame view reads .git-blame-ignore-revs at the root of the repository automatically and shows an “Ignoring revisions in .git-blame-ignore-revs” banner. GitLab reads the same file since 17.11, behind the Ignore specific revisions blame preference. Local Git reads it only when told to.


Case 4: Put it in global config, and blame breaks everywhere else
The obvious shortcut is to set it once in ~/.gitconfig for every repository. Done plainly, that makes blame fatal in every repository that doesn’t have the file.
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# lab-04-global-trap.sh — a global blame.ignoreRevsFile breaks blame in repos without the file
. ./env.sh; cd /tmp/blamelab
git -C desk config --unset blame.ignoreRevsFile
git init -q other && echo hello > other/README && git -C other add README &&
  as Eve 2026-05-01 -C other commit -qm "readme"

git config --global blame.ignoreRevsFile .git-blame-ignore-revs
echo "--- global setting, repo without the file"
git -C other blame README; echo "exit=$?"

git config --global blame.ignoreRevsFile ':(optional).git-blame-ignore-revs'
echo "--- global ':(optional)' setting (Git 2.52+)"
git -C other blame README; echo "exit=$?"
git -C desk blame --date=short -L6,6 pricing.py; echo "exit=$?"

echo "--- the same global file read by an older Git"
/usr/bin/git --version
/usr/bin/git -C desk blame --date=short -L6,6 pricing.py; echo "exit=$?"
--- global setting, repo without the file
fatal: could not open object name list: .git-blame-ignore-revs
exit=128
--- global ':(optional)' setting (Git 2.52+)
^a81f622 (Eve 2026-05-01 09:00:00 +0000 1) hello
exit=0
e226a2a (Ben 2026-02-10 6)     if pct > 30:
exit=0
--- the same global file read by an older Git
git version 2.47.3
fatal: could not open object name list: :(optional).git-blame-ignore-revs
exit=128
blame.ignoreRevsFile names a file that must exist: oidset_parse_file_carefully() dies if it can’t open it. Git 2.52 added the generic :(optional) prefix for path-valued settings (“treated as if it does not exist, if the named path does not exist”, git-config(1)). With it, one global line works in every repository: the repositories that ship the file get it, and the rest are untouched.
The catch is older Git. 2.47.3 doesn’t know the prefix, reads :(optional).git-blame-ignore-revs as a literal file name, and dies in every repository, including the ones that have the file. If your team has Git older than 2.52 anywhere, including CI images and editor plugins that ship their own Git, keep the setting per repository (git config blame.ignoreRevsFile .git-blame-ignore-revs in each clone), or in a conditional include that only matches repositories you know have the file.


Case 5: The squash merge that ignored nothing
The commonest silent failure. A contributor wraps long lines on a branch, adds the branch commit’s hash to the ignore file in the same pull request, and a maintainer squash-merges it.
#!/bin/sh
# check-ignore-revs — every hash in .git-blame-ignore-revs must be a commit in HEAD's history
f=${1:-.git-blame-ignore-revs}; bad=0
for rev in $(sed 's/#.*//' "$f"); do
  if ! git cat-file -e "$rev^{commit}" 2>/dev/null; then
    echo "missing:     $rev"; bad=1
  elif ! git merge-base --is-ancestor "$rev" HEAD; then
    echo "not on HEAD: $rev $(git log -1 --format=%s "$rev")"; bad=1
  fi
done
exit $bad
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# lab-05-squash-trap.sh — a squash merge rewrites the hash you listed; blame says nothing
. ./env.sh; CHECK=$PWD/check-ignore-revs; cd /tmp/blamelab/desk
git config blame.ignoreRevsFile .git-blame-ignore-revs

git switch -qc wrap-lines
python3 - <<'PY'
p = "pricing.py"; s = open(p).read()
s = s.replace('        raise ValueError("discount over 30% needs approval")\n',
              '        raise ValueError(\n            "discount over 30% needs approval"\n        )\n')
open(p, "w").write(s)
PY
git add pricing.py && as Fmt 2026-05-04 commit -qm "style: wrap long lines"
printf '\n# style: wrap long lines, 2026-05-04\n%s\n' "$(git rev-parse HEAD)" >> .git-blame-ignore-revs
git add .git-blame-ignore-revs && as Fmt 2026-05-04 commit -qm "blame: ignore the wrap commit"

git switch -q main && git merge -q --squash wrap-lines &&
  as Maya 2026-05-05 commit -qm "style: wrap long lines (#42)"
git log --oneline --graph --all | head -5
echo "--- blame on main: the squash commit owns the wrapped lines, and nothing warns"
git blame --date=short -L6,9 pricing.py; echo "exit=$?"
echo "--- check-ignore-revs"
$CHECK; echo "exit=$?"
echo "--- after the branch is deleted and gc runs, the object is gone too"
git branch -qD wrap-lines && git reflog expire --expire=now --all && git gc -q --prune=now
$CHECK; echo "exit=$?"
git blame --date=short -L6,9 pricing.py; echo "blame exit=$?"
echo "--- fix: list the commit that is on main, in a follow-up commit"
sq=$(git log -1 --format=%H --grep='(#42)')
sed -i '$d' .git-blame-ignore-revs && echo "$sq" >> .git-blame-ignore-revs
git add .git-blame-ignore-revs && as Maya 2026-05-05 commit -qm "blame: ignore #42 (squash commit)"
$CHECK; echo "exit=$?"
git blame --date=short -L6,9 pricing.py
echo "--- and an abbreviated hash is not 'ignored', it is fatal"
echo "${sq:0:12}" >> .git-blame-ignore-revs
git blame -L6,6 pricing.py; echo "exit=$?"
git checkout -q .git-blame-ignore-revs
Squash commit -- not updating HEAD

| * a778d40 blame: ignore the wrap commit

exit=1

missing:     da6a82d797fdb060cbf9ba1f6d1b9a11a1245d8a
exit=1

exit=0
e226a2a (Ben 2026-02-10 6)     if pct > 30:
e226a2a (Ben 2026-02-10 7)         raise ValueError(
e226a2a (Ben 2026-02-10 8)             "discount over 30% needs approval"
e226a2a (Ben 2026-02-10 9)         )
--- and an abbreviated hash is not 'ignored', it is fatal
fatal: invalid object name: 79b0ee856adc
exit=128
The listed hash da6a82d is a real commit, but not one in main’s history. The squash created 79b0ee8 instead, so blame on main had nothing to ignore. It said nothing about it: blame skips listed hashes it can’t resolve to a commit, and a commit that isn’t in the file’s history is never reached. After the branch was deleted and garbage-collected, the hash didn’t exist at all, and blame still said nothing. Only the check script noticed.
The same happens with rebase-and-merge (the forge re-creates the commits) and with any later history rewrite (filter-repo, a rebase of main). A merge commit is the only merge style that keeps the hash. The fix works with any merge style: list the hash that is on the default branch, in a follow-up commit, and run a check like check-ignore-revs in CI so an entry that doesn’t exist or isn’t on the default branch fails the build.
The opposite mistake is loud: a short hash is not “close enough”, it’s fatal: invalid object name. The file wants full names: 40 hex digits, or 64 in a SHA-256 repository.


Case 6: Code that moved to another file
Ignoring a commit doesn’t help when the code moved. Splitting a module creates new lines in the new file, and plain blame credits the person who moved them. That’s a different problem, with a different flag.
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# lab-06-moved-code.sh — moved and copied code: -C follows it into the new file
. ./env.sh; cd /tmp/blamelab/desk
python3 - <<'PY'
s = open("pricing.py").read()
head, sep, bulk = s.partition("\n\ndef bulk(")
open("pricing.py", "w").write(head.rstrip("\n") + "\n")
open("bulk.py", "w").write("from pricing import discount\n\n\ndef bulk(" + bulk)
PY
git add pricing.py bulk.py && as Dev 2026-06-01 commit -qm "split bulk pricing into bulk.py"
sed -n '/^def net_price/,/^$/p' pricing.py | sed '/^$/d' > tax.py
git add tax.py && as Dev 2026-06-02 commit -qm "tax: start from a copy of net_price"

echo "--- bulk.py: plain blame, then -C (moved from a file changed in the same commit)"
git blame --date=short bulk.py | tail -3
echo "-- -C"
git blame --date=short -C bulk.py | tail -3
echo "--- tax.py: copied from a file the commit did not touch, so it needs -C -C"
git blame --date=short -C tax.py
echo "-- -C -C"
git blame --date=short -C -C tax.py
echo "--- the same -C -C without the ignore file (the repo's blame.ignoreRevsFile cleared)"
git blame --date=short -C -C --ignore-revs-file="" tax.py
--- bulk.py: plain blame, then -C (moved from a file changed in the same commit)
a7ef20e (Dev 2026-06-01 4) def bulk(prices, pct):
a7ef20e (Dev 2026-06-01 5)     total = sum(discount(p, pct) for p in prices)
a7ef20e (Dev 2026-06-01 6)     return round(total, 2)
-- -C
fcd481d pricing.py (Cara 2026-03-03 4) def bulk(prices, pct):
fcd481d pricing.py (Cara 2026-03-03 5)     total = sum(discount(p, pct) for p in prices)
fcd481d pricing.py (Cara 2026-03-03 6)     return round(total, 2)
--- tax.py: copied from a file the commit did not touch, so it needs -C -C
256a406 (Dev 2026-06-02 1) def net_price(gross, vat):
256a406 (Dev 2026-06-02 2)     return round(gross / (1 + vat), 2)
-- -C -C
^97c900f pricing.py (Ana 2026-01-05 1) def net_price(gross, vat):
^97c900f pricing.py (Ana 2026-01-05 2)     return round(gross / (1 + vat), 2)
--- the same -C -C without the ignore file (the repo's blame.ignoreRevsFile cleared)
^97c900f pricing.py (Ana 2026-01-05 1) def net_price(gross, vat):
f2170a20 pricing.py (Fmt 2026-04-01 2)     return round(gross / (1 + vat), 2)

-C looks for lines moved or copied from other files changed in the same commit. Moving bulk() out of pricing.py changed both files, so one -C finds Cara.
-C -C also looks in other files when the commit creates the file, even if that commit didn’t touch them. tax.py was a copy from an untouched pricing.py, so it needs two. (-C -C -C searches every commit, and gets slow on large histories.)
-M does the same within one file, for blocks that moved up or down.
Both have thresholds: at least 20 alphanumeric characters for -M and 40 for -C before blame believes a block moved. Tiny moves stay with the mover.

The last listing shows the two features combine. -C -C finds Ana’s line in pricing.py, but without the ignore file, line 2 then stops at the reformat that touched it there. With both, it goes all the way back.

title: Blame through reformats: .git-blame-ignore-revs
Blame through reformats: .git-blame-ignore-revs
text:
The boring rule
Make every mechanical change its own commit, with no logic changes. Merge it so its hash survives, or list the hash that actually landed on the default branch, in a follow-up commit with a # comment saying what it was. Turn on blame.markIgnoredLines and blame.markUnblamableLines. Check the file in CI. Set blame.ignoreRevsFile per repository, or globally with :(optional) only once every Git in use is 2.52 or newer. When code moves between files, reach for -C rather than the ignore file.

title: Blame through reformats: .git-blame-ignore-revs
text:
Try this

In Case 2’s repository, re-run git blame --ignore-rev without the marks and pick out the guessed lines from the plain output. (You can’t. That’s the argument for turning the marks on.)
Change the Case 1 formatter so it also renames pct to percent. Which lines does --ignore-rev now hand back, and which ones does ? mark? Is every guess right?
Turn check-ignore-revs into a pre-push hook or a CI step that fails when an entry isn’t an ancestor of the default branch. What should it do for a shallow CI clone, where old commits are missing?
Run Case 6’s tax.py with -C -C -C, and time -C, -C -C and -C -C -C on a large repository you have locally. Where does the cost go?
Put blame.ignoreRevsFile in an [includeIf "gitdir:~/src/work/"] file instead of the global config. Which repositories get it, and what happens in one of them that doesn’t have the file?

git blame for -L ranges and line ownership in general.
Pickaxe and –follow for the other half of the hunt: git log -S finds when a string appeared, even after blame has moved on.
