title: Theory
text:
Theory: The Index is a Filter; LFS is a Pointer
Git will store any blob you add. Ignore rules and attributes are policy on what enters the index and how it is treated. LFS replaces a large blob with a tiny pointer blob and puts the real bytes elsewhere.

title: Theory
text:
Invariants

.gitignore applies to untracked files. A tracked file stays tracked until git rm --cached.
Precedence: command-line exclude → .git/info/exclude → .gitignore in-tree → global excludes file.
gitattributes attach behavior to paths: text vs binary, eol, diff, merge, filter (clean/smudge).
Git LFS stores a pointer file (text, few hundred bytes) in Git, and the payload in an LFS object store the forge must provide.

  git add huge.bin     without LFS     blob of huge.bin in .git/objects
  git add huge.bin     with LFS        blob of pointer  version https://git-lfs...
                                       payload ──► LFS store (not in packfiles)

title: Theory
section: Why Git is a bad backup of videos
text:
Why Git is a bad backup of videos
Every clone downloads every version of every blob (unless partial clone / LFS / sparse). A 200 MB binary edited ten times is ~2 GB of packfile. LFS and “do not commit build output” are the same theory: Git’s object store is for source, not for arbitrary bytes.

title: Theory
text:
What can break

Ignoring .env after it was committed (must rm --cached).
CRLF filters on a Linux-only repo.
Pushing LFS pointers to a forge with no LFS storage; clones get pointers, not files.

title: Theory
text:
Theory: A Commit is Immutable; Messages are for Humans and Machines
Once written, a commit object is byte-for-byte fixed. --amend and rebase do not edit it; they write a new object and slide a name. That is why hashes change and why shared history is a social problem.

title: Theory
text:
Invariants

Commit hash = hash of (tree, parents, author, committer, message). Change any field → new hash.
Author and committer can differ (rebase, cherry-pick).
Conventional Commits are a convention, not a Git feature. Hooks and forges can enforce them.
Unstaging moves a path from index toward HEAD; it does not delete working-tree bytes.

  amend

  A ← B ← C     main     C has message "stuff"
  A ← B ← C'    main     C' new object; C remains in reflog

title: Theory
text:
Why messages matter
git log --grep '^fix' only works if subjects are structured. Changelog generators and feat!: breaking-change scanners parse the same text. The object store does not care; your future self and CI do.

title: Theory
text:
What can break

Amending a commit already on origin/main.
Empty subject or WIP on a branch you intended to merge.
Trailers with the wrong spelling (Co-authored-by is magic for some forges).

title: Theory
text:
How to read this chapter
Anatomy, Conventional Commits, amend, unstage, lab; then templates, split/empty, trailers/mailmap, git show.

title: Commit Anatomy
text:
Commit Anatomy
After this page you can read a commit object and say what each field is for.

title: Commit Anatomy
section: A commit is a snapshot plus metadata
text:
A commit is a snapshot plus metadata
cd ~/desk/desk-api
git cat-file -p HEAD
You will see something like:
tree 4b825dc642cb6eb9a060e54bf8d69288fbee4904
parent 9fceb02d0ae598e95dc970b74767f19372d61af8
author Ada Desk <ada@example.com> 1774000000 +0530
committer Ada Desk <ada@example.com> 1774000000 +0530

Document the ping endpoint in README







Field
Meaning




tree
Hash of the directory snapshot this commit names


parent
Previous commit (omitted on the first commit; two lines on a merge)


author
Who wrote the patch, plus timestamp


committer
Who created this commit object, plus timestamp


blank line, then body
The message



The name of the commit is the hash of this object. Change the message, the tree, or a parent → new hash. That is why amend and rebase rewrite history: they write new objects.

title: Commit Anatomy
text:
Author and committer
They match until you rebase, cherry-pick, or apply someone else’s patch. git log shows the author by default. git log --format=fuller shows both.
git log -1 --format=fuller

title: Commit Anatomy
text:
Short names
git rev-parse HEAD
git rev-parse HEAD~1          # first parent, one step back
git rev-parse HEAD^           # same as HEAD~1 on a non-merge
git rev-parse --short HEAD    # abbreviated, unique in this repo
On a merge commit, HEAD^1 is the first parent (the branch you were on) and HEAD^2 is the branch you merged in. HEAD~n walks first-parent only. Chapter 10 uses that when reverting a merge.

title: Commit Anatomy
text:
The tree under it
git ls-tree -r HEAD
Each line is a mode, type, hash, and path. Blobs have no filename inside them; the tree supplies the name. Two commits that share an unchanged src/ping.py share the same blob hash.

title: Commit Anatomy
text:
What git show adds
git show HEAD
git show --stat HEAD
git show --name-only HEAD
git show pretty-prints the commit and, by default, the diff against its first parent. That diff is computed; Git stored the tree, not the patch.
Next page: how to write the message so later git log and automation can parse it.

title: Conventional Commits
text:
Commit Messages That Matter: Conventional Commits
After this page you can write a subject line other people and tools can parse.

title: Conventional Commits
text:
Shape of a message
type(scope): short summary

Optional body: why, not what. Wrap at 72 characters.

Optional footer:
Fixes: #12
BREAKING CHANGE: /ping now returns JSON
The subject is one line, imperative, about 50 characters, no trailing period. Git itself does not enforce this. Forges, changelog generators, and git log --grep benefit when you do.

title: Conventional Commits
text:
Types this book uses



Type
When




feat
A user-visible capability


fix
A bug


docs
README, comments, this book’s desk docs


chore
Tooling, ignore files, no user-facing change


refactor
Same behavior, different code


test
Tests only


ci
Pipeline files (later parts)



scope is optional: feat(api):, fix(web):. For desk-api a scope of ping or auth is enough.
Examples that match the desk:
feat(ping): return JSON from /ping
fix(ping): treat empty name as 400
docs: document GET /ping in README
chore: ignore .env and __pycache__

title: Conventional Commits
text:
Why bother
git log --oneline --grep '^fix'
git log --oneline --grep '^feat(ping)'
Later, platform governance (chapter 31) can require this shape in a server-side hook. A client-side commit-msg hook (chapter 13) can reject a bad subject before the object exists.

title: Conventional Commits
section: What to put in the body
text:
What to put in the body
The subject is what. The body is why and any context git log should keep:
git commit -m "fix(ping): treat empty name as 400" -m "The handler returned 200 and an empty body, so the desk-web health check looked up. Reject empty names at the edge."
Skip the body when the subject is the whole story.

title: Conventional Commits
Conventional Commits
text:
A local alias
git config --global alias.cm '!f() { git commit -m "$1"; }; f'
Aliases are optional. The skill is the subject line, not the shortcut.

title: Amending a Commit Message
text:
Amending and Fixing an Incorrect Commit Message
After this page you can replace the last commit’s message, and you know when that is safe.

title: Amending a Commit Message
text:
The last commit only
cd ~/desk/desk-api
git log -1 --format='%s'
git commit --amend -m "docs: document GET /ping in README"
git log -1 --format='%h %s'
--amend writes a new commit object with the same tree and parent (unless you also staged files) and slides the branch name to it. The old hash disappears from git log. It is still in git reflog for about 30 days (chapter 17).
 before                         after
 A ← B ← C   main               A ← B ← C'  main
              │                        ╲
              └── message "stuff"       C still in reflog
Keep the old message and only restage files:
git add src/ping.py
git commit --amend --no-edit
Open the editor with the old message loaded:
git commit --amend
core.editor (chapter 2) is what opens. On Linux with nvim, you edit, save, quit, and Git takes the buffer.

title: Amending a Commit Message
text:
When this is safe
Safe when all of these hold:

it is HEAD (the latest commit on this branch)
you have not pushed, or you are the only clone
nobody else based work on the old hash

After a push, amending means a force-push (chapter 11). On main shared with a team, prefer a new commit: git commit -m "docs: fix typo in README".

title: Amending a Commit Message
text:
Older than HEAD
--amend cannot retitle commit HEAD~3 by itself. Interactive rebase can (chapter 9, reword). For now, live with old subjects or wait for rebase.

title: Amending a Commit Message
section: Recover if you amended by mistake
text:
Recover if you amended by mistake
git reflog
git reset --soft HEAD@{1}
--soft moves HEAD back and leaves the index and working tree as they are. Chapter 7 is reset in full. The hash you just left is in the reflog (chapter 17). This one-liner is enough if you just amended and panicked.

title: Amending a Commit Message
text:
Identity in an amended commit
Amend rewrites the committer date by default. The author stays. To keep both timestamps:
git commit --amend --no-edit --date="$(git log -1 --format=%aD)"
Rarely needed. Know that git log after an amend shows “now” as the committer time.

title: Unstaging a File
text:
Unstaging an Added File
After this page you can take a path out of the index and leave the working-tree edit in place.

title: Unstaging a File
section: The index is the next commit
text:
The index is the next commit
You git add too much. The file should stay on disk. It should not be in the next snapshot.
cd ~/desk/desk-api
echo "scratch" >> README.md
echo "debug" >> src/ping.py
git add README.md src/ping.py
git status
git restore --staged src/ping.py
git status
README.md is still staged. src/ping.py is modified, not staged. git commit will only record the README line.
 after git add -A                 after restore --staged ping.py

 working   index   HEAD           working   index   HEAD
 ping.py   ping.py  (old)         ping.py   (old)   (old)
 README    README   (old)         README    README  (old)
                                  ▲ still on disk, not in next commit

title: Unstaging a File
text:
Restore vs reset








Command
Index
Working tree




git restore --staged <file>
Matches HEAD
Unchanged (your edit stays)


git restore <file>
Unchanged
Matches the index (edit discarded)


git restore --source=HEAD --staged --worktree <file>
Matches HEAD
Matches HEAD



This book uses git restore. Older guides use git reset HEAD <file> for unstage; same index effect.

title: Unstaging a File
text:
Unstage everything
git restore --staged .
git status
All paths return to “modified” or “untracked.” Nothing is deleted.

title: Unstaging a File
text:
Untracked files
git add of a new file copies it into the index. git restore --staged on that path leaves it untracked (the index no longer knows it). The file remains on disk. git clean would delete untracked files; that is chapter 12. Leave git clean alone until you can name what it removes.

title: Unstaging a File
text:
Partial unstage
git restore --staged -p src/ping.py
Git offers hunks. n keeps the hunk staged, y unstages it. Same interactive idea as git add -p.

title: Unstaging a File
text:
Check before you commit
git diff --staged
git diff
--staged is the next commit. The other is leftover work. Both should match what you intend. The hands-on page next amends a real desk-api commit so this is muscle memory.

title: Hands-On: Amend and Rewrite
text:
Hands-On: Amend and Rewrite a Commit
Practice on ~/desk/desk-api. If that tree is missing, run chapter 3’s tiny-project page first.

title: Hands-On: Amend and Rewrite
text:
1. A sloppy commit
cd ~/desk/desk-api

echo "Returns a fixed string." >> README.md
git add README.md
git commit -m "stuff"
git log -1 --oneline

title: Hands-On: Amend and Rewrite
text:
2. Fix the subject
git commit --amend -m "docs: note that ping returns a fixed string"
git log -1 --format='%h %s'
The hash changed. The tree is the same if you staged nothing else.

title: Hands-On: Amend and Rewrite
text:
3. Forgot a file
cat > src/version.py <<'EOF'
VERSION = "0.1.0"
EOF
git add src/version.py
git commit --amend --no-edit
git show --name-only --oneline HEAD
version.py is now in the same commit as the docs line.

title: Hands-On: Amend and Rewrite
text:
4. Staged too much, then unstaged
echo "WIP" >> src/ping.py
echo "also" >> README.md
git add -A
git restore --staged src/ping.py
git diff --staged
git commit --amend --no-edit
git restore src/ping.py
git status
The WIP line is gone. README’s “also” is in HEAD if it was staged. Status is clean.

title: Hands-On: Amend and Rewrite
text:
5. Confirm the graph
git log --oneline -5
git status
You should be on main, clean, with a conventional subject on HEAD. Next chapter: branches, so this main history can grow a second line of work.

title: Trailers and mailmap: keeping agent commits honest
text:
Trailers and mailmap: keeping agent commits honest
After this page you can say, for any commit, who wrote the change, who wrote the commit object, and which people and tools helped. You can add that last part with git commit --trailer and git interpret-trailers, read it back with --parse and %(trailers), enforce it with a commit-msg hook plus a CI check, and clean up identity drift with .mailmap. The running example is a coding agent called desk-bot that commits next to a human, Kanthi.

title: Trailers and mailmap: keeping agent commits honest
text:
Thesis
A commit has exactly two identity fields in its header: author and committer. Everything else about who was involved lives in trailers. Trailers are Key: value lines in the last paragraph of the message. Git hashes all of it. Git verifies none of it.
So honesty is a convention you have to set up yourself:

An agent commits under its own identity. It does not borrow the human’s user.name.
The agent records what it is in a trailer (Assisted-by:). The humans who shaped the change go in Co-authored-by:.
Only a human adds Signed-off-by:, because that line is a legal statement (the DCO).
A local hook catches mistakes early. A CI check on the pushed range is the gate, because hooks can be skipped.
.mailmap fixes how identities read (in shortlog and log). It never rewrites history.

title: Trailers and mailmap: keeping agent commits honest
text:
Mental model
  commit object (what cat-file -p prints)

  tree       79cc95d1…
  parent     425512d9…
  author     desk-bot <desk-bot@users.noreply.example.com> 1792211400 +0530   ← wrote the change
  committer  Kanthi N <kanthi@example.com>                1792216800 +0530   ← wrote this object
                                                                              (amend, rebase, cherry-pick, am)
  feat: add request timeout                      ← subject
                                                 ← blank line
  Why the timeout exists …                       ← body
                                                 ← blank line
  Assisted-by: desk-bot 2.3                      ┐ trailer block: the LAST paragraph,
  Co-authored-by: Kanthi N <kanthi@example.com>  ┘ every line `Key: value`



Commit header identities and the trailer block, checked locally by a hook, on the server by a range check, and read through .mailmap










Field
Set from
Changes when




author
--author= if given, else GIT_AUTHOR_NAME/EMAIL env, else author.name/email, else user.name/email
Set when the commit is first made. Amend, rebase and cherry-pick keep it unless you pass --reset-author or --author


committer
GIT_COMMITTER_NAME/EMAIL env, else committer.name/email, else user.name/email
Every time the object is rewritten (amend, rebase, cherry-pick, am)


trailers
The message text: --trailer, -s, an editor, a hook
When someone edits the message



The env vars win over config. git-commit(1) says this under COMMIT INFORMATION: author.name and committer.name “override user.name and user.email if set and are overridden themselves by the environment variables”. Case 2 is that sentence going wrong.
Trailer is Git’s word for the structured footer. GitHub reads Co-authored-by: to credit co-authors. The Linux kernel uses Signed-off-by:, Co-developed-by:, Reviewed-by:, and for AI tools Assisted-by:. Git itself only knows the format.

title: Trailers and mailmap: keeping agent commits honest
text:
Worked examples
Tested on Debian 13 (Linux 6.12), Git 2.47.3. Current upstream is Git 2.56.0 (2026-09-28). The trailer behaviour shown here is the same in 2.56, with two exceptions. Both are called out where they matter (Case 4 and Case 8).
Every lab sets GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL=/dev/null and GIT_CONFIG_NOSYSTEM=1 so your own ~/.gitconfig stays out of it. Every lab also pins GIT_AUTHOR_DATE and GIT_COMMITTER_DATE, so the hashes below come out the same on your machine. Run the labs in order. They share /tmp/trailers-lab.

Case 1: Author is not committer
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# lab-01-identities.sh — author vs committer in a throwaway repo
set -euo pipefail
export GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL=/dev/null GIT_CONFIG_NOSYSTEM=1   # ignore your own config
export GIT_AUTHOR_DATE='2026-10-17T10:00:00+05:30'          # pinned so hashes reproduce
export GIT_COMMITTER_DATE="$GIT_AUTHOR_DATE"

rm -rf /tmp/trailers-lab && git init -q -b main /tmp/trailers-lab && cd /tmp/trailers-lab
git config user.name 'Kanthi N'
git config user.email 'kanthi@example.com'

echo 'GET /ping' > README.md && git add README.md
git commit -q -m 'docs: add README'

# The agent commits under its own identity, not the human's.
echo 'pong' > ping.txt && git add ping.txt
git -c user.name='desk-bot' -c user.email='desk-bot@users.noreply.example.com' \
    commit -q -m 'feat: add ping fixture'

echo '--- log: author | committer'
git log --format='%h %an <%ae> | %cn <%ce> | %s'

# The human reviews and amends. Author stays; committer becomes the human.
export GIT_COMMITTER_DATE='2026-10-17T11:30:00+05:30'
git commit -q --amend --no-edit
echo '--- after the human amends'
git log -1 --format='%h %an <%ae> %ad | %cn <%ce> %cd' --date=iso
echo '--- raw object'
git cat-file -p HEAD
./lab-01-identities.sh
--- log: author | committer
8afc755 desk-bot <desk-bot@users.noreply.example.com> | desk-bot <desk-bot@users.noreply.example.com> | feat: add ping fixture
425512d Kanthi N <kanthi@example.com> | Kanthi N <kanthi@example.com> | docs: add README
--- after the human amends
d594efa desk-bot <desk-bot@users.noreply.example.com> 2026-10-17 10:00:00 +0530 | Kanthi N <kanthi@example.com> 2026-10-17 11:30:00 +0530
--- raw object
tree 79cc95d1f5eef5baab6de124179a266390db4f53
parent 425512d9d82623b1baf66b7539cddaececa4a42c
author desk-bot <desk-bot@users.noreply.example.com> 1792211400 +0530
committer Kanthi N <kanthi@example.com> 1792216800 +0530

feat: add ping fixture
The amend changed one header line, committer, and the hash moved from 8afc755 to d594efa. The author line (and its timestamp) stayed. This split is useful: after review, git log --format='%an | %cn' shows both that the agent wrote the change and that a human wrote the final object.


Case 2: A stray GIT_AUTHOR_* wins over -c user.name
Agents and CI wrappers often export identity env vars. If one of them leaks into a later step, that step commits as the wrong person. Nothing warns you.
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# lab-02-stray-env.sh — a leftover GIT_AUTHOR_* beats -c user.name
set -euo pipefail
export GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL=/dev/null GIT_CONFIG_NOSYSTEM=1
export GIT_AUTHOR_DATE='2026-10-17T12:00:00+05:30' GIT_COMMITTER_DATE='2026-10-17T12:00:00+05:30'
cd /tmp/trailers-lab

# Some earlier tool in this shell session exported an identity and never unset it.
export GIT_AUTHOR_NAME='Old Session' GIT_AUTHOR_EMAIL='someone-else@example.com'

BOT=(-c user.name=desk-bot -c user.email=desk-bot@users.noreply.example.com)
echo '--- what Git will use'
git "${BOT[@]}" var GIT_AUTHOR_IDENT
git "${BOT[@]}" var GIT_COMMITTER_IDENT

echo 'v1' > version.txt && git add version.txt
git "${BOT[@]}" commit -q -m 'chore: add version file'
git log -1 --format='%an <%ae> | %cn <%ce>'

echo '--- same command with the stray variables removed'
git reset -q --soft HEAD~1
env -u GIT_AUTHOR_NAME -u GIT_AUTHOR_EMAIL -u GIT_COMMITTER_NAME -u GIT_COMMITTER_EMAIL \
    git "${BOT[@]}" commit -q -m 'chore: add version file'
git log -1 --format='%an <%ae> | %cn <%ce>'
./lab-02-stray-env.sh
--- what Git will use
Old Session <someone-else@example.com> 1792218600 +0530
desk-bot <desk-bot@users.noreply.example.com> 1792218600 +0530
Old Session <someone-else@example.com> | desk-bot <desk-bot@users.noreply.example.com>
--- same command with the stray variables removed
desk-bot <desk-bot@users.noreply.example.com> | desk-bot <desk-bot@users.noreply.example.com>
git var GIT_AUTHOR_IDENT and git var GIT_COMMITTER_IDENT print the identity the next commit will get. Run them before a bot commits. Better: start the commit with env -u GIT_AUTHOR_NAME -u GIT_AUTHOR_EMAIL -u GIT_COMMITTER_NAME -u GIT_COMMITTER_EMAIL so only the identity you pass on the command line can apply.


Case 3: Writing trailers
git commit --trailer (Git 2.32+) runs the message through git interpret-trailers. You get one consistent block, with no hand-typed blank-line mistakes.
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# lab-03-add-trailers.sh — write trailers with git commit --trailer and interpret-trailers
set -euo pipefail
export GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL=/dev/null GIT_CONFIG_NOSYSTEM=1
export GIT_AUTHOR_DATE='2026-10-17T13:00:00+05:30' GIT_COMMITTER_DATE='2026-10-17T13:00:00+05:30'
cd /tmp/trailers-lab
BOT=(-c user.name=desk-bot -c user.email=desk-bot@users.noreply.example.com)

echo 'timeout=5s' > config.ini && git add config.ini
git "${BOT[@]}" commit -q -m 'feat: add request timeout' \
    --trailer 'Assisted-by: desk-bot 2.3' \
    --trailer 'Co-authored-by: Kanthi N <kanthi@example.com>'
echo '--- message as stored'
git log -1 --format=%B

echo '--- aliases: short names for long keys (repo config)'
git config trailer.coauth.key 'Co-authored-by'
git config trailer.assist.key 'Assisted-by'
printf 'fix: clamp timeout\n\nNegative values fell through to 0.\n' |
  git interpret-trailers --trailer 'assist: desk-bot 2.3' \
                         --trailer 'coauth: Kanthi N <kanthi@example.com>'

echo '--- the same trailer twice: default ifExists=addIfDifferentNeighbor'
printf 'x\n\nCo-authored-by: Kanthi N <kanthi@example.com>\n' |
  git interpret-trailers --trailer 'coauth: Kanthi N <kanthi@example.com>'
echo '--- --if-exists=add forces a duplicate'
printf 'x\n\nCo-authored-by: Kanthi N <kanthi@example.com>\n' |
  git interpret-trailers --if-exists=add --trailer 'coauth: Kanthi N <kanthi@example.com>'

echo '--- tokens are prefix-matched against configured keys (case-insensitive)'
printf 'y\n' | git interpret-trailers --trailer 'co: B <b@example.com>' --trailer 'Co-Author: C <c@example.com>'
echo '--- ...but only configured ones: outside this repo they stay as typed'
(cd /tmp && printf 'y\n' | git interpret-trailers --trailer 'Co-Author: C <c@example.com>')
./lab-03-add-trailers.sh
--- message as stored
feat: add request timeout

Assisted-by: desk-bot 2.3
Co-authored-by: Kanthi N <kanthi@example.com>

--- aliases: short names for long keys (repo config)
fix: clamp timeout

Negative values fell through to 0.

Assisted-by: desk-bot 2.3
Co-authored-by: Kanthi N <kanthi@example.com>
--- the same trailer twice: default ifExists=addIfDifferentNeighbor
x

Co-authored-by: Kanthi N <kanthi@example.com>
--- --if-exists=add forces a duplicate
x

Co-authored-by: Kanthi N <kanthi@example.com>
Co-authored-by: Kanthi N <kanthi@example.com>
--- tokens are prefix-matched against configured keys (case-insensitive)
y

Co-authored-by: B <b@example.com>
Co-authored-by: C <c@example.com>
--- ...but only configured ones: outside this repo they stay as typed
y

Co-Author: C <c@example.com>
There are three things to notice:

trailer.<alias>.key turns coauth: into Co-authored-by:. Once a key is configured, any --trailer token that is a case-insensitive prefix of the alias or the key expands to the full key. Here even co: and Co-Author: became Co-authored-by:. Without that config, tokens are written exactly as typed. Case 5 shows this quietly “fixing” a typo before a hook can see it.
The default trailer.ifExists is addIfDifferentNeighbor. Adding the same Co-authored-by again does nothing. --if-exists=add forces the duplicate.
-s / --signoff adds Signed-off-by: with the committer identity. An agent should not use it (Case 5).



Case 4: What Git actually parses as a trailer
A line that looks like a trailer is only a trailer if Git’s parser agrees. git interpret-trailers --parse is the parser. CI should ask it, not grep.
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# lab-04-parse-trailers.sh — what Git actually parses as a trailer
set -euo pipefail
export GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL=/dev/null GIT_CONFIG_NOSYSTEM=1
cd /tmp/trailers-lab

parse() { printf '%s\n' "--- $1"; printf "$2" | git interpret-trailers --parse; echo "[exit $?]"; }

parse 'clean block'           'feat: x\n\nbody\n\nCo-authored-by: A <a@example.com>\nAssisted-by: desk-bot 2.3\n'
parse 'no blank line before'  'feat: x\nCo-authored-by: A <a@example.com>\n'
parse 'one prose line inside (repo has trailer.coauth.key set)' 'feat: x\n\nCo-authored-by: A <a@example.com>\nthanks for the review!\n'
(cd /tmp && parse 'same text, no trailer config at all' 'feat: x\n\nCo-authored-by: A <a@example.com>\nthanks for the review!\n')
parse 'space in the key'      'feat: x\n\nCo authored by: A <a@example.com>\n'
parse 'a URL as the last line' 'feat: x\n\nsee the issue\n\nhttps://example.com/issues/42\n'

echo '--- read trailers out of history'
git log --format='%h %s%n    co-authors: %(trailers:key=co-authored-by,valueonly,separator=%x2C )%n    assisted:   %(trailers:key=Assisted-by,valueonly)' -3
./lab-04-parse-trailers.sh
--- clean block
Co-authored-by: A <a@example.com>
Assisted-by: desk-bot 2.3
[exit 0]
--- no blank line before
[exit 0]
--- one prose line inside (repo has trailer.coauth.key set)
Co-authored-by: A <a@example.com>
[exit 0]
--- same text, no trailer config at all
[exit 0]
--- space in the key
[exit 0]
--- a URL as the last line
https: //example.com/issues/42
[exit 0]
--- read trailers out of history
b77371a feat: add request timeout
    co-authors: Kanthi N <kanthi@example.com>
    assisted:   desk-bot 2.3

aaa3097 chore: add version file
    co-authors: 
    assisted:   
d594efa feat: add ping fixture
    co-authors: 
    assisted:   
Read each result against the rules in git-interpret-trailers(1):

No blank line: the Co-authored-by line is part of the subject paragraph, not a trailer. Anything that parses trailers, including a forge crediting co-authors, will not see it. GitHub’s instructions call for the empty line for this reason.
One prose line inside the block: the block has to be either all trailers, or contain at least one Git-generated or user-configured trailer and be at least 25% trailers. Inside the lab repo, trailer.coauth.key from Case 3 makes Co-authored-by “user-configured”, so it parses. The same text outside any repo parses to nothing. This is why the parse can differ between your laptop and CI. Keep the block clean.
Space in the key: keys are ASCII letters, digits and - only. Co authored by: is prose.
URL as the last line: Git 2.47 reads https://example.com/issues/42 as the trailer https: //example.com/issues/42. That is a real bug. Git 2.56 fixed it (“avoid mistaking lines that begin with a URL … as trailer lines”), and the current manual adds a rule that a candidate whose value starts with // right after the : is not a trailer. On older Git, keep URLs out of the last paragraph or put them in a Refs: trailer.

%(trailers:key=…,valueonly) in --format matches keys case-insensitively. It is the cheapest way to get co-authors or tools out of history for a report.


Case 5: A commit-msg hook, and why it is not enough
The same policy script serves both the local hook and CI. The script parses trailers with Git and applies these rules:

An agent-authored commit (email matching *-bot@* or *[bot]@*) must carry Assisted-by:.
An agent identity must not add Signed-off-by: for itself. The kernel’s coding-assistants.rst says it directly: “AI agents MUST NOT add Signed-off-by tags. Only humans can legally certify the Developer Certificate of Origin.”
Co-authored-by: must be Name <email>, the form GitHub documents.
Unknown keys are rejected, which catches typos the parser does see.

Save trailer-policy.sh, commit-msg and check-range.sh in the same directory as the labs. lab-05-hook.sh copies them into the repo: the policy goes in tools/, where CI can run it, and the hook goes in .git/hooks/.
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# trailer-policy.sh — shared policy for the commit-msg hook and the CI check
# usage: trailer-policy.sh <author-email> <message-file>
set -uo pipefail
author_email=$1 msg=$2
fail=0
err() { printf 'trailer-policy: %s\n' "$*" >&2; fail=1; }

is_bot=0
case $author_email in *-bot@*|*'[bot]'@*) is_bot=1 ;; esac

assisted=0
while IFS= read -r line; do
  key=${line%%:*} val=${line#*: }
  case ${key,,} in
    assisted-by)    assisted=1 ;;
    co-authored-by) [[ $val =~ ^[^\<\>]+\ \<[^\<\>@\ ]+@[^\<\>\ ]+\>$ ]] \
                      || err "Co-authored-by needs 'Name <email>': $val" ;;
    signed-off-by)  [[ $is_bot == 1 && $val == *"<$author_email>"* ]] \
                      && err "an agent identity cannot sign off (DCO is a human statement): $val" ;;
    reviewed-by|acked-by|fixes|refs|change-id) ;;
    *) err "unknown trailer key '$key' (typo? allowed: Assisted-by Co-authored-by Signed-off-by Reviewed-by Acked-by Fixes Refs Change-Id)" ;;
  esac
done < <(git interpret-trailers --parse "$msg")

[[ $is_bot == 1 && $assisted == 0 ]] && err "agent-authored commit ($author_email) needs an Assisted-by: trailer"
exit $fail
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# .git/hooks/commit-msg — runs the shared policy on the message being committed
email=$(git var GIT_AUTHOR_IDENT | sed -E 's/^.*<([^>]*)>.*$/\1/')
exec "$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)/tools/trailer-policy.sh" "$email" "$1"
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# tools/check-range.sh — CI: run the same policy over every commit in a range
# usage: check-range.sh <base>..<head>
set -uo pipefail
bad=0
for rev in $(git rev-list --reverse "$1"); do
  git log -1 --format=%B "$rev" > /tmp/msg.$$
  if tools/trailer-policy.sh "$(git log -1 --format=%ae "$rev")" /tmp/msg.$$ 2>/tmp/err.$$; then
    echo "ok   $(git log -1 --format='%h %ae %s' "$rev")"
  else
    echo "FAIL $(git log -1 --format='%h %ae %s' "$rev")"; sed 's/^/     /' /tmp/err.$$; bad=1
  fi
done
rm -f /tmp/msg.$$ /tmp/err.$$
exit $bad
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# lab-05-hook.sh — enforce the policy locally, then see why CI must enforce it too
set -uo pipefail
export GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL=/dev/null GIT_CONFIG_NOSYSTEM=1
export GIT_AUTHOR_DATE='2026-10-17T14:00:00+05:30' GIT_COMMITTER_DATE='2026-10-17T14:00:00+05:30'
cd /tmp/trailers-lab
mkdir -p tools && cp "$OLDPWD"/{trailer-policy.sh,check-range.sh} tools/ && cp "$OLDPWD/commit-msg" .git/hooks/
chmod +x tools/*.sh .git/hooks/commit-msg
git add tools && git commit -q -m 'ci: add trailer policy' && echo "policy committed: $(git log -1 --format=%h)"
BOT=(-c user.name=desk-bot -c user.email=desk-bot@users.noreply.example.com)

n=0
try() {
  echo "--- $1"; shift
  n=$((n+1)); echo "$n" > n.txt; git add n.txt
  if "$@"; then echo "[committed $(git log -1 --format=%h)]"; git log -1 --format='%(trailers)' | sed '/^$/d;s/^/    /'
  else echo "[rejected, exit $?]"; git reset -q n.txt; fi
}

try 'agent commit, no Assisted-by'  git "${BOT[@]}" commit -q -m 'feat: bump n'
try 'agent signs off as itself'     git "${BOT[@]}" commit -q -s -m 'feat: bump n' --trailer 'Assisted-by: desk-bot 2.3'
try 'misspelled key'                git "${BOT[@]}" commit -q -m 'feat: bump n' --trailer 'Assisted-by: desk-bot 2.3' --trailer 'Coauthored-by: Kanthi N <kanthi@example.com>'
try 'co-author without an email'    git "${BOT[@]}" commit -q -m 'feat: bump n' --trailer 'Assisted-by: desk-bot 2.3' --trailer 'Co-authored-by: Kanthi'
try 'prefix of a configured key'    git "${BOT[@]}" commit -q -m 'feat: bump n' --trailer 'Assisted-by: desk-bot 2.3' --trailer 'Co-Author: Kanthi N <kanthi@example.com>'
try '--no-verify skips the hook'    git "${BOT[@]}" commit -q --no-verify -m 'feat: bump n'
./lab-05-hook.sh
policy committed: 356ca80
--- agent commit, no Assisted-by
trailer-policy: agent-authored commit (desk-bot@users.noreply.example.com) needs an Assisted-by: trailer
[rejected, exit 1]
--- agent signs off as itself
trailer-policy: an agent identity cannot sign off (DCO is a human statement): desk-bot <desk-bot@users.noreply.example.com>
[rejected, exit 1]
--- misspelled key
trailer-policy: unknown trailer key 'Coauthored-by' (typo? allowed: Assisted-by Co-authored-by Signed-off-by Reviewed-by Acked-by Fixes Refs Change-Id)
[rejected, exit 1]
--- co-author without an email
trailer-policy: Co-authored-by needs 'Name <email>': Kanthi
[rejected, exit 1]
--- prefix of a configured key
[committed 7d279bc]
    Assisted-by: desk-bot 2.3
    Co-authored-by: Kanthi N <kanthi@example.com>
--- --no-verify skips the hook
[committed 1b640af]
There are two lessons here:

“Prefix of a configured key” committed with the correct key. --trailer 'Co-Author: …' is a case-insensitive prefix of the configured key Co-authored-by, so Git expanded it before the hook ran. The hook never saw a typo. That is helpful, but it means a hand-typed message and a --trailer argument can produce different text from the same intent.
--no-verify committed a commit that breaks the policy. githooks(5) says commit-msg “can be bypassed with the --no-verify option”. Hooks are not even cloned. Every clone has to install them. A hook is a convenience for honest users. It is not a control.



Case 6: The gate lives on the server
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# lab-06-ci.sh — the server-side half: check every commit since the policy landed
export GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL=/dev/null GIT_CONFIG_NOSYSTEM=1
cd /tmp/trailers-lab
base=$(git log --format=%h --grep='^ci: add trailer policy' -1)
tools/check-range.sh "$base..HEAD"; echo "[check-range exit $?]"
./lab-06-ci.sh
ok   7d279bc desk-bot@users.noreply.example.com feat: bump n
FAIL 1b640af desk-bot@users.noreply.example.com feat: bump n
     trailer-policy: agent-authored commit (desk-bot@users.noreply.example.com) needs an Assisted-by: trailer
[check-range exit 1]
In a real pipeline the range is the pull request’s base..head. Make the job a required status check on the protected branch. Then --no-verify, a missing hook, or a commit made in a web editor all hit the same rule. The script exits non-zero and names the commit, so the fix is git rebase -i with reword on that commit (or, on Git 2.54+, git rebase --trailer; see Case 8).


Case 7: .mailmap fixes how identities read, not what history says
Identities drift. A container commits as root, and a laptop has a work address. .mailmap at the top of the tree maps each of them to one canonical identity.
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# lab-07-mailmap.sh — one person (or agent), many identities; .mailmap fixes the read side
set -euo pipefail
export GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL=/dev/null GIT_CONFIG_NOSYSTEM=1
export GIT_AUTHOR_DATE='2026-10-17T15:00:00+05:30' GIT_COMMITTER_DATE='2026-10-17T15:00:00+05:30'
cd /tmp/trailers-lab
rm -f .git/hooks/commit-msg            # this lab is about reading, not policy

# Before the bot got a real identity, it committed with whatever the container had.
echo a > old.txt && git add old.txt
git -c user.name=root -c user.email=root@buildbox.local commit -q -m 'chore: old bot run'
echo b > work.txt && git add work.txt
git -c user.name='K. N.' -c user.email=kanthi@work.example.com commit -q -m 'docs: from the work laptop'

echo '--- shortlog, no mailmap'
git shortlog -sne HEAD

cat > .mailmap <<'MAP'
Kanthi N <kanthi@example.com> <kanthi@work.example.com>
desk-bot <desk-bot@users.noreply.example.com> root <root@buildbox.local>
MAP
echo '--- shortlog, with .mailmap'
git shortlog -sne HEAD
echo '--- check-mailmap'
git check-mailmap 'root <root@buildbox.local>' '<kanthi@work.example.com>' 'Someone <x@example.com>'
echo '--- %an (raw) vs %aN (mapped); the objects are unchanged'
git log -2 --format='%h raw=%an <%ae>  mapped=%aN <%aE>'
./lab-07-mailmap.sh
--- shortlog, no mailmap
     5  desk-bot <desk-bot@users.noreply.example.com>
     2  Kanthi N <kanthi@example.com>
     1  K. N. <kanthi@work.example.com>
     1  root <root@buildbox.local>
--- shortlog, with .mailmap
     6  desk-bot <desk-bot@users.noreply.example.com>
     3  Kanthi N <kanthi@example.com>
--- check-mailmap
desk-bot <desk-bot@users.noreply.example.com>
Kanthi N <kanthi@example.com>
Someone <x@example.com>
--- %an (raw) vs %aN (mapped); the objects are unchanged
b0821b0 raw=K. N. <kanthi@work.example.com>  mapped=Kanthi N <kanthi@example.com>
6c42fda raw=root <root@buildbox.local>  mapped=desk-bot <desk-bot@users.noreply.example.com>
The mapping format is Proper Name <proper@email> [Commit Name] <commit@email> (gitmailmap(5)). git shortlog always applies it. git log and git show apply it because log.mailmap is true by default. In --format, use %aN/%aE (mapped) or %an/%ae (raw). The commits 6c42fda and b0821b0 are unchanged: same author bytes, same hashes. Two caveats:

%(trailers) is not mailmapped. A Co-authored-by: with an old address stays old.
The trailer-policy.sh check in Case 6 reads raw %ae. That is deliberate. Policy should judge what was recorded, not what it is displayed as.



Case 8: What is newer than this box’s Git
These were not run here, because Git 2.47.3 does not have them. They come from the upstream release notes and manuals:

Git 2.54: git rebase --trailer=<trailer> appends a trailer to every rebased commit through the interpret-trailers machinery. It implies --force-rebase, so every commit in the range gets a new hash and a new committer line. That is the one-command fix for “the agent forgot Assisted-by: on six commits”. It is still a history rewrite, so do it before the branch is shared.
Git 2.56: the URL-as-trailer fix from Case 4, and an updated git-interpret-trailers(1) that defines keys (alphanumeric and hyphen) and documents how comment lines are handled.

title: Trailers and mailmap: keeping agent commits honest
text:
The trap
The commit looks fine in a forge UI, and you assume the metadata is checked. It isn’t. Git hashes whatever identity your environment produced: a stale GIT_AUTHOR_NAME, the human’s user.email borrowed by an agent, or a Co-authored-by glued to the subject line with no blank line before it. A commit-msg hook only helps on machines where someone installed it and nobody passed --no-verify. Then .mailmap makes shortlog look tidy and hides the drift. The record you meant to be honest is honest only by accident.

title: Trailers and mailmap: keeping agent commits honest
text:
The boring rule

Agents commit as themselves, with stray GIT_* identity variables unset. They say what they are in Assisted-by: and never sign off. Humans who shaped the change go in Co-authored-by: Name <email> as the last paragraph. Parse trailers with git interpret-trailers --parse, never grep. Enforce the rule on the pushed range in a required CI check. Use the hook only as an early warning. Use .mailmap for display, never as a substitute for correct identities.

title: Trailers and mailmap: keeping agent commits honest
text:
Try this

Run git var GIT_AUTHOR_IDENT in the shell your agent uses. Then export GIT_AUTHOR_EMAIL=x@example.com and run it again. Put an env -u … wrapper in front of the agent’s commit command.
Add trailer.assist.key "Assisted-by" to a repo and commit with --trailer 'assist: <tool> <version>'. Read it back with git log --format='%h %(trailers:key=Assisted-by,valueonly)'.
Feed git interpret-trailers --parse a message whose last line is a URL. If your Git is older than 2.56, you will see the bogus https: trailer. Decide where URLs go in your messages.
Wire tools/check-range.sh "$BASE..$HEAD" into your CI and make it a required check. Push a --no-verify commit to a test branch and watch it fail.
Write a .mailmap for your own repo and compare git shortlog -sne before and after.

title: Git Diff Algorithms — myers, patience, histogram
text:
Thesis
git diff is not one algorithm. myers (default) is fast and good enough for most patches. patience and histogram spend more care on unique lines so moved blocks stay together in noisy files. This chapter diffs the same rewrite under all three. (The Argo CD book section on diff algorithms is about rendered app diffs — this chapter is everyday Git.)

title: Git Diff Algorithms — myers, patience, histogram
text:
Mental model
  git -c diff.algorithm=myers|patience|histogram diff



Algorithm
Intent




myers
Classic LCS-style; default


patience
Prefer unique lines as anchors


histogram
patience-like with histogram heuristics

title: Git Diff Algorithms — myers, patience, histogram
text:
Worked examples
Git on this box: 2.47.3.
=== myers ===
diff --git a/f.txt b/f.txt
index e63706e..fc15405 100644
--- a/f.txt
+++ b/f.txt
@@ -1,10 +1,13 @@
 alpha
 bravo
-charlie
-delta
+CHANGED-1
+CHANGED-2
 echo
 foxtrot
 golf
+NEW-BLOCK-A
+NEW-BLOCK-B
+NEW-BLOCK-C
 hotel
 india
 juliet
=== patience ===
diff --git a/f.txt b/f.txt
index e63706e..fc15405 100644
--- a/f.txt
+++ b/f.txt
@@ -1,10 +1,13 @@
 alpha
 bravo
-charlie
-delta
+CHANGED-1
+CHANGED-2
 echo
 foxtrot
 golf
+NEW-BLOCK-A
+NEW-BLOCK-B
+NEW-BLOCK-C
 hotel
 india
 juliet
=== histogram ===
diff --git a/f.txt b/f.txt
index e63706e..fc15405 100644
--- a/f.txt
+++ b/f.txt
@@ -1,10 +1,13 @@
 alpha
 bravo
-charlie
-delta
+CHANGED-1
+CHANGED-2
 echo
 foxtrot
 golf
+NEW-BLOCK-A
+NEW-BLOCK-B
+NEW-BLOCK-C
 hotel
 india
 juliet
git version 2.47.3
On this small rewrite all three produced the same hunks — expected for a tidy change. Divergence shows up on large, copy-heavy files.

Leave myers for day-to-day. Switch to histogram when a review is hard to read because of moved blocks.

title: git range-diff for Rewritten Series
text: git range-diff for Rewritten Series

title: git range-diff for Rewritten Series
text:
Thesis
git range-diff compares two revisions of a patch series — after rebase, amend, or squash — and shows how each commit changed. It answers “what did I alter while rewriting?” better than a single diff of tips.

title: git range-diff for Rewritten Series
text:
Mental model
  old: A—B—C
  new: A'—B'—C'   (rebased)
  range-diff old...new
       → per-commit pairwise diffs of patches
Matching uses patch-id heuristics; order and subject help correspondence.

title: git range-diff for Rewritten Series
text:
Worked example
# create a tiny series, rebase-edit, then range-diff
git range-diff <old-tip>...<new-tip>
# or after a rebase:
git range-diff ORIG_HEAD...HEAD
1:  8a2c39b < -:  ------- add f
2:  62c3d72 = 1:  7c1560d patch1
3:  2aebe57 < -:  ------- patch2
-:  ------- > 2:  1ad4b63 patch2 v2

title: git range-diff for Rewritten Series
text:
Trap
Diffing only old..new trees. That shows net effect, not which commit in the series absorbed the change. Also: heavy squashing into one commit makes range-diff less informative — there is nothing left to pair.

title: git range-diff for Rewritten Series
text:
Boring rule
After interactive rebase of a published-but-not-merged series, run git range-diff ORIG_HEAD...HEAD before force-push and paste the interesting hunks into the PR.

title: git range-diff for Rewritten Series
text:
Try this

Reorder two commits with rebase -i and read the range-diff.
Amend a commit message only — range-diff should show a message-only change.
Compare with git range-diff --creation-factor=100.

title: git notes — Annotations outside the Tree
text: git notes — Annotations outside the Tree

title: git notes — Annotations outside the Tree
text:
Thesis
git notes attach free-form text to an object (usually a commit) without changing its hash. Review commentary, CI URLs, and backport hints can ride along without rewriting history.

title: git notes — Annotations outside the Tree
text:
Mental model
  commit abc123  ←── notes/commits → "Reviewed-by: …"
  (tree unchanged; notes live in refs/notes/*)
Default ref: refs/notes/commits. Fetch/push notes explicitly — they are not part of ordinary branch fetch unless configured.

title: git notes — Annotations outside the Tree
text:
Worked example
# lab identity already set for this demo
git notes add -m "lab note: verified on box" HEAD
git notes show HEAD
git log -1 --notes
git notes remove HEAD   # cleanup when done
=== notes show ===
review: LGTM after nits
=== log --notes ===
8a2c39b add f
Notes:
    review: LGTM after nits
Sharing:
git push origin refs/notes/commits
git fetch origin refs/notes/commits:refs/notes/commits

title: git notes — Annotations outside the Tree
text:
Trap
Expecting notes to clone by default. They will not. Also: amending a commit changes its OID — notes stay on the old OID unless rewritten. Notes are the wrong tool for signed release metadata that must be immutable and always-present; use tags or the commit message for that.

title: git notes — Annotations outside the Tree
text:
Boring rule
Use notes for optional, discardable annotations. Document the notes ref in the repo README if the team relies on them, and add an explicit fetch refspec.

title: git notes — Annotations outside the Tree
text:
Try this

Add a note, git commit --amend, and observe the note no longer shows on HEAD.
Configure fetch = +refs/notes/*:refs/notes/* in a test remote.
Compare notes vs git interpret-trailers in commit messages.

title: Theory
text:
Theory: Reset Moves Names; Restore Copies Bytes; Revert Adds a Commit
Three different operations get called “undo.” They act on different trees and different audiences.

title: Theory
text:
Invariants








Tool
What it moves
History




git restore
Working tree and/or index, from a source
Names unchanged


git reset (no path)
HEAD (and maybe index, working tree)
Branch name slides; old commit may become unreachable


git reset (with path)
Index (mixed) for those paths
HEAD stays


git revert
Nothing; writes a new commit
History goes forward



Soft / mixed / hard is which of the three trees follow HEAD when you reset a commit:
              HEAD     index          worktree
  --soft      moves    stays          stays
  --mixed     moves    matches HEAD   stays          (default)
  --hard      moves    matches HEAD   matches HEAD

title: Theory
text:
Why checkout split
Old git checkout meant both “switch branch” and “restore file.” Git 2.23+ splits them: switch for branches, restore for files. This book uses the split so a command’s name is its theory.

title: Theory
text:
What can break

reset --hard on a shared main.
Confusing mixed reset (unstage all) with hard (throw away tracked work).
Expecting --hard or restore to delete untracked files. They stay. Removing them is git clean.

title: Theory
text:
How to read this chapter
Three modes, the comparison table as practice, path reset, switch/restore/checkout, then a lab that walks one commit through soft, mixed, and hard on Linux.

title: Soft, Mixed, and Hard Reset
text:
Soft, Mixed, and Hard Reset
After this page you can predict git status after --soft, --mixed, and --hard, and you can put the branch name back with ORIG_HEAD.

title: Soft, Mixed, and Hard Reset
text:
One commit, three trees
Start from a clean main on ~/desk/desk-api (chapter 3). This page adds one scratch commit, tries each mode, and removes that commit at the end.
cd ~/desk/desk-api
git switch main
git status
Ignored files such as .env are fine. Commit or restore any other uncommitted work before you continue.
echo "scratch" >> README.md
git add README.md
git commit -m "lab: reset modes"
 A ← B ← S     main
 HEAD, index, and worktree all name S
S is the scratch commit. Each mode below starts from S. Git records the old tip in ORIG_HEAD whenever a reset moves the branch, so git reset --hard ORIG_HEAD returns to S.

title: Soft, Mixed, and Hard Reset
text:
--soft moves the name
git reset --soft HEAD~1
git status
 HEAD → B
 index still S       "Changes to be committed"
 worktree still S
main now names B. The scratch line is staged. git log no longer shows lab: reset modes. The commit object stays in the reflog (chapter 17).
git reset --hard ORIG_HEAD
git log --oneline -1
You are back on the scratch commit. The line is in README.md, and status is clean.

title: Soft, Mixed, and Hard Reset
section: --mixed moves the name and the index
text:
--mixed moves the name and the index
--mixed is the default. git reset HEAD~1 and git reset --mixed HEAD~1 are the same command.
git reset HEAD~1
git status
git diff
Git prints Unstaged changes after reset:.
 HEAD → B
 index matches B      the scratch line is not staged
 worktree still S     "Changes not staged for commit"
The patch is in the working tree. The next commit includes it only after git add.
git reset --hard ORIG_HEAD

title: Soft, Mixed, and Hard Reset
text:
--hard moves all three
git reset --hard HEAD~1
git status
grep scratch README.md || echo "scratch line is gone"
 HEAD, index, and worktree all match B
 tracked files match B
The line is gone from disk. Untracked files are still on disk. --hard rewrites tracked files to the commit you named and leaves untracked and ignored files alone.
git reset --hard ORIG_HEAD
The scratch commit is the branch tip again, and the line is back. ORIG_HEAD is the immediate undo. After other commands have moved HEAD, the reflog is the record (chapter 17). The lab at the end of this chapter recovers with HEAD@{1} on purpose.

title: Soft, Mixed, and Hard Reset
text:
Remove the scratch commit
git reset --hard HEAD~1
git status
git log --oneline -5
lab: reset modes is off the log. README.md has no scratch line. The object remains in the reflog until it expires.

title: Soft, Mixed, and Hard Reset
text:
Where this is safe
Use these modes on a local branch nobody else has fetched. On a main other people already have, moving the name and pushing is a force-push (chapter 11). A published undo is git revert (chapter 10). The next page is how to choose restore, reset, or revert.

title: restore vs reset vs revert
text:
Restore, Reset, and Revert
After this page you can pick the undo that matches what is wrong and who else has the commit.

title: restore vs reset vs revert
text:
Three audiences
 uncommitted                    unpublished                     published
 working tree or index          only this clone has the hash    someone else may have it
 restore                        reset or amend                  revert








Situation
Command
Branch tip




Edited a tracked file, not staged
git restore <file>
stays


Staged too soon
git restore --staged <file>
stays


Last local commit should be redone
git reset --soft HEAD~1, then commit
parent; changes stay staged


Last local commit should be an unstaged edit
git reset HEAD~1
parent; changes stay in the worktree


Last local commit and its files should disappear
git reset --hard HEAD~1
parent; tracked files match the parent


Last local commit needs a new message or one more file
git commit --amend
new hash, same parent (chapter 6)


A shared commit should be undone
git revert <hash>
moves forward (chapter 10)



restore copies bytes. The branch name stays. reset with no path slides the branch name. revert adds a commit.

title: restore vs reset vs revert
text:
Amend and soft reset
Both replace an unpublished tip.
Amend keeps one commit at the tip: same parent, new hash. You are still one commit ahead of the parent. Chapter 6 is amend.
Soft reset takes the tip off the branch and leaves that tree staged. You can drop a file, split the change, or commit it again with an ordinary message. The previous page is that mode.

title: restore vs reset vs revert
text:
Revert goes forward
git revert writes a new commit whose patch is the inverse of an older one. The old hash stays reachable. Use it when the commit is on a shared main, or when you are unsure whether anyone fetched it. Chapter 10 includes un-merging with git revert -m 1.
 published:   A ← B ← C ← R      R undoes C; C is still reachable
 local only:  A ← B              reset moved main off C; C is in the reflog

title: restore vs reset vs revert
text:
A test you can apply
Ask where the hash lives.

In the working tree or the index only: restore.
On this branch, and you have not pushed it (or there is no remote yet): reset or amend.
On a forge, or a teammate has pulled: revert.

Chapter 11 is the force-push that follows a reset of something you already pushed. On shared main, revert.

title: Resetting Paths
text:
Resetting Paths
After this page you can change one path in the index while the branch name stays put.

title: Resetting Paths
section: A path means the branch stays
text:
A path means the branch stays
With no path, git reset moves HEAD. With a path, HEAD stays and Git copies that path from a commit into the index only.
cd ~/desk/desk-api
git switch main
git status
BEFORE=$(git rev-parse --short HEAD)
echo "path lab" >> README.md
git add README.md
git commit -m "lab: path reset"
git reset HEAD~1 -- README.md
git rev-parse --short HEAD
echo "parent was $BEFORE"
git status
git diff -- README.md
git diff --staged -- README.md
The short hash is the commit you just made, lab: path reset. It is not $BEFORE. Status lists README.md in two places:

Changes to be committed. The index holds the parent’s blob.
Changes not staged for commit. The working tree still has the path lab line.

That is one edit, seen from both sides. git diff shows the line added. git diff --staged shows the line removed. Git also prints Unstaged changes after reset:.
 HEAD stays on "lab: path reset"
 index README     ← parent blob
 worktree README  ← still has "path lab"
Older notes unstage with git reset HEAD -- README.md. This book unstages with git restore --staged (chapters 3 and 6). The path form is how you aim the index at an older blob, and how you read a script that still uses it.

title: Resetting Paths
section: Put the file back, then drop the commit
text:
Put the file back, then drop the commit
HEAD is still the scratch commit. Copy that commit’s README.md into the index and the working tree:
git restore --source=HEAD --staged --worktree -- README.md
git status
Status is clean. The log still shows lab: path reset.
git reset --hard HEAD~1
git log --oneline -3
The scratch commit is off main, and README.md has no path lab line. The path reset did not do that. The last command is a branch reset from the first page of this chapter.

title: Resetting Paths
text:
Whole tree versus one path
 git reset HEAD~1
     main slides to the parent

 git reset HEAD~1 -- README.md
     main stays; the index path changes

 git restore --source=HEAD~1 --staged --worktree -- README.md
     main stays; index and worktree take the old blob
The third command is how you make a file look like an older commit and then record that with a new commit. The older commit stays in history. switch and restore on the next page are the same split: names versus bytes.

title: switch, restore, and checkout
text:
switch, restore, and checkout
After this page you can change branches with git switch and files with git restore, and you can translate an old git checkout line.

title: switch, restore, and checkout
text:
Two commands, two jobs
Until Git 2.23, git checkout did both jobs. It still does, including in Git 2.55. Checking out a branch moves HEAD. Checking out a path copies bytes. One word for both is how a file gets overwritten when the goal was to change branches.
git switch moves HEAD and refuses a path. git restore copies bytes and leaves HEAD where it is.







Older command
Command in this book




git checkout main
git switch main


git checkout -b feat/x
git switch -c feat/x


git checkout -- README.md
git restore README.md


git checkout HEAD -- README.md
git restore --source=HEAD --staged --worktree -- README.md


git checkout <hash>
git switch --detach <hash>



Scripts and old notes still say checkout. Translate them with the table. Type switch and restore yourself.

title: switch, restore, and checkout
text:
Switch branches
cd ~/desk/desk-api
git switch main
git switch -c feat/switch-lab
git switch main
git switch -
git branch --show-current
git switch - uses @{-1}, the checkout you were on before this one. The last command prints feat/switch-lab.
git switch main
git branch -d feat/switch-lab
-d deletes a branch whose tip is already reachable from HEAD. You are on main, and feat/switch-lab names that same commit, so the delete succeeds.

title: switch, restore, and checkout
section: A path is not a branch
text:
A path is not a branch
git switch README.md
Git stops with fatal: invalid reference: README.md. The file is unchanged.

title: switch, restore, and checkout
section: Local edits that would be overwritten
text:
Local edits that would be overwritten
git switch -c feat/switch-lab
echo "other side" >> README.md
git add README.md
git commit -m "lab: other side"
git switch main
echo "main side" >> README.md
git switch feat/switch-lab
Git aborts. The message still says the files would be overwritten by checkout. README.md on main still ends with main side. feat/switch-lab still has other side.
git restore README.md
git branch -D feat/switch-lab
git status
-D deletes a branch even when main does not contain its commits. Use it here to discard the throwaway lab: other side commit. When you need to keep the uncommitted line and still change branches, stash it (chapter 12).

title: switch, restore, and checkout
text:
Detached HEAD
git switch --detach HEAD
git switch main
--detach points HEAD at a commit and at no branch. Chapter 1 is the trap: a commit made there needs a new branch before you leave it. From a detached HEAD with no new commit, git switch main attaches you again.
The lab next walks one scratch commit through soft, mixed, and hard, then brings it back from the reflog.

title: Hands-On: Reset Lab
text:
Hands-On: Reset Lab
Walk one commit through soft, mixed, and hard on desk-api. Lose the line on purpose, and take it back from the reflog.

title: Hands-On: Reset Lab
text:
Setup
cd ~/desk/desk-api
git switch main
git status
START=$(git rev-parse HEAD)
echo "$START"
Status is clean, aside from ignored files such as .env. If git switch main refuses, restore or commit the work left from the previous page.
echo "lab line" >> README.md
git add README.md
git commit -m "lab: scratch line"

title: Hands-On: Reset Lab
text:
Soft
git reset --soft HEAD~1
git status
git diff --staged -- README.md
The line is under “Changes to be committed”. git log --oneline does not show lab: scratch line.
git commit -m "lab: scratch line"
Same tree, new hash. The next mode starts from a commit again.

title: Hands-On: Reset Lab
text:
Mixed
git reset HEAD~1
git status
git diff -- README.md
Git prints Unstaged changes after reset:. The line is in the file and not in the index.
git add README.md
git commit -m "lab: scratch line"

title: Hands-On: Reset Lab
text:
Hard, and an untracked file
echo "not tracked" > notes.tmp
git reset --hard HEAD~1
git status
grep "lab line" README.md || echo "line gone"
ls notes.tmp
Tracked files match the commit in $START. notes.tmp is still in the directory. --hard left it there.

title: Hands-On: Reset Lab
text:
Recover with the reflog
git reflog -5
The first line is this reset (HEAD@{0}). The next line (HEAD@{1}) is commit: lab: scratch line. HEAD@{1} means “where HEAD was one move ago.” That is a different question from HEAD~1, the parent of the current commit. Chapter 17 is that difference in full.
git reset --hard HEAD@{1}
grep "lab line" README.md
git log --oneline -1
The line is back. main names the scratch commit again.

title: Hands-On: Reset Lab
section: Leave the repo as you found it
text:
Leave the repo as you found it
git reset --hard "$START"
rm -f notes.tmp
git status
git log --oneline -5
$START is the tip from the start of the lab, so this last reset also drops lab: scratch line.

title: Hands-On: Reset Lab
text:
Done when

git status is clean (an ignored .env is fine)
notes.tmp is gone
the log has no lab: scratch line
README.md has no lab line
you saw that line staged, then unstaged, then missing, then restored from HEAD@{1}

Chapter 8 creates branches from this same desk-api. A reset of shared main waits; merging and rebasing come first.

title: Theory
text:
Theory: A Branch is a Name; a Merge is a Node with Two Parents
Creating a branch does not copy files. It writes a ref. Merging either slides that ref (fast-forward) or writes a commit with two parents (a join).

title: Theory
text:
Invariants

git switch -c feat = write refs/heads/feat at current HEAD, point HEAD at it.
Fast-forward is legal iff the current tip is an ancestor of the other tip.
A three-way merge diffs base→ours and base→theirs and applies both to the base. The merge base is the unique best common ancestor (usually).
Conflict markers are unmerged index stages (1 base, 2 ours, 3 theirs) spilled into the working tree.
During a merge, --ours is HEAD. During a rebase, --ours is the upstream. That swap is the theory, not a bug.

 fast-forward          three-way merge

 A ← B ← C   main      A ← B ← C ← M   main
           ← D ← E           ↑     ↑
                             D ← E

title: Theory
text:
Why merge commits exist
They record that two lines of work met, and they keep both sides’ hashes stable. Rebase prefers a straight first-parent chain and pays with new hashes. Neither changes the fact that Git stores snapshots.

title: Theory
text:
What can break

Merging with uncommitted work that overlaps the incoming tree.
Resolving markers but forgetting git add (merge stays open).
git merge --abort after the merge commit exists (too late).

title: Theory
text:
How to read this chapter
Create/switch, merge types, three-way, conflicts, fast-forward, lab; then mergetool, ours/theirs, orphan, comparing branches, rerere.

title: Creating and Switching Branches
text:
Branch to Create a Safe Working Area
After this page you can create, switch, list, and delete branches on Linux without touching main.

title: Creating and Switching Branches
text:
A branch is a name
cd ~/desk/desk-api
git branch
git switch -c feat/ping-json
git branch
git switch -c creates feat/ping-json at current HEAD and points HEAD at it. git branch (no args) lists local names; * is where HEAD is.
git switch main
git switch feat/ping-json
git switch is the modern command. git checkout still works; this book uses switch for branches.

title: Creating and Switching Branches
section: Name them so later pages stay readable
text:
Name them so later pages stay readable
feat/…     a capability
fix/…      a bug
chore/…    tooling
Slashes are fine on Linux. The name is a file under .git/refs/heads/ (or a line in packed-refs). feat/ping-json is the path refs/heads/feat/ping-json.

title: Creating and Switching Branches
text:
Work on the branch
git switch feat/ping-json
# edit, add, commit as in chapter 3
git log --oneline --graph --all --decorate
main stays where you left it. Commits on feat/ping-json are extra nodes in the DAG.
 A ← B ← C                 main
           ↖
             D ← E         feat/ping-json   HEAD

title: Creating and Switching Branches
text:
List and see
git branch -v                 # last commit on each
git branch --show-current
git log --oneline main..HEAD  # commits on this branch that main does not have
A..B means reachable from B, not from A.

title: Creating and Switching Branches
text:
Delete
git switch main
git branch -d feat/ping-json     # refuses if not merged
git branch -D feat/ping-json     # delete anyway
-d is the default you want. -D is when you meant to throw the line of work away.

title: Creating and Switching Branches
text:
Rename
git branch -m feat/ping-json feat/ping
Renames the current branch if you omit the old name. After you publish a branch, renaming locally does not rename it on the remote; chapter 11.

title: Creating and Switching Branches
section: Stuck with a dirty working tree
text:
Stuck with a dirty working tree
Git refuses to switch if the switch would overwrite uncommitted edits. Commit, stash (chapter 12), or restore first.
git status
git switch main

title: Merge Types
text:
Merge Types: Fast-Forward, Recursive, and Octopus
After this page you can name the three merge shapes Git actually writes.

title: Merge Types
text:
Fast-forward
main is an ancestor of feat/ping-json. Merging can just slide main forward. No new commit.
A ← B ← C                 main
          ← D ← E         feat/ping-json

# after git switch main && git merge feat/ping-json

A ← B ← C ← D ← E         main, feat/ping-json
git switch main
git merge feat/ping-json
git log shows a straight line. git merge --no-ff forces a merge commit even when a fast-forward is possible (Git Flow likes that; trunk-based usually does not).

title: Merge Types
text:
Recursive (two parents)
The branches diverged. Git writes a merge commit with two parents.
A ← B ← C ← M             main
     ↑      ↑
     D ← E                feat/ping-json
The default strategy for two heads is ort (the current “recursive” replacement). You rarely pass -s. Git finds a merge base (common ancestor), diffs both sides against it, and applies both diffs to the base.
git switch main
git merge feat/ping-json -m "merge feat/ping-json"
git log --oneline --graph --decorate

title: Merge Types
text:
Octopus (three or more parents)
git merge topic-a topic-b topic-c
One merge commit with several parents. Git only does this when there are no overlapping conflicts. If two topics touch the same hunk, octopus refuses; merge them pairwise instead. You will almost never need octopus on desk-api. Know the name so git log --graph with a commit that has three parents is not a mystery.
 A ← B ← C ← M          main     M has three parents
      ↑  ↑   ↑
      D  E   F          three topic tips

title: Merge Types
text:
See the parents
git cat-file -p HEAD
git rev-parse HEAD^1 HEAD^2
HEAD^1 is the first parent (the branch you had checked out). HEAD^2 is what you merged in.

title: Merge Types
text:
Abort
git merge --abort
Returns the three trees to the pre-merge state while a merge is in progress (MERGE_HEAD exists). After the merge commit exists, abort is too late; git reset (chapter 7) or git revert -m 1 (chapter 10).

title: Three-Way Merge
text:
Three-Way Merge Explained
After this page you can draw the three inputs Git uses when two branches diverged.

title: Three-Way Merge
text:
The three trees
Call them:



Name
What




Base
Merge base: latest common ancestor of both tips


Ours
The branch you have checked out (HEAD)


Theirs
The branch you named in git merge



Git diffs base→ours and base→theirs, then applies both diffs to the base. That is a three-way merge. A two-way merge (ours vs theirs only) cannot tell “we both added the same line” from “they added a line we never had.”
          C  base     (merge-base main feat)
         / \
        /   \
      G     E         ours = main, theirs = feat
        \   /
         \ /
          M  result   two-parent merge commit

title: Three-Way Merge
text:
See the base
cd ~/desk/desk-api
git merge-base main feat/ping-json
git log --oneline --graph main feat/ping-json
merge-base prints one hash. git log --graph should make that node obvious.

title: Three-Way Merge
section: Stages in the index during a conflict
text:
Stages in the index during a conflict
When both sides changed the same hunk, Git records three stages for that path in the index:



Stage
Content




1
base


2
ours


3
theirs



git ls-files -u
git checkout --ours path / --theirs path copies stage 2 or 3 into the working tree. You still git add after you edit. The next page is the full conflict loop.

title: Three-Way Merge
section: Why this matters for a forge
text:
Why this matters for a forge
A pull request / merge request is this same three-way merge, run on the server when you click Merge. The conflict you see in the UI is stages 2 and 3 plus markers. Learning it locally means the UI is not a new theory.

title: Three-Way Merge
text:
zdiff3 markers
With merge.conflictstyle zdiff3 (chapter 2) a conflicted file shows the common ancestor as well as ours and theirs. That extra block is the base. Read it before you delete markers.

title: Merge Conflicts
text:
Merge Conflicts: In Git and in Teams
After this page you can finish a conflicted merge on Linux and leave a clean main.

title: Merge Conflicts
text:
What a conflict is
Both branches changed the same region of a file (or one side changed a file the other deleted). Git writes conflict markers into the working tree and leaves the merge unfinished.
<<<<<<< HEAD
return "ok"
=======
return {"status": "ok"}
>>>>>>> feat/ping-json
With zdiff3 you also get an ancestor block (|||||||).

title: Merge Conflicts
text:
The loop
git switch main
git merge feat/ping-json
# Git stops and prints "fix conflicts and then commit"

git status
# both modified: src/ping.py
Edit the file in nvim. Remove every <<<<<<<, =======, >>>>>>> (and ||||||| if present). Leave the code you want.
git add src/ping.py
git status          # "all conflicts fixed"
git commit          # default message is "Merge branch 'feat/ping-json'"
Git opens core.editor for the merge message if you omit -m. A conventional subject is optional here; merge commits are often left as Git’s default so git log --first-parent stays readable.

title: Merge Conflicts
text:
Abort vs continue
git merge --abort     # give up; back to pre-merge
After git add, there is no --continue for merge; git commit finishes it. Rebase does use --continue (chapter 9).

title: Merge Conflicts
text:
Binary files and deletes
git status will say deleted by them or added by us. Pick a side:
git restore --ours --worktree --staged path
git restore --theirs --worktree --staged path
git rm path
Then git add / git commit as usual.

title: Merge Conflicts
text:
Teams
A conflict is a data problem (two diffs) plus a people problem (whose behavior should win). On a forge, the same markers appear in the pull-request UI. Resolve on your laptop, commit, push. Do not resolve only in the UI if you cannot run the tests; Linux is where desk-api actually runs.
rerere (chapter 2) records how you resolved a hunk and reapplies it if the same conflict comes back. Leave it enabled.

title: Merge Conflicts
text:
After the merge
git log --oneline --graph --decorate --all
git branch -d feat/ping-json
-d succeeds once the work is reachable from main.

title: Fast-Forward for Clean History
text:
Creating a Fast-Forward Merge for a Clean History
After this page you can keep main a straight line when the feature branch is ahead of it.

title: Fast-Forward for Clean History
text:
When a fast-forward is possible
main has not moved since you branched. Every commit on the feature is a descendant of main.
 before --ff-only                   after --ff-only

 A ← B ← C          main            A ← B ← C ← D ← E   main
           ← D ← E  feat                        feat
cd ~/desk/desk-api
git switch main
git merge --ff-only feat/ping-json
--ff-only fails if Git would need a merge commit. That is the setting you already put in pull.ff only for pulls. Use it on purpose for local merges when you want a linear main.

title: Fast-Forward for Clean History
text:
If it fails
Someone committed to main while you worked. Options:

Merge anyway (git merge feat/ping-json) → merge commit, history shows the join.
Rebase the feature onto main (chapter 9), then --ff-only.
git merge --no-ff feat/ping-json → always a merge commit (Git Flow release style).

title: Fast-Forward for Clean History
text:
See it
git log --oneline --graph --decorate
A fast-forward looks like a single chain. A merge commit is a join with two parents.

title: Fast-Forward for Clean History
text:
first-parent
git log --first-parent --oneline
Walks only ^1. After --no-ff merges, this is “what landed on main.” After a fast-forward, it is the same as a normal log. Chapter 15 picks a branching strategy; this page is the mechanism that strategy will call.

title: Hands-On: A Real Merge Conflict
text:
Hands-On: Simulate a Real Merge Conflict
Two branches edit src/ping.py on Linux. You merge, resolve markers, and delete the feature branch.

title: Hands-On: A Real Merge Conflict
text:
Setup
Start from a clean ~/desk/desk-api (chapter 3 hands-on).
cd ~/desk/desk-api
git switch main
git status

title: Hands-On: A Real Merge Conflict
text:
Branch A — JSON ping
git switch -c feat/ping-json
cat > src/ping.py <<'EOF'
def ping():
    return {"status": "ok"}
EOF
git add src/ping.py
git commit -m "feat(ping): return a dict"
git switch main

title: Hands-On: A Real Merge Conflict
section: Branch B — string change on main
text:
Branch B — string change on main
cat > src/ping.py <<'EOF'
def ping():
    return "OK"
EOF
git add src/ping.py
git commit -m "feat(ping): shout the status"
main and feat/ping-json have diverged.
 A ← B ← C ← shout     main          ping.py returns "OK"
           ↖
             dict      feat/ping-json  ping.py returns {"status": "ok"}

title: Hands-On: A Real Merge Conflict
text:
Merge and conflict
git merge feat/ping-json
git status
cat src/ping.py
You should see markers. Open the file in nvim (or your editor) and make it:
def ping():
    return {"status": "OK"}
No marker lines left.
git add src/ping.py
git commit -m "merge feat/ping-json"
git log --oneline --graph --decorate -8
git branch -d feat/ping-json

title: Hands-On: A Real Merge Conflict
text:
Done when

git status is clean on main
src/ping.py returns a dict with "OK"
feat/ping-json is deleted
git log --graph shows a merge commit (two parents)

If you want to retry: git reset --hard to the commit before the merge (only on this lab clone), or copy the repo and run the page again. Chapter 9 rebases this same divergence into a straight line instead.
