title: Git 2.56 for Daily Work
text: Git 2.56 for Daily Work: add --resolved, branch --delete-merged, and Friends

title: Git 2.56 for Daily Work
text:
Thesis
Git 2.56.0 (tagged 28 September 2026) adds two commands to the end of the merge cycle that most people have been scripting by hand:

git add --resolved stages exactly the conflicted paths you have finished, and nothing else. It refuses the whole batch if any of them still contain conflict markers.
git branch --delete-merged <upstream> deletes local branches whose work has already landed on the upstream they track. Use --dry-run to preview it.

There are also three smaller tools: git bisect run --reset-when-found cleans up after itself, git history drop removes one commit from a branch (and the branches stacked on it) without an interactive rebase, and git branch --forked lists branches by what they track. On top of that, git merge-base and git branch --contains got faster without any change on your side.
Each new flag is a sharp, narrow tool. --resolved only knows what a conflict marker is, so it does not know whether you resolved a conflict well. --delete-merged only removes branches that track something other than their own push destination, and most people’s branches don’t. This page shows both behaviours on real repositories, so you know which of your branches and conflicts the new flags will and won’t handle.
Everything below was run with git version 2.56.0. Earlier versions reject these options as unknown.

title: Git 2.56 for Daily Work
text:
Mental model
end of a merge                                     end of a topic's life

  git status --short                                local          upstream
   M README.md   (yours, unrelated)                 fix/typo  ──►  origin/main  tip reachable?  ─┐
  UU app.py      (resolved)                         feat/wip  ──►  origin/main  no              │
  UU config.toml (resolved)                         feat/x    ──►  origin/feat/x  (push target) │
                                                                                                ▼
  git add -u          stages all three             git branch --delete-merged origin
  git add --resolved  stages only the UU paths       deletes fix/typo only
                      and refuses if any still
                      has <<<<<<< / ======= / >>>>>>>








Command
What it does
What it does not do




git add --resolved [<pathspec>]
Stages unmerged paths that have no conflict markers left. One leftover marker anywhere and nothing is staged
It does not look at binary or modify/delete conflicts. Those have no markers, so they are staged as whatever is in the working tree


git branch --delete-merged <pattern> [<branch-glob>…]
Deletes local branches whose upstream matches <pattern> (a ref, a remote name meaning its HEAD, or a glob) and whose tip is reachable from that upstream
It skips branches that track their own push destination, branches whose upstream is gone, and squash-merged branches, all without a word


--dry-run
With --delete-merged, prints Would delete branch … and touches nothing



branch.<name>.deleteMerged=false
Exempts one branch, and says so (Skipping '…')
Does not affect git branch -d


git branch --forked <pattern>
Lists branches by upstream. It’s the same match --delete-merged uses, without the reachability check



git bisect … --reset-when-found[=original\|found]
Ends the bisection by itself once the first bad commit is found
Can’t be combined with --no-checkout


git history drop <commit>
Removes one commit and replays its descendants, including other branches stacked on top
It won’t drop root or merge commits, and it won’t stop for conflicts. It aborts instead

title: Git 2.56 for Daily Work
text:
Worked examples (Cases)
Every case uses throwaway repositories under /tmp/g256. Source this file first so your hashes match the transcripts. It also shuts out your global config, so your aliases and push.default don’t change the results:
# env.sh — source this so your hashes match the transcripts (needs git 2.56+)
export GIT_AUTHOR_NAME="Dev" GIT_AUTHOR_EMAIL="dev@example.com"
export GIT_COMMITTER_NAME="Dev" GIT_COMMITTER_EMAIL="dev@example.com"
export GIT_AUTHOR_DATE="2026-10-01T09:00:00Z" GIT_COMMITTER_DATE="2026-10-01T09:00:00Z"
export GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL=/dev/null GIT_CONFIG_NOSYSTEM=1
export GIT_CONFIG_COUNT=2
export GIT_CONFIG_KEY_0=init.defaultBranch GIT_CONFIG_VALUE_0=main
export GIT_CONFIG_KEY_1=advice.detachedHead GIT_CONFIG_VALUE_1=false

Case 1: Stage what you resolved, not what you happened to touch
git add -u after a conflict is a habit, and it’s how unrelated edits end up inside merge commits. Set up a merge with two conflicts while an uncommitted note sits in README.md:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# setup-conflict.sh — a merge with two conflicted files and one unrelated local edit
set -euo pipefail
rm -rf /tmp/g256/conflict && mkdir -p /tmp/g256/conflict && cd /tmp/g256/conflict
git init -q
printf 'port = 8080\nlog = "info"\n' > config.toml
printf 'def greet():\n    return "hello"\n' > app.py
printf '# demo\n' > README.md
git add . && git commit -qm "base"
git switch -qc feature
printf 'port = 9090\nlog = "info"\n' > config.toml
printf 'def greet():\n    return "hello, world"\n' > app.py
git commit -qam "feature: new port and greeting"
git switch -q main
printf 'port = 8081\nlog = "info"\n' > config.toml
printf 'def greet():\n    return "hi"\n' > app.py
git commit -qam "main: different port and greeting"
echo "local note, not part of the merge" >> README.md   # unrelated, uncommitted
git merge feature || true
$ source env.sh && ./setup-conflict.sh
Auto-merging app.py
CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in app.py
Auto-merging config.toml
CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in config.toml
Automatic merge failed; fix conflicts and then commit the result.
$ cd /tmp/g256/conflict
$ git status --short
 M README.md
UU app.py
UU config.toml
$ printf 'def greet():\n    return "hello, world"\n' > app.py
$ git add --resolved; echo "exit=$?"
fatal: the following paths still have conflict markers:
    config.toml

exit=128
$ git status --short
 M README.md
UU app.py
UU config.toml
$ printf 'port = 9090\nlog = "info"\n' > config.toml
$ git add --resolved
$ git status --short
 M README.md
M  app.py
M  config.toml
$ git add --resolved -u
fatal: options '-u/--update' and '--resolved' cannot be used together
$ git commit -q --no-edit
$ git status --short
 M README.md
Three things to read off this:

With app.py fixed and config.toml still marked, --resolved staged nothing, not even app.py. It is all or nothing on purpose, so the index never shows a half-finished merge as resolved.
Once both were clean it staged both, and README.md stayed M. The merge commit holds the merge and nothing else, and your note is still waiting in the working tree.
--resolved can’t be combined with -u or -A, because those mean “stage everything tracked”. You can narrow it with a pathspec: git add --resolved src/ stages only the resolved paths under src/.



Case 2: Set topics up the way --delete-merged expects
--delete-merged matches on a branch’s upstream, so it works best when each topic tracks the branch it will land on (origin/main) and is pushed to a branch of its own name. Git already does the first half for you. A branch started from a remote-tracking branch gets that branch as its upstream (branch.autoSetupMerge=true is the default). The push needs one setting:
$ git switch -c fix/readme origin/main
Switched to a new branch 'fix/readme'
branch 'fix/readme' set up to track 'origin/main'.
$ echo r > r.txt && git add r.txt && git commit -qm 'fix/readme'
$ git push
fatal: The upstream branch of your current branch does not match
the name of your current branch.  To push to the upstream branch
on the remote, use

    git push origin HEAD:main

To push to the branch of the same name on the remote, use

    git push origin HEAD

To choose either option permanently, see push.default in 'git help config'.

To avoid automatically configuring an upstream branch when its name
won't match the local branch, see option 'simple' of branch.autoSetupMerge
in 'git help config'.

$ git config push.default current
$ git push
To /tmp/g256/br/origin.git
 * [new branch]      fix/readme -> fix/readme
$ git branch -vv --list fix/readme
* fix/readme 08b47a1 [origin/main: ahead 1] fix/readme
push.default=simple, the default, refuses to push a branch to a name that differs from its upstream. push.default=current pushes fix/readme to origin/fix/readme and leaves the upstream on origin/main. Now git status says how far you are from main, which is the comparison you care about for a topic. Once the work is merged, --delete-merged origin will recognise it.


Case 3: Preview, then sweep
This script builds a clone with eight topic branches (plus main), covering every state you’ll meet: merged, unfinished, squash-merged, tracking its own remote branch, upstream deleted, checked out in another worktree, opted out, and tracking a release branch that never got the fix:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# setup-branches.sh — a clone with eight local branches in different states
set -euo pipefail
rm -rf /tmp/g256/br && mkdir -p /tmp/g256/br && cd /tmp/g256/br
git init -q --bare origin.git
git clone -q origin.git work 2>/dev/null && cd work
echo base > app.txt && git add app.txt && git commit -qm "base" && git push -q origin main

topic() {  # topic <branch> <upstream>: branch from origin/main tracking <upstream>, one commit
  git switch -qc "$1" --track "$2" 2>/dev/null || git switch -qc "$1" origin/main
  echo "$1" > "${1//\//-}.txt" && git add . && git commit -qm "$1"
}

# 1. merged: tracks origin/main, merged upstream with a merge commit
topic fix/typo origin/main;        git push -q origin fix/typo
# 2. not merged yet
topic feat/wip origin/main
# 3. squash-merged upstream (different commit, same content)
topic feat/squashed origin/main;   git push -q origin feat/squashed
# 4. tracks its own remote branch, merged, then the remote branch was deleted
git switch -qc feat/gone origin/main && echo gone > gone.txt && git add . && git commit -qm "feat/gone" && git push -qu origin feat/gone
# 5. tracks its own remote branch, merged, remote branch still there
git switch -qc feat/same-name origin/main && echo same > same.txt && git add . && git commit -qm "feat/same-name" && git push -qu origin feat/same-name
# 6. merged, but checked out in a linked worktree
topic fix/in-worktree origin/main; git push -q origin fix/in-worktree
# 7. merged, but opted out
topic feat/round-two origin/main;  git push -q origin feat/round-two
git config branch.feat/round-two.deleteMerged false
# 8. merged into main, tracks a release branch that does not have it
git push -q origin main:release/1.0
git fetch -q
topic fix/backport origin/release/1.0; git push -q origin fix/backport
git switch -q main

# "upstream" merges everything except feat/wip; feat/squashed is squashed
rm -rf ../hub && git clone -q ../origin.git ../hub 2>/dev/null && cd ../hub
for b in fix/typo feat/gone feat/same-name fix/in-worktree feat/round-two fix/backport; do
  git merge -q --no-ff --no-edit "origin/$b" >/dev/null
done
git merge -q --squash origin/feat/squashed >/dev/null 2>&1 && git commit -qm "feat/squashed (squashed)"
git push -q origin main
git push -q origin --delete feat/gone
cd ../work
git fetch -q --prune
git worktree add -q ../wt fix/in-worktree
$ source env.sh && ./setup-branches.sh && cd /tmp/g256/br/work
$ git branch -vv
  feat/gone       db5921d [origin/feat/gone: gone] feat/gone
  feat/round-two  e157f1f [origin/main: behind 12] feat/round-two
  feat/same-name  0401489 [origin/feat/same-name] feat/same-name
  feat/squashed   d74a4cc [origin/main: ahead 1, behind 13] feat/squashed
  feat/wip        2fc13cf [origin/main: ahead 1, behind 13] feat/wip
  fix/backport    d76cc42 [origin/release/1.0: ahead 1] fix/backport
+ fix/in-worktree 15ead81 (/tmp/g256/br/wt) [origin/main: behind 12] fix/in-worktree
  fix/typo        fdcf8be [origin/main: behind 12] fix/typo
* main            9d063a9 [origin/main: behind 13] base
$ git branch --forked origin/main
  feat/round-two
  feat/squashed
  feat/wip
+ fix/in-worktree
  fix/typo
* main
$ git branch --dry-run --delete-merged origin
Skipping 'feat/round-two' (branch.feat/round-two.deleteMerged is false)
Would delete branch fix/typo (was fdcf8be).
$ git branch --dry-run --delete-merged origin 'fix/*'
Would delete branch fix/typo (was fdcf8be).
$ git branch --delete-merged origin
Skipping 'feat/round-two' (branch.feat/round-two.deleteMerged is false)
Deleted branch fix/typo (was fdcf8be).
$ git branch --list
  feat/gone
  feat/round-two
  feat/same-name
  feat/squashed
  feat/wip
  fix/backport
+ fix/in-worktree
* main
Read the result branch by branch:








Branch
Outcome
Why




fix/typo
deleted
Tracks origin/main, and its tip is reachable from it


feat/round-two
kept, reported
branch.feat/round-two.deleteMerged=false


fix/in-worktree
kept, silent
Checked out in /tmp/g256/br/wt


feat/wip
kept, silent
Not merged yet


feat/squashed
kept, silent
A squash merge creates a new commit, so the branch tip is never reachable from origin/main


feat/same-name, main
kept, silent
git push would update their own upstream. Right after a pull, such a branch is always “merged”, so Git refuses to guess


feat/gone
kept, silent
Its upstream origin/feat/gone was pruned after the merge


fix/backport
kept, silent
Merged into main, but its upstream origin/release/1.0 doesn’t have it



Passing origin means “the branch origin/HEAD points at”, so origin/main here. 'origin/*' widens the match to every upstream on that remote, and you can repeat --delete-merged to name several. A trailing 'fix/*' limits which local branches are even considered. --forked uses the same upstream match as a listing filter, so git branch --forked origin/main is a cheap way to see the candidates before anything is checked for reachability.
Deleted branches print their old tip (was fdcf8be). Until gc prunes the commits, git branch fix/typo fdcf8be puts it back.


Case 4: A bisect that cleans up after itself
git bisect run used to leave you on a detached HEAD in the middle of the bisection state until you remembered git bisect reset. Now it can finish the job:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# setup-bisect.sh — 16 commits; commit 11 breaks check.sh
set -euo pipefail
rm -rf /tmp/g256/bisect && mkdir -p /tmp/g256/bisect && cd /tmp/g256/bisect
git init -q
printf '#!/bin/sh\ngrep -q "^limit=10$" limits.conf\n' > check.sh && chmod +x check.sh
echo "limit=10" > limits.conf
git add . && git commit -qm "c1: add check"
for i in $(seq 2 16); do
  [ "$i" -eq 11 ] && echo "limit=100" > limits.conf
  echo "change $i" >> CHANGELOG && git add . && git commit -qm "c$i"
done
git switch -qc topic && git switch -q main
$ source env.sh && ./setup-bisect.sh && cd /tmp/g256/bisect
$ git switch -q topic
$ git bisect start main main~15
Bisecting: 7 revisions left to test after this (roughly 3 steps)
[977dff1cd080a1d2dc267fd03fad3d5bd34aedae] c8
$ git bisect run --reset-when-found ./check.sh
running './check.sh'
Bisecting: 3 revisions left to test after this (roughly 2 steps)
[17edb82aa1019346897ab8763f8baf74af113808] c12
running './check.sh'
Bisecting: 1 revision left to test after this (roughly 1 step)
[e7ccdbe0a5c6e71b2fea6e0f448dc4aba80c7f52] c10
running './check.sh'
Bisecting: 0 revisions left to test after this (roughly 0 steps)
[09ee7e9ff3cff397a539e7e73d2b9ac5d3a6ff5f] c11
running './check.sh'
09ee7e9ff3cff397a539e7e73d2b9ac5d3a6ff5f is the first 'bad' commit
commit 09ee7e9ff3cff397a539e7e73d2b9ac5d3a6ff5f
Author: Dev <dev@example.com>
Date:   Thu Oct 1 09:00:00 2026 +0000

    c11

 CHANGELOG   | 1 +
 limits.conf | 2 +-
 2 files changed, 2 insertions(+), 1 deletion(-)
bisect found first 'bad' commit
$ git status --short --branch
## topic
$ git bisect log
error: We are not bisecting.
$ git bisect start --reset-when-found=found main main~15
Bisecting: 7 revisions left to test after this (roughly 3 steps)
[977dff1cd080a1d2dc267fd03fad3d5bd34aedae] c8
$ git bisect run ./check.sh >/dev/null
$ git status --short --branch
## HEAD (no branch)
$ git log -1 --oneline
09ee7e9 c11
--reset-when-found (that is, =original) put us back on topic, with no bisection state left: We are not bisecting. =found leaves the culprit checked out (detached at 09ee7e9 c11) and still clears the state. That’s what you want when the next step is git show or a build of the bad commit. You can give the option to bisect start, as in the second run, or to bisect run. It’s refused with --no-checkout (options '--reset-when-found' and '--no-checkout' cannot be used together), because there is no checkout to return from.


Case 5: Drop one commit without an interactive rebase
git history is still marked experimental. 2.56 adds drop next to reword, split, and fixup:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# setup-history.sh — a short topic with one commit that should never have happened
set -euo pipefail
rm -rf /tmp/g256/hist && mkdir -p /tmp/g256/hist && cd /tmp/g256/hist
git init -q
echo "app" > app.txt && git add . && git commit -qm "base"
git switch -qc feat/report
echo "query"  > query.sql  && git add . && git commit -qm "add report query"
echo "debug=1" > .env.local && git add . && git commit -qm "WIP: local debug settings"
echo "render" > render.py  && git add . && git commit -qm "render report"
git branch feat/report-ui                       # a branch stacked on top
echo "ui" > ui.js && git switch -q feat/report-ui && git add . && git commit -qm "report UI"
git switch -q feat/report
$ source env.sh && ./setup-history.sh && cd /tmp/g256/hist
$ git log --oneline --decorate --graph feat/report-ui
* 4ff5f05 (feat/report-ui) report UI
* 6021dd1 (HEAD -> feat/report) render report
* e3d4de1 WIP: local debug settings
* 99efa11 add report query
* e135d0b (main) base
$ git history drop HEAD~1 --dry-run
update refs/heads/feat/report 5c85b08fe93e8dcbebb35bcd5e0fd6b7b8b725df 6021dd1b2c922ee1fa03f10a65d75d3012da1a89
update refs/heads/feat/report-ui 83fe96025062c342ad0ad189b968ba7766bd58f1 4ff5f05abfefe16eb8dd35c9382d9f8b17c0f457
$ git history drop HEAD~1
$ git log --oneline --decorate --graph feat/report-ui
* 83fe960 (feat/report-ui) report UI
* 5c85b08 (HEAD -> feat/report) render report
* 99efa11 add report query
* e135d0b (main) base
$ ls
app.txt
query.sql
render.py
--dry-run prints the ref updates it would make, in update-ref --stdin form (update <ref> <new> <old>). The real run made the same updates: feat/report and the stacked feat/report-ui both moved, so the stack stayed in one piece. To move only the current branch, pass --update-refs=head. Unlike rebase -i, it never stops halfway. If a descendant doesn’t replay cleanly, nothing changes at all:
$ echo 'app v2' > app.txt && git commit -qam 'bump to v2'
$ echo 'app v3' > app.txt && git commit -qam 'bump to v3'
$ git history drop HEAD~1; echo "exit=$?"
error: failed replaying descendants
exit=255
$ git log --oneline -3
9be6c5a bump to v3
97e8f92 bump to v2
5c85b08 render report
The 9be6c5a on top is the same commit as before the failed command. No sequencer state is left behind and there is no --abort to remember. When the drop needs a real conflict resolution, use git rebase -i.


What you get for free
There are two speedups with no new syntax, both from the release notes:

git merge-base now stops walking once one side’s exclusive commits run out, which makes queries with a one-sided history much faster. Merges, rebases, and git log A...B all compute merge bases. The same release also fixes a case where git merge-base (without --all) could return a wrong answer on repositories with v1 commit-graphs and clock skew.
git branch --contains and git for-each-ref --contains now use the memoised traversal that git tag --contains already had.

The release notes describe these as significant speedups without benchmark numbers. Measure on your own repository before you quote one.

title: Git 2.56 for Daily Work
text:
The trap
--resolved checks for markers. It does not check that you resolved anything. Three common conflicts break that assumption in three ways:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# setup-traps.sh — three conflicts that have no conflict markers to find
set -euo pipefail
rm -rf /tmp/g256/traps && mkdir -p /tmp/g256/traps && cd /tmp/g256/traps
git init -q
printf 'Release notes\n=======\n\n- v1\n' > NOTES.md
printf 'logo\0v1' > logo.png
echo "legacy" > legacy.cfg
git add . && git commit -qm "base"
git switch -qc side
printf 'Release notes\n=======\n\n- v2\n' > NOTES.md
printf 'logo\0v2' > logo.png
echo "legacy, patched" > legacy.cfg
git commit -qam "side: notes, new logo, patch legacy.cfg"
git switch -q main
printf 'Release notes\n=======\n\n- v3\n' > NOTES.md
printf 'logo\0v3' > logo.png
git rm -q legacy.cfg
git commit -qam "main: notes, other logo, drop legacy.cfg"
git merge side || true
$ source env.sh && ./setup-traps.sh >/dev/null && cd /tmp/g256/traps
$ git status --short
UU NOTES.md
DU legacy.cfg
UU logo.png
$ printf 'Release notes\n=======\n\n- v2\n- v3\n' > NOTES.md
$ git add --resolved
fatal: the following paths still have conflict markers:
    NOTES.md

$ git add --resolved logo.png legacy.cfg
$ git status --short
UU NOTES.md
A  legacy.cfg
$ git diff --cached --stat HEAD
 NOTES.md   | Unmerged
 legacy.cfg | 1 +
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+)

False positive. NOTES.md is cleanly resolved, but its Markdown heading is underlined with exactly seven =. That is the same shape as a conflict separator, so --resolved refuses. Either stage that file explicitly after reading it (git add NOTES.md), or set NOTES.md conflict-marker-size=32 in .gitattributes before merging. Git then writes 32-character markers, and seven = no longer looks like one.
Silent “resolution” of a binary. logo.png was UU, and now it isn’t listed at all. --resolved staged the working-tree copy, which for a binary conflict is ours. The staged diff against HEAD is empty, so their logo is gone without a trace.
Silent resurrection. legacy.cfg was deleted on main and modified on side (DU). It has no markers, so --resolved staged the surviving copy (A legacy.cfg) and brought back a file your branch had deleted on purpose.

The other trap is the flip side of Case 3: --delete-merged is quiet about everything it doesn’t delete. If your team’s flow is “push to origin/<same-name>, squash-merge on the forge, delete the remote branch”, none of your branches qualify. They all track their own push destination, are squash-merged, or have a pruned upstream. The command prints nothing and deletes nothing, which looks the same as having nothing to clean up.

title: Git 2.56 for Daily Work
text:
The boring rule

After a conflicted merge, run git status --short and deal with every DU, UD, AA, and binary UU deliberately (git checkout --ours/--theirs <path>, or git rm). Then use git add --resolved for the text files and read any refusal it gives you. Never git add -u or git add . in the middle of a merge.
Start topics from origin/main, set push.default=current, and clean up with git fetch --prune && git branch --dry-run --delete-merged origin before the real run. Mark long-lived topics with branch.<name>.deleteMerged=false. Delete squash-merged and same-name branches yourself with git branch -D after checking git log origin/main..<branch>.

title: Git 2.56 for Daily Work
text:
Try this

Rerun Case 1, but after resolving both files use git add -u instead of --resolved. Commit with git commit --no-edit, then run git show --stat HEAD and find README.md, your unrelated note, inside the merge commit.
Copy setup-traps.sh and add echo 'NOTES.md conflict-marker-size=32' > .gitattributes just before the base commit. Rerun it, resolve NOTES.md the same way, and confirm that git add --resolved NOTES.md now succeeds while logo.png and legacy.cfg stay unmerged.
In the Case 3 clone, run git branch --forked 'origin/*' -vv and predict, before running it, what git branch --dry-run --delete-merged 'origin/*' will print.
In the Case 3 clone, run git cherry origin/main feat/squashed and git cherry origin/main feat/wip. A - line means an equivalent patch is already upstream, which is the evidence you want before git branch -D on a squash-merged branch.
Write a git sweep alias that runs fetch --prune, then branch --dry-run --delete-merged origin, asks y/N, and only then runs the real thing.

title: git add –resolved for Conflict Markers
text: git add –resolved for Conflict Markers

title: git add –resolved for Conflict Markers
text:
Thesis
git add --resolved (Git 2.56+) stages a path only if conflict markers are gone. It catches the classic failure mode: you “fix” a merge but leave <<<<<<< in the file and git add happily stages the mess.

title: git add –resolved for Conflict Markers
text:
Mental model
  conflicted path
       │
       ├─ git add file          → stages whatever is on disk (markers OK)
       └─ git add --resolved file
              → refuses if <<<<<<< / ======= / >>>>>>> remain

title: git add –resolved for Conflict Markers
text:
Worked example
This writing box has Git 2.47.3 — --resolved is not present yet. Confirmed:
Git 2.47.3 on this box; git add --resolved arrived in Git 2.56. Chapter written from release notes and git-add docs.
git version 2.47.3
Documented behaviour (Git 2.56 release notes / docs): after a conflicted merge, edit the file clean, then:
git add --resolved path/to/file
# error if markers remain; stages when clean
git status
Until you upgrade, a cheap guard is:
# pre-2.56 hygiene
if grep -nE '^(<<<<<<<|=======|>>>>>>>)' path/to/file; then
  echo "markers remain" >&2; exit 1
fi
git add path/to/file

title: git add –resolved for Conflict Markers
text:
Trap
Assuming CI will catch markers. Many test suites never open the conflicted asset (docs, JSON, lockfiles). --resolved (or the grep guard) belongs in the human merge path and in pre-commit hooks.

title: git add –resolved for Conflict Markers
text:
Boring rule
On Git ≥ 2.56, prefer git add --resolved for every path leaving a conflicted state. On older Git, script the marker grep before git add.

title: git add –resolved for Conflict Markers
text:
Try this

On a 2.56+ lab: leave markers in, watch --resolved fail; remove them and succeed.
Add a pre-commit hook that greps staged files for conflict markers.
Read the Git 2.56 release notes entry for --resolved.

title: git add –resolved for Conflict Markers
text:
Sources

Git 2.56 release notes / git add documentation (--resolved)
git merge conflict marker conventions (<<<<<<<, etc.)

title: Theory
text:
Theory: Rebase Copies Commits; It Does Not Slide Them
A rebase walks a range of commits, takes each patch against its parent, and applies it onto a new base. Each successful apply writes a new commit (new hash, usually same author, you as committer).

title: Theory
text:
Invariants

Original commits remain in the object store until GC; the branch name moves to the copied tip.
Conflicts happen once per copied commit, not once at a join.
Interactive rebase is the same machine plus a todo list (pick, squash, fixup, reword, edit, drop).
pull --rebase = fetch + rebase local-only commits onto @{u}.
--onto is “take this range and replay it on that commit,” the general form of rebase.

 before                         after git rebase main

 A ← B ← C ← G     main         A ← B ← C ← G          main
      ↑                                     ↖
      D ← E        feat                       D' ← E'  feat

title: Theory
text:
Why teams fight about it
Merge preserves hashes and adds a node. Rebase rewrites hashes and can keep main linear. Unpublished feature branches are the safe audience. Published main is not.

title: Theory
text:
What can break

Rebasing commits other people have based work on (force-push incident).
--ours/--theirs confusion vs merge.
Empty commits after rebase (--skip vs keep).

title: Theory
text:
How to read this chapter
Why, interactive, conflicts, pull –rebase, vs merge, lab; then --onto, autosquash, --exec, --update-refs.

title: Why Rebase
text:
Why Rebase? Clean History vs Merge Commits
After this page you can say what rebase copies, and why the hashes change.

title: Why Rebase
section: Replay commits on a new parent
text:
Replay commits on a new parent
You branched from main at C. main moved to G. Rebase copies your commits D and E as D' and E' with parent G:
A ← B ← C ← G                main
          ← D ← E            feat/ping-json

# git switch feat/ping-json && git rebase main

A ← B ← C ← G                main
              ← D' ← E'      feat/ping-json
D' has a new hash. The patch is similar; the parent is G. Git then fast-forwards or you --ff-only merge into main.
cd ~/desk/desk-api
git switch feat/ping-json
git rebase main

title: Why Rebase
text:
What you gain

main can stay a single chain (fast-forward).
Reviewers read your commits on top of current main, not an old base.
git log --first-parent on main after --ff-only is your feature commits, not a merge node.

title: Why Rebase
text:
What you pay

New hashes. Anyone who fetched D and E now has stale names.
Conflicts are replayed per copied commit, not once in a merge commit.

Rebase unpublished work (your feature branch). Merge published history you share (main that others pulled). Chapter 11 is force-push if you already pushed the old D and E.

title: Why Rebase
section: rebase vs merge in one line
text:
rebase vs merge in one line
Merge adds a join. Rebase copies a chain onto a new base. Both produce a tree that contains both sides of the work. The graph looks different. The next pages are interactive rebase, conflicts, pull --rebase, and when to pick which.

title: Interactive Rebase
text:
Interactive Rebase: Squash, Reorder, Fixup, Polish
After this page you can rewrite a short chain of local commits on Linux without a GUI.

title: Interactive Rebase
text:
Open the todo list
cd ~/desk/desk-api
git switch feat/ping-json
git rebase -i HEAD~3
Git writes a file and opens core.editor (nvim in this book). Each line is a commit, oldest first:
pick a1b2c3d feat(ping): return a dict
pick d4e5f6a docs: mention JSON
pick 98ab765 fix typo
You edit the verbs, save, quit. Git replays from the top.

title: Interactive Rebase
text:
Verbs you will use







Verb
Effect




pick
Keep this commit


reword
Keep, edit the message


edit
Stop here so you can amend


squash
Fold into the previous commit; editor for a combined message


fixup
Fold into the previous commit; keep the previous message


drop
Omit this commit



Reorder lines to reorder commits. Delete a line to drop (same as drop).

title: Interactive Rebase
text:
Linux without the editor (labs)
For a scripted squash of everything after the first of the last three:
GIT_SEQUENCE_EDITOR="sed -i '2,\$s/^pick /fixup /'" git rebase -i HEAD~3
sed -i on GNU sed (Linux) edits in place. This is for labs and hooks. Day to day, use nvim.

title: Interactive Rebase
text:
Stop and amend (edit)
Git stops at that commit. You git add / git commit --amend, then:
git rebase --continue

title: Interactive Rebase
text:
Abort
git rebase --abort
Back to the pre-rebase branch tip. Safe while the rebase is in progress.

title: Interactive Rebase
text:
Range
git rebase -i main rebases each commit reachable from HEAD but not from main. That is the usual “update my feature onto main” todo list.
Do this on a feature branch. Interactive rebase of shared main rewrites hashes everyone already has.

title: Rebase Conflicts
text:
Rebase Conflicts: How They Differ from Merge Conflicts
After this page you can finish a conflicted rebase one commit at a time.

title: Rebase Conflicts
text:
One commit at a time
A merge conflict happens once, at the join. A rebase conflict happens each time a copied commit does not apply onto the new parent.
 merge: one fight at M

 A ← B ← C ← M
      ↑      ↑
      D ← E

 rebase: a fight at D', then maybe again at E'

 A ← B ← C ← G ← D'  ←  E'
                 ▲ stop    ▲ stop
Markers look the same (<<<<<<<). git status during a rebase says rebase in progress and names the commit being applied.
git rebase main
# CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in src/ping.py
git status

title: Rebase Conflicts
text:
The loop

Edit files, remove markers.
git add the resolved paths.
git rebase --continue (not git commit, unless Git asks you to).
Repeat until Git prints Successfully rebased.

nvim src/ping.py
git add src/ping.py
git rebase --continue
If the commit becomes empty (your patch is already in the new base):
git rebase --skip
Give up:
git rebase --abort

title: Rebase Conflicts
section: Ours / theirs are swapped from merge
text:
Ours / theirs are swapped from merge
During merge, --ours is the branch you had checked out (main). During rebase, you checked out the feature and Git replays onto main: --ours is the upstream (the new base), --theirs is the commit being replayed.
That swap surprises everyone once. Prefer reading the markers over --ours until it is boring.

title: Rebase Conflicts
text:
rerere
With rerere.enabled (chapter 2), Git records the resolution. A later rebase that hits the same hunk applies it again. On a long-lived feature branch that rebases onto main daily, this is the difference between pain and a two-second continue.

title: Rebase Conflicts
text:
After success
git log --oneline --graph --decorate main feat/ping-json
A straight line from main through your copied commits. Then git switch main && git merge --ff-only feat/ping-json.

title: Pull with Rebase
text:
Pull with Rebase When Your Branch Is Out of Date
After this page you can update a local branch from a remote without a merge commit from git pull.

title: Pull with Rebase
text:
pull is fetch plus integrate
git pull
means git fetch then, by default, a merge of @{u} (the upstream) into HEAD. If both you and the remote moved, you get a merge commit that only exists because you pulled.
 after fetch, both moved

 origin/main   A ← B ← C ← G
 local main    A ← B ← C ← D ← E

 git pull              (merge)     A ← B ← C ← G ← M
                                         D ← E ↗

 git pull --rebase                 A ← B ← C ← G ← D' ← E'
Chapter 2 set:
git config --global pull.ff only
Then git pull fails instead of merging. You choose:
git pull --rebase
# or
git fetch
git rebase @{u}
--rebase copies your local-only commits onto the updated upstream, then fast-forwards your branch name.

title: Pull with Rebase
section: When this is the right shape
text:
When this is the right shape
You committed two fixes on main locally. Someone else pushed to origin/main. git pull --rebase replays your two fixes on top of theirs. History stays linear. Conflicts are per commit (previous page).

title: Pull with Rebase
text:
When to merge instead
You want a merge commit that records “I integrated upstream at this point.” Feature branches that you share, or main policies that require merge commits, use git pull --no-rebase or an explicit git merge.

title: Pull with Rebase
section: Set it for this branch only
text:
Set it for this branch only
git config pull.rebase true          # this repo
git config --global pull.rebase true # every repo (overrides pull.ff only)
This book leaves pull.ff only as the global default so a surprise pull fails closed. Type --rebase when you mean it, until the habit is there.

title: Pull with Rebase
text:
After a rebase pull
git status
git log --oneline --graph --decorate -12
Your branch is ahead of 'origin/main' by N commits means you still need git push. If you had already pushed the old hashes, you need a force-with-lease (chapter 11).

title: Rebase vs Merge
text:
The Debate: Rebase vs Merge
After this page you can pick a default for desk-api and know what you are giving up.

title: Rebase vs Merge
text:
Same trees, different graphs
Both operations can produce a working tree that contains both sides of the work. Merge records a join. Rebase copies a chain.
 start                         after merge

 A ← B ← C ← G   main          A ← B ← C ← G ← M   main
      ↑                             ↑          ↑
      D ← E      feat               D ← E      feat

 start                         after rebase feat onto main

 A ← B ← C ← G   main          A ← B ← C ← G          main
      ↑                                      ↖
      D ← E      feat                          D' ← E'  feat




Merge
Rebase




Hashes of your old commits
Unchanged
New


Extra commit
Often a merge commit
None if you fast-forward after


Conflicts
Once, at the join
Once per copied commit


Safe on published main
Yes
Usually no


Safe on your unpushed feature
Yes
Yes, and often cleaner

title: Rebase vs Merge
text:
A default that scales

Feature branch you own: rebase onto main, then fast-forward main (or open a pull request that the forge squash-merges).
main / shared long-lived branch: merge or fast-forward only. Do not rebase commits other people have.
Hotfix already on main: revert (chapter 10), do not rebase main.

Forges add a third option: squash merge (many commits become one on main). That is a server-side rewrite. Chapter 15 and chapter 31. Locally, rebase is how you squash before you push.

title: Rebase vs Merge
text:
rerere, tests, Linux
Run the test command you actually have after every --continue. On Linux that is whatever desk-api uses (python -m pytest, a shell script, make test). Rebase does not run tests for you.

title: Rebase vs Merge
text:
You can mix
Rebase the feature. Merge into main with --no-ff if the team wants a join node for git log --first-parent. That is Git Flow’s “feature into develop” shape. Trunk-based skips the join and fast-forwards.
There is no global winner. There is a default per branch class. Write it down in the repo (chapter 15). The hands-on page next squashes a messy feature on Linux.

title: Hands-On: Clean Up a Messy History
text:
Hands-On: Clean Up a Messy History
Make three noisy commits on a feature branch, then squash them into one conventional commit with interactive rebase.

title: Hands-On: Clean Up a Messy History
text:
Setup
cd ~/desk/desk-api
git switch main
git switch -c feat/health-header

title: Hands-On: Clean Up a Messy History
text:
Three messy commits
echo "# health" >> README.md
git add README.md
git commit -m "wip"

echo "Health endpoint later." >> README.md
git add README.md
git commit -m "more"

echo "See src/ping.py for now." >> README.md
git add README.md
git commit -m "typo fix later"
git log --oneline -5

title: Hands-On: Clean Up a Messy History
text:
Squash with GNU sed (Linux)
Keep the first of the three; fixup the rest:
GIT_SEQUENCE_EDITOR="sed -i '2,\$s/^pick /fixup /'" git rebase -i HEAD~3
git log --oneline -5
One commit remains, message still wip. Retitle:
git commit --amend -m "docs: mention a future health endpoint"
git log --oneline -3

title: Hands-On: Clean Up a Messy History
text:
Optional: rebase onto main
If main moved, replay this one commit:
git rebase main
git log --oneline --graph --decorate -8

title: Hands-On: Clean Up a Messy History
text:
Cleanup
git switch main
git merge --ff-only feat/health-header
git branch -d feat/health-header
If --ff-only refuses, main moved; rebase the feature first or merge.

title: Hands-On: Clean Up a Messy History
text:
Done when

git log on main shows one docs: commit for this work, not three wips
git status is clean
The feature branch is deleted

text: update-refs and keep-base

title: update-refs and keep-base
text:
Thesis
A plain rebase moves one branch name: the one you are on. Real work often comes as a stack: feat/api ← feat/ui ← feat/docs, each reviewed as its own pull request. If you rebase the top of the stack, every branch name under it is left pointing at the old commits. Two flags fix this:

--update-refs force-moves every local branch that points into the rebased range, so the whole stack moves together.
--keep-base rewrites commits in place, on the same merge base. You can tidy a stack (fixups, rewording) without also pulling in whatever landed on main overnight.

Use them together and you can edit any commit in the stack, from the top branch, in one command.
--update-refs arrived in Git 2.38 and --keep-base in Git 2.24. The transcripts on this page come from Git 2.47. The behaviour is the same in current releases (2.56 as of October 2026).

title: update-refs and keep-base
text:
Mental model
before: a stack of three branches (api, ui, docs = feat/*); main has moved on to B ── M

  B ── A1 ── A2 ── U1 ── U2 ── D1
  ▲          ▲           ▲     ▲
  base       api         ui    docs

plain `git rebase main`: only HEAD's branch moves

  B ── M ── A1' ── A2' ── U1' ── U2' ── D1'   ← feat/docs
  └── A1 ── A2 ── U1 ── U2                     ← feat/api, feat/ui left behind

`git rebase --update-refs main`: every branch inside the range moves

  B ── M ── A1' ── A2' ── U1' ── U2' ── D1'
                   ▲             ▲      ▲
                   api           ui     docs

`git rebase -i --keep-base --update-refs main`: rewrite in place on B

  B ── A1' ── A2' ── U1' ── U2' ── D1'        (M stays off to the side)







Piece
What it does




--update-refs
Adds an update-ref refs/heads/<name> line to the todo list after the last commit of each branch inside the range. The refs move only when the rebase finishes, so --abort leaves them alone


rebase.updateRefs=true
Makes --update-refs the default. Turn it off for one run with --no-update-refs


--keep-base <upstream>
New base = merge-base(<upstream>, HEAD). Same as --onto <upstream>...HEAD <upstream>, and also implies --reapply-cherry-picks and --no-fork-point


Branches checked out in another worktree
Never updated. The todo shows a # Ref … checked out at … comment instead


Refs outside the rebased range
Untouched. Rebase from the top of the stack, or descendants get left behind



--keep-base cannot be combined with --onto or --root. It is a way of choosing the onto point, so those flags would conflict with it.

title: update-refs and keep-base
text:
Worked examples (Cases)
Every case starts from the same throwaway repository. Source the environment file so your commit hashes match the transcripts.
# stack-env.sh — source this so your hashes match the transcripts on this page
export GIT_AUTHOR_NAME="Dev" GIT_AUTHOR_EMAIL="dev@example.com"
export GIT_COMMITTER_NAME="Dev" GIT_COMMITTER_EMAIL="dev@example.com"
export GIT_AUTHOR_DATE="2026-10-02T10:00:00+05:30"
export GIT_COMMITTER_DATE="2026-10-02T10:00:00+05:30"
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# setup-stack.sh — build a three-branch stack on top of main, then move main
set -euo pipefail
export GIT_AUTHOR_NAME="Dev" GIT_AUTHOR_EMAIL="dev@example.com"
export GIT_COMMITTER_NAME="Dev" GIT_COMMITTER_EMAIL="dev@example.com"
export GIT_AUTHOR_DATE="2026-10-01T09:00:00+05:30"
export GIT_COMMITTER_DATE="$GIT_AUTHOR_DATE"

git init -q -b main "${1:-stack}" && cd "${1:-stack}"
c() { echo "$2" >> "$1"; git add "$1"; git commit -q -m "$3"; }

c README.md "# shop"                    "init: README"
c lib.sh    "price() { echo 100; }"     "main: add lib.sh"

git switch -q -c feat/api                # bottom of the stack
echo "timeout=3" > api.conf && git add api.conf
c api.sh    "get_price() { price; }"    "api: add get_price"
c api.sh    "list_items() { :; }"       "api: add list_items"

git switch -q -c feat/ui                 # middle: builds on feat/api
c ui.sh     "render() { get_price; }"   "ui: render price"
c ui.sh     "render_list() { list_items; }" "ui: render list"

git switch -q -c feat/docs               # top: builds on feat/ui
c docs.md   "Prices come from get_price." "docs: describe pricing"

git switch -q main                       # meanwhile, main moves on
c lib.sh    "tax() { echo 18; }"        "main: add tax()"
git switch -q feat/docs
mkdir -p /tmp/vcs && cd /tmp/vcs        # save both files here first
chmod +x setup-stack.sh
source ./stack-env.sh
./setup-stack.sh && cd stack
git log --graph --oneline --decorate --all
* 87455ba (HEAD -> feat/docs) docs: describe pricing
* 576a711 (feat/ui) ui: render list
* 42dfa4c ui: render price
* 87584b9 (feat/api) api: add list_items
* f2f0cff api: add get_price
| * c6a0e25 (main) main: add tax()
|/  
* 6b188b4 main: add lib.sh
* 2a401c6 init: README
To reset between cases, run cd /tmp/vcs && rm -rf stack && ./setup-stack.sh && cd stack.

Case 1: The stale stack (what goes wrong without the flag)
git rebase main
git log --graph --oneline --decorate --all
git log --oneline main..feat/ui
Successfully rebased and updated refs/heads/feat/docs.
* 1861481 (HEAD -> feat/docs) docs: describe pricing
* f0527d0 ui: render list
* 55affa4 ui: render price
* 49a9b11 api: add list_items
* 58ab280 api: add get_price
* c6a0e25 (main) main: add tax()
| * 576a711 (feat/ui) ui: render list
| * 42dfa4c ui: render price
| * 87584b9 (feat/api) api: add list_items
| * f2f0cff api: add get_price
|/  
* 6b188b4 main: add lib.sh
* 2a401c6 init: README
576a711 ui: render list
42dfa4c ui: render price
87584b9 api: add list_items
f2f0cff api: add get_price
feat/docs moved and the other two did not. The repository now holds two copies of the api and ui commits. If you push feat/ui now, its pull request still targets the old base. If you push feat/docs, its pull request shows four extra commits that “belong” to other PRs. The old way to repair this was one git branch -f per branch, with hashes copied by hand.


Case 2: --update-refs moves the whole stack
git rebase --update-refs main
git log --graph --oneline --decorate --all
Successfully rebased and updated refs/heads/feat/docs.
Updated the following refs with --update-refs:
    refs/heads/feat/api
    refs/heads/feat/ui
* 1861481 (HEAD -> feat/docs) docs: describe pricing
* f0527d0 (feat/ui) ui: render list
* 55affa4 ui: render price
* 49a9b11 (feat/api) api: add list_items
* 58ab280 api: add get_price
* c6a0e25 (main) main: add tax()
* 6b188b4 main: add lib.sh
* 2a401c6 init: README
Prove that the rewrite only replayed the commits and changed none of them. range-diff pairs each old commit with its new version, and = means “identical patch”:
git range-diff main feat/docs@{1} feat/docs
git reflog -2 feat/ui
1:  f2f0cff = 1:  58ab280 api: add get_price
2:  87584b9 = 2:  49a9b11 api: add list_items
3:  42dfa4c = 3:  55affa4 ui: render price
4:  576a711 = 4:  f0527d0 ui: render list
5:  87455ba = 5:  1861481 docs: describe pricing
f0527d0 feat/ui@{0}: rewritten during rebase
576a711 feat/ui@{1}: commit: ui: render list
Each moved branch gets a rewritten during rebase reflog entry, so git branch -f feat/ui feat/ui@{1} undoes one branch if you need to.


Case 3: Fix the bottom commit from the top, without moving the base
Review on feat/api asks for timeout=30. You are on feat/docs, and main has moved, but you do not want to drag main: add tax() into three open pull requests just to fix one line.
sed -i 's/timeout=3/timeout=30/' api.conf
git commit -q -am "fixup! api: add get_price"
git log --oneline -1
GIT_SEQUENCE_EDITOR=cat git rebase -i --autosquash --keep-base --update-refs main
git log --graph --oneline --decorate --all
GIT_SEQUENCE_EDITOR=cat prints the todo list and accepts it unchanged. In real work you would let your editor open it. Comment lines are omitted below:
ddf1e1f fixup! api: add get_price
pick f2f0cff api: add get_price
fixup ddf1e1f fixup! api: add get_price
pick 87584b9 api: add list_items
update-ref refs/heads/feat/api
pick 42dfa4c ui: render price
pick 576a711 ui: render list
update-ref refs/heads/feat/ui
pick 87455ba docs: describe pricing
Successfully rebased and updated refs/heads/feat/docs.
Updated the following refs with --update-refs:
    refs/heads/feat/api
    refs/heads/feat/ui
* 6824a87 (HEAD -> feat/docs) docs: describe pricing
* 76f2b7a (feat/ui) ui: render list
* c08e7a1 ui: render price
* b46d23a (feat/api) api: add list_items
* 7e3a228 api: add get_price
| * c6a0e25 (main) main: add tax()
|/  
* 6b188b4 main: add lib.sh
* 2a401c6 init: README
Three things to notice:

--autosquash moved the fixup next to its target. --update-refs put each update-ref line after the branch’s last commit, so feat/api now includes the fix.
--keep-base kept the fork point at 6b188b4. main is still off to the side, and each pull request’s diff against its base changed only where you meant it to.
The update-ref lines are ordinary todo commands. You can move them, delete one (that branch then stays where it was), or add one (update-ref refs/heads/feat/ui-split) to cut a new branch boundary in the middle of the stack.

Verify what changed. --creation-factor raises the threshold for pairing commits, which helps when a commit is tiny and the fix is a large share of it:
git range-diff --creation-factor=95 "$(git merge-base main feat/docs)" feat/docs@{1} feat/docs
1:  f2f0cff ! 1:  7e3a228 api: add get_price
    @@ Commit message
     
      ## api.conf (new) ##
     @@
    -+timeout=3
    ++timeout=30
     
      ## api.sh (new) ##
     @@
2:  87584b9 = 2:  b46d23a api: add list_items
3:  42dfa4c = 3:  c08e7a1 ui: render price
4:  576a711 = 4:  76f2b7a ui: render list
5:  87455ba = 5:  6824a87 docs: describe pricing
6:  ddf1e1f < -:  ------- fixup! api: add get_price
One ! (changed) commit, four =, and the fixup gone: exactly the intended edit.


Case 4: Make it the default
git config rebase.updateRefs true          # this repo; use --global for all repos
git rebase main
git config --show-origin rebase.updateRefs
Successfully rebased and updated refs/heads/feat/docs.
Updated the following refs with --update-refs:
    refs/heads/feat/api
    refs/heads/feat/ui
file:.git/config    true
git rebase --no-update-refs main opts out for one run. That is useful when you deliberately want to fork a copy of a stack and leave the original branches alone.


Case 5: Publish the moved stack in one atomic push
A rewritten stack needs a force push. Push all the branches together, so a reviewer never sees feat/ui rebased while feat/api is still old:
git init -q --bare ../origin.git && git remote add origin ../origin.git
git push -q origin main feat/api feat/ui feat/docs      # the "already published" state
git rebase -q --update-refs main
git push --force-with-lease --atomic origin feat/api feat/ui feat/docs
To ../origin.git
 + 87584b9...49a9b11 feat/api -> feat/api (forced update)
 + 87455ba...1861481 feat/docs -> feat/docs (forced update)
 + 576a711...f0527d0 feat/ui -> feat/ui (forced update)
--force-with-lease refuses to overwrite a branch someone else pushed to since your last fetch. --atomic makes the server accept all three ref updates or none of them.


Case 6: The bottom branch was squash-merged
feat/api lands on main as one squash commit. Its original commits will never appear on main, so git rebase main would try to replay them and conflict, or produce empty commits. Cut them off explicitly with --onto:
git switch -q main && git merge -q --squash feat/api && git commit -q -m "api: get_price and list_items (#41)"
git switch -q feat/docs
git rebase --update-refs --onto main feat/api feat/docs
git log --graph --oneline --decorate --all
Successfully rebased and updated refs/heads/feat/docs.
Updated the following refs with --update-refs:
    refs/heads/feat/ui
* 49a9441 (HEAD -> feat/docs) docs: describe pricing
* 9faa213 (feat/ui) ui: render list
* cb443ba ui: render price
* a49d524 (main) api: get_price and list_items (#41)
* c6a0e25 main: add tax()
| * 87584b9 (feat/api) api: add list_items
| * f2f0cff api: add get_price
|/  
* 6b188b4 main: add lib.sh
* 2a401c6 init: README
The range feat/api..feat/docs excludes the squashed commits. feat/ui moves because it points inside the range. feat/api does not, because it is the boundary. Delete it (git branch -D feat/api) and retarget the feat/ui pull request to main.

title: update-refs and keep-base
text:
The trap
Rebasing from the middle of the stack, or from a worktree, silently strands branches.
--update-refs only touches refs that point into the commits being rewritten. Rebase feat/ui and its descendant feat/docs is not in that range:
git switch -q feat/ui
git rebase --update-refs main
git log --graph --oneline --decorate --all
Successfully rebased and updated refs/heads/feat/ui.
Updated the following refs with --update-refs:
    refs/heads/feat/api
* f0527d0 (HEAD -> feat/ui) ui: render list
* 55affa4 ui: render price
* 49a9b11 (feat/api) api: add list_items
* 58ab280 api: add get_price
* c6a0e25 (main) main: add tax()
| * 87455ba (feat/docs) docs: describe pricing
| * 576a711 ui: render list
| * 42dfa4c ui: render price
| * 87584b9 api: add list_items
| * f2f0cff api: add get_price
|/  
* 6b188b4 main: add lib.sh
* 2a401c6 init: README
The second failure is quieter. A branch that is checked out in another worktree is skipped, and a non-interactive rebase gives no warning at all:
git worktree add -q ../wt-ui feat/ui
GIT_SEQUENCE_EDITOR=cat git rebase -i --update-refs main | grep -E 'update-ref|checked out'
update-ref refs/heads/feat/api
# Ref refs/heads/feat/ui checked out at '/tmp/vcs/wt-ui'
The run then reports Updated the following refs with --update-refs: refs/heads/feat/api only. feat/ui stays on the old commits, and the next git push from that worktree re-publishes the stale stack.
Recovery is cheap, because nothing is lost. Run git switch feat/docs && git rebase --update-refs main from the true top. For a worktree, remove it or detach its HEAD first (git -C ../wt-ui switch --detach), then rebase again.

title: update-refs and keep-base
text:
The boring rule

Turn on rebase.updateRefs. Rebase stacks only from the top branch, with no stack branch checked out in another worktree. Use --keep-base when you are tidying and plain <upstream> when you are catching up. Prove every rewrite with git range-diff, and publish with git push --force-with-lease --atomic naming every branch in the stack.

title: update-refs and keep-base
text:
Try this

Build the stack, then run git rebase -i --keep-base --update-refs main and reword ui: render price. Use git range-diff to confirm that only that commit shows !, and only in its message.
In the todo list, add update-ref refs/heads/feat/ui-price right after pick … ui: render price. Check that the new branch exists after the rebase and points at the rewritten commit.
Start a rebase that conflicts (edit ui.sh on main first), then git rebase --abort. Confirm with git log --oneline -1 feat/api that no stack branch moved: the refs only update when the rebase completes.
Reproduce the worktree trap, then fix it with git -C ../wt-ui switch --detach and a fresh rebase from feat/docs.
Set git config --global rebase.updateRefs true and rebase.autoSquash true. For a week, write review fixes as git commit --fixup=<sha> and land them with one git rebase -i --keep-base <base>.

title: Interactive Rebase from the Merge-Base
text:
Thesis
git rebase -i main rebases onto main’s tip. Sometimes you only want to edit commits unique to your branch since it forked — that set is merge-base(HEAD, main)..HEAD. Starting the todo from the merge-base keeps upstream commits out of your squash/reword list.

title: Interactive Rebase from the Merge-Base
text:
Mental model
  o----o----o  main
   \
    a----b----c  feature
  merge-base = o
  rebase -i $(git merge-base HEAD main)  → todo: a, b, c

title: Interactive Rebase from the Merge-Base
text:
Worked examples
Lab output:
main=40c708e feature=3541637
merge-base=6a07c0a
--- log feature ---
3541637 f3
bb6b435 f2
261afe9 f1
--- after: git rebase -i $(git merge-base HEAD main) would open todo for: ---
261afe9 f1
bb6b435 f2
3541637 f3

title: Interactive Rebase from the Merge-Base
text:
Trap
Confusing this with git rebase --onto. See 07-rebase-onto.qmd for --onto.

title: Interactive Rebase from the Merge-Base
text:
Boring rule
When cleaning a feature branch before review, open the interactive todo from the merge-base so you only see your commits.

title: Interactive Rebase from the Merge-Base
text:
Try this

Add a conflicting upstream commit and finish the rebase.
Compare git rebase -i main todo vs merge-base todo after main moves.

title: Theory
text:
Theory: Cherry-Pick and Revert are Patches with New Hashes
Both operations take a diff (commit vs its parent, or the inverse) and apply it to HEAD, writing a new commit. They do not move the original node.

title: Theory
text:
Invariants

Cherry-pick(C) ≈ apply diff(parent(C), C) onto HEAD.
Revert(C) ≈ apply diff(C, parent(C)) onto HEAD (the inverse patch).
The original commit remains reachable if any name still points at it.
Revert of a merge needs -m to choose which parent is the mainline; Git then considers those changes “already merged” for future merges.
-x records cherry picked from in the message; it does not link objects.

 cherry-pick D onto main          revert C on main

 feat  A ← B ← C ← D ← E          A ← B ← C ← R
 main  A ← B ← C                  R undoes C; C stays
 after A ← B ← C ← D'

title: Theory
text:
Why not reset on production
Reset moves a name backward. Clones that already have the old tip cannot fast-forward. Revert lets them fast-forward to a commit that cancels the bad one. That is the distributed-model consequence, not etiquette.

title: Theory
text:
What can break

Cherry-picking a merge without -m.
Reverting a merge then trying to merge the same feature again (Git thinks it is in).
Secrets: revert does not purge blobs from history.

title: Theory
text:
How to read this chapter
Cherry-pick, hotfixes, revert, emergencies; then ranges/-x, empty picks.

title: Cherry-Pick
text:
Cherry-Pick: Moving Commits Surgically
After this page you can copy one commit onto another branch without merging the whole feature.

title: Cherry-Pick
text:
Copy the patch, new hash
cd ~/desk/desk-api
git switch main
git cherry-pick <hash>
Git takes the diff of that commit against its parent, applies it onto HEAD, and writes a new commit. The new object has a new hash. Author is preserved; you are the committer.
 feat    A ← B ← C ← D ← E          pick D only
 main    A ← B ← C

 after   A ← B ← C ← D'             main   (D' ≈ patch of D, new hash)
 feat    A ← B ← C ← D ← E          unchanged
git log -1 --format=fuller

title: Cherry-Pick
text:
Several commits
git cherry-pick abc123 def456
git cherry-pick main~3..feat/ping-json
A range A..B is commits reachable from B excluding A. Oldest is applied first.

title: Cherry-Pick
text:
Conflicts
Same markers as merge. Then:
git add src/ping.py
git cherry-pick --continue
git cherry-pick --abort
git cherry-pick --skip
Same loop as rebase, one commit at a time.

title: Cherry-Pick
text:
Empty pick
If main already contains the change, Git says the pick is empty. --skip or --allow-empty.

title: Cherry-Pick
text:
What cherry-pick is for

A hotfix that lives on a release branch and also needs to be on main
A commit that landed on the wrong branch
Backporting a fix to an older release/* line

What it is a poor fit for: dragging a whole feature. Merge or rebase the branch instead so you get the whole chain and a honest graph.
Next page: hotfixes and backports as a desk scenario.

title: Hotfixes and Backports
text:
Deploying Hotfixes Without Merging Features
After this page you can land a one-commit fix on main and on a release branch without dragging unreleased work.

title: Hotfixes and Backports
text:
The situation
feat/big-refactor is half done. Production (main or release/1.x) needs a one-line fix that you already committed on the feature branch.
Merging the feature would ship unfinished work. Cherry-pick the fix commit only.
 feat/big-refactor   A ← B ← fix ← D ← E     (D,E not ready)
 main                A ← B

 cherry-pick fix     A ← B ← fix'            main
                     A ← B ← fix ← D ← E     feat  (untouched)
cd ~/desk/desk-api
git log feat/big-refactor --oneline -5
# copy the hash of the fix

git switch main
git cherry-pick <hash>

title: Hotfixes and Backports
text:
Release branch
git switch -c release/1.2 main   # or an existing release line
git cherry-pick <hash>
Now both lines have the fix, as two commits with different hashes and the same author.

title: Hotfixes and Backports
text:
Backport the other direction
The fix landed on main first. An older release still needs it:
git switch release/1.1
git cherry-pick <hash-on-main>
If the older tree cannot apply the patch (the surrounding code moved), resolve like a rebase conflict or rewrite the fix by hand and commit normally. Cherry-pick is a tool, not a guarantee.

title: Hotfixes and Backports
Hotfixes and Backports
text:
After the pick
Run whatever desk-api uses to check itself on Linux (python -c 'from src.ping import ping; print(ping())' is enough for the toy module). Then merge or push according to chapter 11. Do not merge feat/big-refactor until that feature is done.

title: Revert and Unmerge
text:
git revert and Unmerging Changes
After this page you can undo a published commit by adding a new commit, including a merge.

title: Revert and Unmerge
text:
Revert writes history forward
cd ~/desk/desk-api
git switch main
git revert HEAD --no-edit
git log --oneline -3
The bad commit is still in the graph. A new commit applies the inverse patch. Shared clones can fast-forward. This is the safe undo on main.
 reset --hard HEAD~1     (local only)     A ← B            main
                                          C still in reflog

 revert HEAD             (shared)         A ← B ← C ← R    main
                                          R undoes C; C remains
--no-edit keeps Git’s default message (Revert "…"). Edit with git revert HEAD if you need a fix: subject.

title: Revert and Unmerge
text:
Several commits
git revert --no-edit HEAD~2..HEAD
Reverts newest first (the range is exclusive on the left). Conflicts: git add and git revert --continue, or git revert --abort.

title: Revert and Unmerge
text:
Revert a merge commit
A merge has two parents. Git needs to know which parent is “the mainline” to diff against:
git revert -m 1 <merge-hash>
-m 1 means “keep first parent’s tree; undo what the merged branch brought in.” -m 2 is the other parent (almost never what you want on main).
After reverting a merge, Git considers that feature’s commits already merged. Cherry-picking them back later can no-op. To re-land the feature, revert the revert, or rebase the feature into new hashes.

title: Revert and Unmerge
text:
Revert vs reset vs restore








Goal
Command
History




Throw away uncommitted edits
git restore
Unchanged


Replace last unpublished commit
git commit --amend / reset
Rewritten


Undo a published commit
git revert
New commit



git reset --hard on shared main is a force-push incident. Revert instead.

title: Revert and Unmerge
text:
Un-merge without -m
If the merge was never pushed and is HEAD:
git reset --hard HEAD~1
That moves main to first parent and drops the merge commit from the branch name. Only on a lab clone or an unpublished branch. Chapter 7 is reset in full. The merge commit stays in the reflog (chapter 17) until it expires.

title: Production Emergency Scenarios
text:
Real Production Emergency Scenarios
After this page you have a short playbook for “production is wrong and Git is how we talk about it.”
Assume Linux, ~/desk/desk-api, and a main that is already on a remote. You are in a terminal, not a GUI.

title: Production Emergency Scenarios
section: 1. Bad commit is HEAD on main, already pulled by others
text:
1. Bad commit is HEAD on main, already pulled by others
git switch main
git pull --ff-only
git revert HEAD --no-edit
# run tests
git push

title: Production Emergency Scenarios
section: 2. Bad commit is in the middle of main
text:
2. Bad commit is in the middle of main
git log --oneline -20
git revert --no-edit <hash>
# tests
git push
If several commits are one logical change, revert the range newest-first, or revert the merge with -m 1.

title: Production Emergency Scenarios
section: 3. Fix exists on a feature branch, production cannot wait
text:
3. Fix exists on a feature branch, production cannot wait
git log feat/whatever --oneline
git switch main
git cherry-pick -x <fix-hash>
# tests
git push
Leave the feature branch as-is. The pick is a new hash on main.

title: Production Emergency Scenarios
text:
4. You committed a secret
git revert does not remove the secret from history; it only removes it from HEAD. Anyone who fetched still has the blob. Rotate the secret at the provider. History cleanup is chapter 20 (git filter-repo). For the next five minutes: revert or a follow-up commit that deletes the file, rotate, tell the team.

title: Production Emergency Scenarios
section: 5. Merge to main was wrong, merge commit is HEAD, not pushed
text:
5. Merge to main was wrong, merge commit is HEAD, not pushed
git reset --hard HEAD~1
If it was pushed, revert with -m 1 instead.

title: Production Emergency Scenarios
section: 6. You are not sure what main is
text:
6. You are not sure what main is
git status
git log --oneline --graph --decorate -15
git reflog -10
Status, graph, reflog. Then pick revert (shared) or reset (local only).
Write the team a one-line message: hash reverted, why, who is rotating secrets if any. Git is the record; the pager is the people.

title: Theory
text:
Theory: A Remote is Another Repository Plus a Nickname
origin is not special to Git. It is a default name for a URL. Fetch copies objects and updates remote-tracking refs. Push asks the other repository to move a name it owns.

title: Theory
text:
Invariants

git fetch does not move your main. It updates refs/remotes/origin/main.
git pull = fetch + merge or rebase of @{u} into HEAD.
Non-fast-forward push is rejected because it would drop commits the remote still names.
--force-with-lease succeeds only if the remote ref still matches what you last fetched.
Several remotes means several photographs of the same DAG, not several Git identities.

  laptop                         origin (bare or forge)
  refs/heads/main                refs/heads/main
  refs/remotes/origin/main  ◄──  (fetch updates this)
         │ push ──────────────────►  (moves theirs if fast-forward)

title: Theory
section: Why PRs are not Git objects
text:
Why PRs are not Git objects
A pull request is a forge row: “please integrate this ref into that ref,” plus comments and checks. The Git underneath is still fetch + merge/rebase/squash on the server.

title: Theory
text:
What can break

git pull on a dirty tree.
Force-push of main.
Two remotes with the same objects but different main (divergent policy).

title: Theory
text:
How to read this chapter
Fetch/pull/push, extra remotes, force-with-lease, PRs, two-clone lab; then upstream, refspecs, bundle, prune, fork vs clone.

title: Fetch, Pull, and Push
text:
Remote Mechanics: Fetch, Pull, Push
After this page you can talk to another Git repository on Linux without confusing fetch with pull.

title: Fetch, Pull, and Push
section: A remote is a named URL
text:
A remote is a named URL
cd ~/desk/desk-api
git remote add origin git@host:ada/desk-api.git
git remote -v
origin is a convention. The URL is SSH (chapter 2) or https://. For labs on one machine, a bare repo on disk is a valid remote:
 ~/desk/desk-api                         origin
 working tree + .git                     (bare) objects + refs
      │  git fetch    origin/main ──►    refs/heads/main
      │  git push     main ──────────►   refs/heads/main
      ▼
 refs/heads/main          refs/remotes/origin/main
git init --bare ~/desk/desk-api.git
git remote add origin ~/desk/desk-api.git
file:// and a path both work on Linux. Bare means no working tree — the shape a forge stores.

title: Fetch, Pull, and Push
text:
Fetch
git fetch origin
git fetch --all
git log --oneline --graph --decorate --all
Fetch downloads objects and updates remote-tracking names (origin/main). It does not move your main. Safe to run any time.

title: Fetch, Pull, and Push
text:
Push
git push -u origin main
-u sets upstream so later git push and git pull know the default. After that:
git push
git status
# Your branch is up to date with 'origin/main'
Push refuses if the remote has commits you do not. Fetch, integrate, push again.

title: Fetch, Pull, and Push
text:
Pull
git pull
Fetch plus integrate @{u} into HEAD. With pull.ff only (chapter 2), it fast-forwards or fails. git pull --rebase copies your local commits onto the updated upstream (chapter 9).
Prefer git fetch then look at git log --oneline main..origin/main before you integrate.

title: Fetch, Pull, and Push
text:
Tracking
git branch -vv
git rev-parse --abbrev-ref --symbolic-full-name '@{u}'
@{u} is the upstream of the current branch. git push -u is how it gets set.

title: Fetch, Pull, and Push
text:
Delete a remote branch
git push origin --delete feat/ping-json
Local delete is still git branch -d. The two are independent.

title: Multiple Remotes
text:
Understanding Multiple Remotes
After this page you can push the same desk-api history to two places.

title: Multiple Remotes
text:
Extra remotes are normal
cd ~/desk/desk-api
git remote add origin git@forgejo.home:ada/desk-api.git
git remote add github git@github.com:ada/desk-api.git
git remote -v
Fetch both:
git fetch --all
git branch -r
origin/main and github/main are separate photographs.
                    git push origin
                 ┌──────────────────►  Forgejo
 laptop desk-api ┤
                 └──────────────────►  GitHub
                    git push github

 refs/remotes/origin/main
 refs/remotes/github/main

title: Multiple Remotes
text:
Push to both
git push origin main
git push github main
A convenience:
git remote add all git@forgejo.home:ada/desk-api.git
git remote set-url --add --push all git@forgejo.home:ada/desk-api.git
git remote set-url --add --push all git@github.com:ada/desk-api.git
git push all main
One git push all updates both push URLs. Fetch still uses the first URL of that remote unless you add more fetch URLs. Many people just type two pushes.

title: Multiple Remotes
text:
Independence preview
Chapter 22 is lock-in. The Git-level move is this page: the objects live in every clone. Two remotes means a forge outage does not strand desk-api. Issues and CI still live on each forge; Git history does not.

title: Multiple Remotes
text:
Rename and remove
git remote rename origin forgejo
git remote remove github
Removing a remote deletes remote-tracking refs for it. Local branches stay.

title: Multiple Remotes
text:
origin on a USB disk
git init --bare /media/ada/stick/desk-api.git
git remote add stick /media/ada/stick/desk-api.git
git push -u stick main
Linux mounts the stick; Git sees a path. Same protocol family as ~/desk/desk-api.git.

title: Force Push
text:
Force Push Dangers
After this page you can update a remote after a rebase without clobbering someone else’s commits.

title: Force Push
text:
Why push refuses
You rebased feat/ping-json. Local hashes are new. The remote still has the old chain. A plain git push is a non-fast-forward and Git rejects it.
 origin/feat    A ← B ← C ← D ← E
 local feat     A ← B ← C ← G ← D' ← E'     (rebased onto new main)

 plain push     rejected (not a fast-forward)
 --force-with-lease
   if origin still at E  →  origin becomes E'
   if teammate added F   →  lease fails, fetch first

title: Force Push
text:
--force-with-lease
git push --force-with-lease origin feat/ping-json
Git checks that the remote ref still points at what you last fetched. If a teammate pushed in the meantime, the lease fails and you fetch again. That is the default force this book uses.

title: Force Push
text:
--force
git push --force origin feat/ping-json
Overwrites the remote ref even if it moved. Use on a branch only you own, and only when you meant to throw away the remote’s extra commits. Never a habit on main.

title: Force Push
text:
main
Do not force-push main on a shared remote. Revert instead (chapter 10). Forges often deny force on the default branch (chapter 31).

title: Force Push
section: Recover if you force-pushed by mistake
text:
Recover if you force-pushed by mistake
The old commits may still be on your laptop (git reflog) or another clone. Push them back:
git reflog
git push --force-with-lease origin <old-hash>:main   # only if you own this recovery
That is an emergency. Coordinate on chat first.

title: Force Push
text:
Lease plus fetch
Always:
git fetch origin
git log --oneline --graph --decorate HEAD origin/feat/ping-json
git push --force-with-lease
Look at the graph. Then push.

title: Pull Requests and Code Review
text:
Pull Requests, Code Review, and Handling Conflicts in Teams
After this page you can describe a pull request as Git operations plus a forge UI.

title: Pull Requests and Code Review
section: Git has no pull request object
text:
Git has no pull request object
A pull request (GitHub, Gitea, Forgejo, Bitbucket) or merge request (GitLab) is:

A branch you pushed (feat/ping-json)
A request that another branch (main) integrate it
Discussion, checks, and a button that runs merge, squash merge, or rebase merge on the server

Gerrit uses Change-Ids (chapter 27). SourceHut uses mailing lists (chapter 28). The Git underneath is still fetch + merge or rebase.
 origin/main     A ← B ← C
 origin/feat     A ← B ← C ← D ← E     ← you pushed this

 forge PR        "merge feat into main"
                 = merge, squash, or rebase on the server

title: Pull Requests and Code Review
text:
Local shape
git switch -c feat/ping-json
# commits
git push -u origin feat/ping-json
On the forge: open a PR from feat/ping-json into main. Reviewers fetch that branch:
git fetch origin feat/ping-json
git log --oneline main..origin/feat/ping-json
git switch -c review-ping origin/feat/ping-json

title: Pull Requests and Code Review
text:
Conflicts in a PR
The server’s merge is the same three-way merge as chapter 8. Resolve on Linux in your clone:
git fetch origin
git switch feat/ping-json
git rebase origin/main          # or: git merge origin/main
# fix, add, rebase --continue
git push --force-with-lease
The PR updates because the branch name moved.

title: Pull Requests and Code Review
text:
Review comments
Comments live on the forge. They are not Git objects. Closing a PR without merging leaves the branch on the remote until you delete it. Merging may delete the branch if the forge is set to.

title: Pull Requests and Code Review
text:
Hands-on next
The next page uses two directories on one Linux machine as “you” and “origin,” so you can push and fetch without an account.

title: Hands-On: Two Clones
text:

Simulate a remote with a bare repo on Linux. No forge account required.

title: Hands-On: Two Clones
text:
Origin (bare)
 ~/desk/desk-api          ~/desk/desk-api.git         ~/desk/desk-api-b
 (clone A, you)           (bare origin)               (clone B, teammate)
      │ push/fetch              ▲                      │ fetch/merge
      └─────────────────────────┴──────────────────────┘
mkdir -p ~/desk
git init --bare ~/desk/desk-api.git

title: Hands-On: Two Clones
text:
Your clone
If ~/desk/desk-api already has history:
cd ~/desk/desk-api
git remote remove origin 2>/dev/null || true
git remote add origin ~/desk/desk-api.git
git push -u origin main
If you are starting empty:
git clone ~/desk/desk-api.git ~/desk/desk-api
cd ~/desk/desk-api
# if clone was empty, make the chapter 3 tiny project first, then:
git push -u origin main

title: Hands-On: Two Clones
section: A second clone (teammate or your own review checkout)
text:
A second clone (teammate or your own review checkout)
git clone ~/desk/desk-api.git ~/desk/desk-api-b
cd ~/desk/desk-api-b
git log --oneline -3

title: Hands-On: Two Clones
section: Feature on A, fetch on B
text:
Feature on A, fetch on B
cd ~/desk/desk-api
git switch -c feat/readme-note
echo "Lab remote: ~/desk/desk-api.git" >> README.md
git add README.md
git commit -m "docs: note the local origin path"
git push -u origin feat/readme-note
cd ~/desk/desk-api-b
git fetch origin
git log --oneline main..origin/feat/readme-note
git merge origin/feat/readme-note
On a forge, that merge on B is the reviewer’s local check; the PR merge happens on the server into main. Here, integrate on A:
cd ~/desk/desk-api
git switch main
git merge --ff-only feat/readme-note
git push origin main
git branch -d feat/readme-note
git push origin --delete feat/readme-note
cd ~/desk/desk-api-b
git fetch origin
git switch main
git merge --ff-only origin/main

text:
Done when

~/desk/desk-api.git has main with the docs commit
Both clones’ main match git rev-parse HEAD
Feature branch is gone locally and on origin

You just did clone, branch, commit, push, fetch, and integrate. A pull-request button is that last integrate, with a UI. Next: stash, tags, and cleanup on a single clone.
