title: Theory
text:
Theory: Stash is Commits; a Tag is a Name Meant to Stay Put
git stash writes commit objects (index state + working-tree state) and points refs/stash at them. A lightweight tag is a ref. An annotated tag is an object (message, tagger, date) that then points at a commit.

title: Theory
text:
Invariants

Stash does not change HEAD’s commit; it makes the working tree match HEAD (plus options for untracked).
stash@{n} is reflog syntax on refs/stash.
Tags are not pushed by default (git push origin v1.0.0).
git clean deletes untracked files Git never hashed; there is no Git undo.
git describe finds the nearest reachable annotated tag and counts commits after it.

  stash push                     annotated tag

  HEAD C  (unchanged)            refs/tags/v0.1.0 → tag object → commit C
  WD    clean
  refs/stash → W  (WIP commit)
                parent C

title: Theory
text:
Why stash vs a branch
A branch is a name you can push and PR. A stash is local, easy to drop, easy to lose in stash clear. If the WIP will survive the afternoon, switch -c wip/… and commit.

title: Theory
text:
What can break

stash pop with conflicts (entry may still drop).
Moving a published tag (-f) while others have already fetched it.
git clean -f -x deleting ignored .env.

title: Theory
text:
How to read this chapter
Stash, tags, cleanup, lab; then stash branch, describe, archive.

title: Stash
text:
Stash Mechanics, Including Patch Stashes
After this page you can park uncommitted work, switch branches, and bring the work back.

title: Stash
section: A stash is a commit Git keeps on the side
text:
A stash is a commit Git keeps on the side
cd ~/desk/desk-api
echo "wip" >> README.md
git stash push -m "wip readme"
git status
git stash list
Working tree is clean. stash@{0} holds the diff. Switch branches, then:
 before stash                 after stash push

 working  dirty README        working  clean
 index    clean               index    clean
 HEAD     C                   HEAD     C
                              stash@{0}  ──► a pair of commits
                                           (index + working tree)
git stash pop
# or
git stash apply
pop applies and drops. apply applies and keeps the stash entry.

title: Stash
text:
Include untracked
git stash push -u -m "wip plus new files"
Without -u, untracked files stay in the way and can block a switch.

title: Stash
text:
Patch stash (-p)
git stash push -p -m "only the ping hunk"
Git offers hunks, same as git add -p. Stash the ones that are in the way; leave the rest in the working tree.

title: Stash
Stash
text:
Conflicts on apply
Markers appear. Add and continue as a normal working-tree conflict. The stash entry remains if you used apply; pop may still drop — prefer apply when you are unsure.

title: Stash
text:
Stash vs commit
A commit on a throwaway branch is easier to push and to recover. Stash is for “I must switch in the next ten seconds.” If the WIP will last, git switch -c wip/… and commit.

title: Tags
text:
Tags: Lightweight vs Annotated
After this page you can mark a commit as a release and push that name.

title: Tags
text:
Two kinds
cd ~/desk/desk-api
git tag v0.1.0                    # lightweight: a ref file
git tag -a v0.1.0 -m "desk-api 0.1.0"   # annotated: a tag object
Lightweight is a name pointing at a commit (like a branch that you do not move).
Annotated is a real object: message, tagger, date, optional signature (chapter 20). Releases should be annotated.
 lightweight                         annotated

 refs/tags/v0.1.0 ──► commit C       refs/tags/v0.1.0 ──► tag object
                                                              │
                                                              ▼
                                                         commit C
                                         tag object has message, tagger, date
If v0.1.0 already exists, Git refuses. git tag -f overwrites locally; moving a published tag surprises clones. Prefer v0.1.1.

title: Tags
text:
List and show
git tag
git tag -l 'v0.1.*'
git show v0.1.0

title: Tags
text:
Push
Tags are not pushed by default.
git push origin v0.1.0
git push origin --tags
--tags pushes all local tags. Prefer naming one tag for a release.

title: Tags
text:
Checkout
git switch --detach v0.1.0
Detached HEAD (chapter 1). Build or inspect, then git switch main. To develop from a tag: git switch -c hotfix/0.1.1 v0.1.0.

title: Tags
text:
Delete
git tag -d v0.1.0
git push origin --delete v0.1.0
Forges may still show a release page; that is forge metadata, not the Git tag.

title: Cleanup Commands
text:
Cleanup Commands
After this page you can delete merged branches, drop stashes, and remove untracked files on purpose.

title: Cleanup Commands
text:
Merged branches
cd ~/desk/desk-api
git switch main
git branch --merged
git branch -d feat/readme-note
--merged lists names whose tips are reachable from HEAD. -d refuses otherwise; -D deletes anyway.
Remote leftovers:
git fetch --prune
git branch -r
--prune deletes remote-tracking names that the remote no longer has.

title: Cleanup Commands
text:
Stashes
git stash list
git stash drop stash@{0}
git stash clear          # every stash
clear is permanent for the stash reflog’s practical purposes. Apply first if you need the diff.

title: Cleanup Commands
text:
Untracked files: git clean
git clean -n             # dry run
git clean -n -d          # include untracked directories
git clean -f -d          # delete
-n is mandatory the first time you run it on a tree you care about. -f is required (Git refuses to delete without it). -x also removes ignored files (build artifacts listed in .gitignore). That can delete .env if it is ignored — check -n -x first.
On Linux you can recover a deleted untracked file only from backups or the editor; Git never had a blob.

title: Cleanup Commands
text:
Garbage collection
git gc --aggressive --prune=now
Packs objects, drops unreachable ones older than the prune date. Rarely needed by hand; Git runs gc in the background. After a huge filter-repo (chapter 20) you will run it on purpose.

title: Cleanup Commands
text:
git fsck (peek)
git fsck --full
Reports dangling objects (often old amended commits) and real corruption. Dangling is normal. Missing blobs is chapter 21.

title: Hands-On: Stash and Switch
text:
Hands-On: Stash, Work on Another Branch, Apply
Park a README edit, fix a typo on main, come back, apply the stash.

title: Hands-On: Stash and Switch
text:
Park work
echo "TODO: metrics" >> README.md
git stash push -m "metrics todo"
git status
git stash list

title: Hands-On: Stash and Switch
text:
Other work
git switch -c fix/readme-typo
echo "typo-lab $(date -Iseconds)" >> README.md
git add README.md
git commit -m "docs: lab timestamp"
git switch main
git merge --ff-only fix/readme-typo
git branch -d fix/readme-typo

title: Hands-On: Stash and Switch
text:
Restore the stash
git stash list
git stash apply stash@{0}
cat README.md
git add README.md
git commit -m "docs: TODO for metrics"
git stash drop stash@{0}
git stash list
git status
If apply conflicted, resolve markers, git add, commit, then drop.

title: Hands-On: Stash and Switch
text:
Tag this point
git tag -a v0.1.0-lab -m "after stash lab"
git show v0.1.0-lab --quiet
git tag -d v0.1.0-lab

title: Theory
text:
Theory: Hooks are Local Policy; the Server is Real Policy
A hook is an executable Git runs by filename. Exit non-zero aborts the Git operation. Client hooks are not cloned (by design: a clone must not execute a stranger’s scripts). Therefore they are courtesy. Server pre-receive / update and CI are enforcement.

title: Theory
text:
Invariants

.git/hooks/pre-commit runs on this clone only, unless core.hooksPath points at a shared dir.
--no-verify skips client pre-commit and commit-msg.
The web editor on a forge never runs your laptop hooks.
core.hooksPath and init.templateDir are how a Linux user shares hooks without committing .git.

  git commit
     → pre-commit → commit-msg → object exists

  git push
     → pre-push (client) → network → pre-receive (server) → CI

title: Theory
text:
Why both
Client hooks fail in milliseconds (whitespace, WIP subject). CI fails in minutes (tests, secret scan) and cannot be skipped with --no-verify. Put the same checks in both; put policy on the server.

title: Theory
text:
What can break

Forgetting chmod +x.
Hooks that print to stdout and corrupt commit-msg files.
Assuming teammates have your hooks after git clone.

title: Theory
text:
How to read this chapter
Types, writing, templates vs CI, lab; then prepare-commit-msg, post-checkout/merge, --no-verify; then config-based hooks (Git 2.54+), which define several named hooks per event in any config file.

title: Hook Types
text:
Hook Types: Pre-Commit, Commit-Msg, Pre-Push
After this page you can name the client hooks this book uses and where they live on Linux.

title: Hook Types
section: A hook is a program Git runs
text:
A hook is a program Git runs
Executable files in .git/hooks/. Git looks at the filename. If pre-commit exists and is executable (chmod +x), Git runs it before it writes a commit object. Exit status 0 continues. Non-zero aborts.
 git commit
    │
    ▼
 pre-commit      exit ≠ 0 ──► abort, no object
    │ 0
    ▼
 commit-msg      exit ≠ 0 ──► abort, no object
    │ 0
    ▼
 commit object written, main slides forward

 git push
    │
    ▼
 pre-push        exit ≠ 0 ──► abort, remote unchanged
    │ 0
    ▼
 objects uploaded
Sample files are *.sample and are not run. Copy and chmod:
cd ~/desk/desk-api
ls .git/hooks
install -m 0755 .git/hooks/pre-commit.sample .git/hooks/pre-commit
# then edit; or write your own
install -m 0755 is the Linux way to copy and set the executable bit in one step.

title: Hook Types
text:
Client hooks you will write








Hook
When
Typical job




pre-commit
After you type git commit, before the object exists
Lint, block secrets, git diff --check


commit-msg
After you save the message
Conventional Commits pattern


pre-push
After you type git push, before objects upload
Tests, block WIP branches



There are more (prepare-commit-msg, post-commit, post-checkout). Start with these three.

title: Hook Types
text:
Server hooks (later)
A forge runs pre-receive / update / post-receive on the server when you push. Chapter 23 names them; chapter 31 uses them for policy. Your laptop hooks do not run on the server. A teammate can skip pre-commit with git commit --no-verify. Server hooks are the ones that actually enforce.

title: Hook Types
text:
Environment
Hooks run with a POSIX shell on Linux unless the shebang says otherwise. Always start with:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
Git sets GIT_DIR and runs with the working tree as cwd for client hooks (with nuances for worktrees, chapter 14). Print to stderr so you do not pollute commit output:
echo "pre-commit: running" >&2

title: Writing a Hook
text:
Writing Your First Hook
After this page you have a pre-commit that refuses a commit containing a tab-only whitespace error, and a commit-msg that checks a conventional subject.

title: Writing a Hook
text:
pre-commit
cat > ~/desk/desk-api/.git/hooks/pre-commit <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
git diff --cached --check
EOF
chmod +x ~/desk/desk-api/.git/hooks/pre-commit
git diff --cached --check flags leftover conflict markers and bad whitespace in the index. Exit status non-zero aborts the commit.
Try:
cd ~/desk/desk-api
printf 'bad \n' >> README.md    # trailing space
git add README.md
git commit -m "docs: trigger hook"
Fix the line, git add, commit again.

title: Writing a Hook
text:
commit-msg
Git passes the path to a temporary file that holds the message:
cat > ~/desk/desk-api/.git/hooks/commit-msg <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
file="$1"
subject="$(head -n1 "$file")"
if [[ "$subject" == WIP* ]]; then
  echo "commit-msg: subject cannot start with WIP" >&2
  exit 1
fi
EOF
chmod +x ~/desk/desk-api/.git/hooks/commit-msg
A stricter conventional check can wait until the team agrees on types. Start by blocking WIP.

title: Writing a Hook
text:
pre-push
Git passes the remote name and URL, and on stdin: local ref, local hash, remote ref, remote hash.
cat > ~/desk/desk-api/.git/hooks/pre-push <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
while read -r local_ref local_sha remote_ref remote_sha; do
  if [[ "$remote_ref" == refs/heads/main && "$local_sha" != "$remote_sha" ]]; then
    echo "pre-push: running tests before updating main" >&2
    # python -m pytest -q || exit 1
  fi
done
EOF
chmod +x ~/desk/desk-api/.git/hooks/pre-push
Uncomment the test command when desk-api has tests.

title: Writing a Hook
text:
--no-verify
git commit --no-verify -m "docs: skip hooks"
Emergency only. Treat it as breaking the seatbelt.

title: Hook Templates and CI
text:
Hook Templates: Sharing Hooks Across Repos
After this page you can point new repos at a shared hooks directory, and you know why CI still has to run on the server.

title: Hook Templates and CI
text:
.git/hooks is local
Cloning does not copy hooks (Git ignores them in the payload on purpose: a clone would otherwise execute someone else’s scripts). Each clone needs its own install step.

title: Hook Templates and CI
text:
core.hooksPath
mkdir -p ~/desk/git-hooks
# put pre-commit, commit-msg, … there, chmod +x
git config --global core.hooksPath ~/desk/git-hooks
Every repo on this Linux user account now runs those hooks. A repo can override with git config core.hooksPath .githooks (a directory inside the project that you do commit).
Project-local, committed:
mkdir -p ~/desk/desk-api/.githooks
# copy scripts, chmod +x, commit them
git config core.hooksPath .githooks
New clones still must run the git config once, or a Makefile / just recipe / bin/install-hooks script. Document that in README.md.

title: Hook Templates and CI
text:
init.templateDir
mkdir -p ~/desk/git-template/hooks
# scripts in that hooks dir
git config --global init.templateDir ~/desk/git-template
git init and git clone copy the template’s hooks/ into the new .git/hooks. Good for your laptop. Teammates need the same config.

title: Hook Templates and CI
section: CI is the hook you cannot skip
text:
CI is the hook you cannot skip
A pre-commit hook is a courtesy. git commit --no-verify and a forge’s web editor skip it. CI on the forge (chapter 32, GitHub Actions in Part VI) runs on the server after push. Put the same checks there: git diff --check, tests, secret scanning.
 laptop                         forge
 .git/hooks/pre-commit          pre-receive / CI job
    │ skippable                    │ not skippable
    ▼                              ▼
 git commit                     git push accepted
    │                              │
    └──────── git push ────────────┘
Client hooks catch mistakes in milliseconds on Linux. CI is the policy. Use both.

title: Hook Templates and CI
text:
Frameworks
pre-commit.com is a Python manager that installs a tiny .git/hooks/pre-commit and runs a YAML list of linters. Optional. Raw bash hooks in this chapter teach the mechanism; a framework is fine in production if the team already uses it.

title: Hands-On: A Pre-Commit Hook
text:
Hands-On: Create a Pre-Commit Hook
Install a pre-commit that runs git diff --cached --check on desk-api.

title: Hands-On: A Pre-Commit Hook
text:
Fail on purpose
printf 'trailing space \n' >> README.md
git add README.md
git commit -m "docs: should fail the hook"
Expect a non-zero exit and no new commit. git log -1 --oneline is unchanged.

title: Hands-On: A Pre-Commit Hook
text:
Pass
git restore --staged README.md
git restore README.md
echo "hooks lab" >> README.md
git add README.md
git commit -m "docs: hooks lab"
git status
Clean status, new commit. Remove the hook when you are done with the lab, or leave it — --check is a good default:
rm -f .git/hooks/pre-commit
Leave it in place if you want the check on this clone.

title: Config-based hooks: sharing hooks without copying files into .git/hooks
text:
Config-based hooks: sharing hooks without copying files into .git/hooks
After this page you can define Git hooks in configuration instead of as files named after events: several hooks per event, defined once in ~/.gitconfig and reused by every repository, switched off per repository, shipped with a project through include.path, and (for server-side events) run in parallel. You will also know the four places this goes wrong: an event-wide off switch that doesn’t switch everything off, an included hook file that runs whatever the last pull brought, older Git versions that ignore all of it silently, and parallel hooks that don’t overlap.

title: Config-based hooks: sharing hooks without copying files into .git/hooks
text:
Thesis
Until Git 2.54 a hook was a file: Git looked for an executable called pre-commit (or commit-msg, pre-push, …) in $GIT_DIR/hooks, or in core.hooksPath if set, and ran it. One event, one file. Sharing it meant copying it into every clone, or pointing every clone’s core.hooksPath at one directory and writing a dispatcher script to run several checks from it.
Git 2.54 (2026-04-20) added config-based hooks. A hook is now a named block in any Git config file:
[hook "no-todo"]
    event = pre-commit
    command = ~/bin/no-todo

hook.<name>.event is multi-valued: one hook can serve many events, and many hooks can serve one event.
hook.<name>.command is a path or a shell one-liner. The last value parsed wins.
hook.<name>.enabled = false switches one hook off, for example in one repository’s .git/config, while it stays defined in ~/.gitconfig.
Git 2.55 (2026-06-29) added hook.<name>.parallel and hook.jobs / hook.<event>.jobs to run several hooks for the same event at once, and the event-wide hook.<event>.enabled switch. The git-hook(1) manual is unchanged in 2.56.

What did not change: client-side hooks are still a local convenience. They are not cloned, --no-verify still skips them, and the real policy still lives on the server and in CI. Config-based hooks make the local half easier to share. They don’t make it enforceable.

title: Config-based hooks: sharing hooks without copying files into .git/hooks
text:
Mental model



Where Git 2.54+ finds the hooks for one event: config sources in parse order, the run list, and the switches


git commit
  └─ event "pre-commit"
       run list = configured hooks, in the order their hook.<name>.event lines were parsed
                  (system → global → local → worktree → -c; include.path files where included)
                + the traditional hook file (core.hooksPath, else .git/hooks), LAST
       every enabled hook runs; any non-zero exit aborts the commit








Key (scope)
Meaning
Since




hook.<name>.command
What to run: a path or a shell one-liner. Last value wins
2.54


hook.<name>.event
Which event(s) run it. Multi-valued; an empty value resets the list
2.54


hook.<name>.enabled
false switches this hook off without deleting it
2.54


hook.<event>.enabled
false switches off the configured hooks for that event (see Case 2)
2.55


hook.<name>.parallel
true declares this hook safe to run concurrently with the others
2.55


hook.jobs, hook.<event>.jobs
How many hooks may run at once (-1 = CPU count). Default 1
2.55


git hook list [--show-scope] <event>
Print the run list for an event, with the config scope of each hook
2.54


git hook run [-j N] <event> [-- args]
Run an event’s hooks by hand, the way Git would
2.36 (config hooks 2.54, -j 2.55)



A <name> must not be an event name: hook.pre-commit.command is a fatal error, because hook.pre-commit.enabled and hook.pre-commit.jobs already mean “the event” (git-config(1), hook.<friendly-name>.event).

title: Config-based hooks: sharing hooks without copying files into .git/hooks
text:
Worked examples (Cases)
Run on Debian 13 (Linux 6.12) with Git 2.56.0, the current release (2026-09-28), built from the release tarball in user space. The box’s distribution Git is 2.47.3, and Case 4 uses it on purpose. Every listing below was run, and every output block is pasted from the run.
Source this file first. It keeps your own ~/.gitconfig out of the way by pointing “global” at a throwaway file, so Case 1 can write to it safely:
# env.sh — source this so your hashes match the transcripts (needs git 2.55+)
export GIT_AUTHOR_NAME="Dev" GIT_AUTHOR_EMAIL="dev@example.com"
export GIT_COMMITTER_NAME="Dev" GIT_COMMITTER_EMAIL="dev@example.com"
export GIT_AUTHOR_DATE="2026-10-01T09:00:00Z" GIT_COMMITTER_DATE="2026-10-01T09:00:00Z"
export GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL=/tmp/hooklab/global.gitconfig GIT_CONFIG_NOSYSTEM=1
export GIT_CONFIG_COUNT=1 GIT_CONFIG_KEY_0=init.defaultBranch GIT_CONFIG_VALUE_0=main
Run the cases in order; they share /tmp/hooklab.

Case 1: Two hooks on one event, defined once for every repository
Two small checks, no-todo and no-big, live in ~/bin-style scripts and are registered in the global config. The repository has no hook files at all:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# lab-01-one-event-two-hooks.sh — two named hooks on pre-commit, defined in config, no files in .git/hooks
set -euo pipefail
rm -rf /tmp/hooklab && mkdir -p /tmp/hooklab/bin && cd /tmp/hooklab
: > global.gitconfig
cat > bin/no-todo <<'SH'
#!/bin/sh
# bin/no-todo — refuse staged lines that add "TODO"
if git diff --cached -U0 | grep -q '^+.*TODO'; then
  echo "no-todo: staged change adds a TODO" >&2; exit 1
fi
echo "no-todo: ok"
SH
cat > bin/no-big <<'SH'
#!/bin/sh
# bin/no-big — refuse staged files over 1 MiB
git diff --cached --name-only -z | xargs -0 -r -I{} sh -c \
  'test $(wc -c < "{}") -le 1048576 || { echo "no-big: {} is over 1 MiB" >&2; exit 1; }' || exit 1
echo "no-big: ok"
SH
chmod +x bin/*
git config set --global hook.no-todo.command /tmp/hooklab/bin/no-todo
git config set --global --append hook.no-todo.event pre-commit
git config set --global hook.no-big.command /tmp/hooklab/bin/no-big
git config set --global --append hook.no-big.event pre-commit
git init -q repo && cd repo
ls .git/hooks | grep -v '\.sample$' || echo "(no active hook files in .git/hooks)"
git hook list --show-scope pre-commit
echo 'print("hi")' > app.py && git add app.py
git commit -qm "add app" && git log --oneline
echo '# TODO: remove' >> app.py && git add app.py
git commit -qm "add todo" || echo "commit refused, exit $?"
(no active hook files in .git/hooks)
global  no-todo
global  no-big
no-todo: ok
no-big: ok
f652878 add app
no-todo: staged change adds a TODO
no-big: ok
commit refused, exit 1
Three things to read off this:

.git/hooks has only the .sample files git init copies in. The hooks come entirely from config, and git hook list --show-scope says from which scope.
On the refused commit both hooks ran: no-big: ok is printed after no-todo failed. Git runs every hook for the event and then refuses if any of them exited non-zero. Write each hook as if it were the only one, with its own clear message.
git config set --append is the Git 2.46+ spelling. With the older git config syntax, the equivalent of --append is --add; git config --global --append … is rejected as an unknown option.



Case 2: Order, the hooks directory, and the off switches
Add a traditional .git/hooks/pre-commit file to the same repository and try each way of turning hooks off:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# lab-02-order-and-off-switches.sh — config hooks + a .git/hooks file: order, disabling, --no-verify
set -euo pipefail
cd /tmp/hooklab/repo
git restore --staged app.py && git checkout -q -- app.py
printf '#!/bin/sh\necho "legacy .git/hooks/pre-commit"\n' > .git/hooks/pre-commit
chmod +x .git/hooks/pre-commit
git hook list --show-scope pre-commit
echo "--- run the event by hand"
git hook run pre-commit
echo "--- this repo opts out of one global hook"
git config set --local hook.no-big.enabled false
git hook list --show-scope pre-commit
echo "--- switch the whole event off for this repo"
git config set --local hook.pre-commit.enabled false
git hook run pre-commit; echo "exit $?"
git config unset --local hook.pre-commit.enabled
echo "--- --no-verify skips config hooks too"
echo '# TODO: later' >> app.py && git add app.py
git commit -q --no-verify -m "wip: todo (skipped hooks)" && git log --oneline -1
global  no-todo
global  no-big
hook from hookdir
--- run the event by hand
no-todo: ok
no-big: ok
legacy .git/hooks/pre-commit
--- this repo opts out of one global hook
global  no-todo
global  disabled    no-big
hook from hookdir
--- switch the whole event off for this repo
legacy .git/hooks/pre-commit
exit 0
--- --no-verify skips config hooks too
092fc2a wip: todo (skipped hooks)

The traditional hook is still honoured and runs last, after every configured hook. git hook list shows it as hook from hookdir. If core.hooksPath is set, that directory replaces .git/hooks as the “hookdir” and the configured hooks still run; on this box, setting core.hooksPath to a shared directory made git hook list pre-commit print no-todo, no-big, hook from hookdir, and the hookdir hook it ran was the shared one.
hook.no-big.enabled=false in .git/config turns off a hook defined in ~/.gitconfig for this repository only, and the list marks it disabled. This is the clean way to opt one repository out of a personal or company-wide hook.
hook.pre-commit.enabled=false switched off both configured hooks, but the .git/hooks/pre-commit file still ran. git-config(1) describes the event switch as “no hooks fire for that event”. In Git 2.56.0 the code that applies it (list_hooks_add_configured() in hook.c) marks only configured hooks as event-disabled; list_hooks_add_default() adds the hookdir hook afterwards without that check. Don’t rely on this switch to silence a legacy hook file; remove or rename the file.
--no-verify skipped the configured hooks as well as the file, and the TODO was committed. It skips pre-commit and commit-msg hooks of every kind.



Case 3: Shipping hook config with the project
Config is not cloned, any more than .git/hooks is. What a project can ship is a tracked config file that each developer chooses to include. The project keeps the hook script and its definition under .githooks/; a clone opts in once with include.path:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# lab-03-shared-from-repo.sh — ship hook config in the repo; each clone opts in with include.path
set -euo pipefail
cd /tmp/hooklab && rm -rf proj proj.git alice && : > global.gitconfig
git init -q proj && cd proj
mkdir .githooks
cat > .githooks/check-subject <<'SH'
#!/bin/sh
# .githooks/check-subject — commit-msg: subject line at most 50 characters
len=$(head -n1 "$1" | wc -c)
[ "$len" -le 51 ] || { echo "check-subject: subject is $((len-1)) chars (max 50)" >&2; exit 1; }
SH
chmod +x .githooks/check-subject
cat > .githooks/hooks.gitconfig <<'CFG'
# .githooks/hooks.gitconfig — reviewed hook definitions; clones opt in with include.path
[hook "check-subject"]
    event = commit-msg
    command = .githooks/check-subject
CFG
git add .githooks && git commit -qm "ship commit-msg policy" && cd ..
git clone -q --bare proj proj.git && git clone -q proj.git alice && cd alice
echo "--- fresh clone: nothing runs"
git hook list commit-msg || true
git config set --local include.path ../.githooks/hooks.gitconfig
echo "--- after opting in"
git hook list --show-scope commit-msg
git config list --show-origin | grep '^file:.*hook\.'
git commit -q --allow-empty -m "this subject line is far too long to pass the policy check" || echo "refused"
git commit -q --allow-empty -m "short subject" && git log --oneline -1
echo "--- from a subdirectory: the relative command still resolves"
mkdir -p src && cd src && git commit -q --allow-empty -m "from src/" && git log --oneline -1
--- fresh clone: nothing runs
warning: no hooks found for event 'commit-msg'
--- after opting in
local   check-subject
file:.git/../.githooks/hooks.gitconfig  hook.check-subject.event=commit-msg
file:.git/../.githooks/hooks.gitconfig  hook.check-subject.command=.githooks/check-subject
check-subject: subject is 58 chars (max 50)
refused
7831542 short subject
--- from a subdirectory: the relative command still resolves
1c40431 from src/

A fresh clone runs nothing. Opting in is one git config set --local include.path ../.githooks/hooks.gitconfig; the path is relative to the directory of the including file, .git/, which is why --show-origin prints .git/../.githooks/hooks.gitconfig.
git hook list --show-scope reports an included hook under the scope of the file that included it: local.
Hooks run from the top of the working tree (githooks(5)), so command = .githooks/check-subject works from src/ too.

Compared with core.hooksPath=.githooks, this keeps the project’s hooks and your own global ones, needs no dispatcher script, and lets a developer disable one project hook with hook.<name>.enabled=false without editing tracked files.


Case 4: The teammate on an older Git
Same clone, same policy, two Git versions:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# lab-04-old-git.sh — the same clone, committed with an older Git: config hooks silently do nothing
set -uo pipefail
cd /tmp/hooklab/alice
for g in git /usr/bin/git; do
  echo "--- $($g --version)"
  $g hook list commit-msg 2>&1 | head -1
  $g commit -q --allow-empty -m "a subject line that is much longer than fifty characters" \
    && { echo "commit accepted: $($g log -1 --format=%s)"; $g reset -q --soft HEAD~1; } \
    || echo "commit refused"
done
--- git version 2.56.0
check-subject
check-subject: subject is 56 chars (max 50)
commit refused
--- git version 2.47.3
error: unknown subcommand: `list'
commit accepted: a subject line that is much longer than fifty characters
Git 2.47.3 has no idea what hook.check-subject.* means, and unknown config keys are not an error in Git, so the over-long subject was accepted without a word. Git 2.47.3 does have git hook run (it dates from 2.36), but not git hook list. That is the safest single check to put in a setup script: if git hook list commit-msg fails, the developer’s hooks are not running. Stating “requires Git 2.54+” in the contributing guide matters more than usual here, because the failure is silent.


Case 5: An included hook runs whatever the last pull brought
include.path to a tracked file, like core.hooksPath to a tracked directory, means “run the version of these files that is checked out right now”. Another contributor changes the hook script, the change is merged, Alice pulls:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# lab-05-trust-on-pull.sh — an included hook file runs whatever the last pull brought
set -euo pipefail
cd /tmp/hooklab && rm -rf mallory
git clone -q proj.git mallory && cd mallory
cat > .githooks/check-subject <<'SH'
#!/bin/sh
# .githooks/check-subject — (changed upstream)
echo "check-subject: this line arrived with the last pull and runs as $(id -un)" >&2
SH
git commit -qam "tweak subject check" && git push -q origin main
cd ../alice && git pull -q --rebase origin main
echo "--- review what the pull changed under .githooks before the next commit"
git diff --stat ORIG_HEAD HEAD -- .githooks
git commit -q --allow-empty -m "next commit"
--- review what the pull changed under .githooks before the next commit
 .githooks/check-subject | 5 ++---
 1 file changed, 2 insertions(+), 3 deletions(-)
check-subject: this line arrived with the last pull and runs as box
The new script ran on Alice’s next commit, under her user, with her credentials and SSH agent in reach. Nothing asked. This is not a Git bug; it is what opting in to a tracked hook means, and it is the reason git clone never runs hooks in the first place. Treat .githooks/ like CI workflow files:

Protect the path with code-owner review on the server (a CODEOWNERS rule for /.githooks/) so changes to it need a named reviewer.
After a pull, check git diff --stat ORIG_HEAD HEAD -- .githooks (as above) or git log -p ORIG_HEAD..HEAD -- .githooks before your next commit.
Point command at something that cannot change under you when it matters: a tool installed from a package with a pinned version, rather than a script in the working tree.



Case 6: Parallel hooks on the server
Parallelism is for slow, independent hooks such as notifications after a push. Commit-time hooks always run one at a time: git-hook(1) lists applypatch-msg, pre-commit, prepare-commit-msg, commit-msg, post-commit, post-checkout and push-to-checkout as always serial, because they share the index, working tree or message file. post-receive on a bare repository is a good candidate. Two hooks each sleep one second to stand in for a slow webhook; the push is timed:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# lab-06-parallel-post-receive.sh — two slow server-side hooks: serial vs hook.<event>.jobs
set -euo pipefail
cd /tmp/hooklab && rm -rf srv.git dev && : > global.gitconfig
git init -q --bare srv.git
cat > notify <<'SH'
#!/bin/sh
# notify — post-receive: read the first "<old> <new> <ref>" line, then a slow "webhook"
read -r old new ref
start=$(date +%s%N); sleep 1
echo "$1: $ref, slow part began at +$(( (start - $(cat /tmp/hooklab/t0)) / 1000000 )) ms"
SH
cat > notify-drain <<'SH'
#!/bin/sh
# notify-drain — same, but read ALL of stdin (to EOF) before the slow part
refs=$(cat)
start=$(date +%s%N); sleep 1
echo "$1: slow part began at +$(( (start - $(cat /tmp/hooklab/t0)) / 1000000 )) ms"
SH
chmod +x notify notify-drain
git -C srv.git config set hook.chat.command "/tmp/hooklab/notify chat"
git -C srv.git config set --append hook.chat.event post-receive
git -C srv.git config set hook.ci.command "/tmp/hooklab/notify ci"
git -C srv.git config set --append hook.ci.event post-receive
git init -q dev && cd dev && git remote add origin ../srv.git
push() { git commit -q --allow-empty -m "$1"; date +%s%N > /tmp/hooklab/t0
         s=$(date +%s%N); git push -q origin main 2>&1 | sed 's/^remote: /  remote: /; s/ *$//'
         echo "  push took $(( ($(date +%s%N) - s) / 1000000 )) ms"; }
echo "--- default: serial"; push one
git -C ../srv.git config set hook.post-receive.jobs 2
echo "--- jobs=2, but no hook declares parallel=true: still serial"; push two
git -C ../srv.git config set hook.chat.parallel true
git -C ../srv.git config set hook.ci.parallel true
echo "--- jobs=2 and both hooks parallel=true"; push three
git -C ../srv.git config set hook.chat.command "/tmp/hooklab/notify-drain chat"
git -C ../srv.git config set hook.ci.command "/tmp/hooklab/notify-drain ci"
echo "--- same, but each hook drains stdin to EOF first"; push four
--- default: serial
  remote: chat: refs/heads/main, slow part began at +12 ms
  remote: ci: refs/heads/main, slow part began at +1017 ms
  push took 2023 ms
--- jobs=2, but no hook declares parallel=true: still serial
  remote: chat: refs/heads/main, slow part began at +13 ms
  remote: ci: refs/heads/main, slow part began at +1017 ms
  push took 2023 ms
--- jobs=2 and both hooks parallel=true
  remote: chat: refs/heads/main, slow part began at +14 ms
  remote: ci: refs/heads/main, slow part began at +14 ms
  push took 1020 ms
--- same, but each hook drains stdin to EOF first
  remote: chat: slow part began at +1021 ms
  remote: ci: slow part began at +17 ms
  push took 2028 ms

Serial by default. ci starts about 1,000 ms after chat; the push takes 2 s.
hook.post-receive.jobs=2 alone changes nothing. Every configured hook for the event must also declare hook.<name>.parallel=true. One hook without it keeps the whole event serial. That is deliberate: the hook’s author, not the admin, says whether it is safe to run alongside others.
Both declared parallel: both start at +14 ms and the push takes 1 s.
The same hooks reading stdin to EOF first: the push is back to 2 s. ci starts at +17 ms, but chat doesn’t get end-of-file on its stdin until ci exits. While the hooks were running, /proc/<pid>/fd of the second hook process showed two extra pipe descriptors (fd 8 and 9) besides its own stdin and stdout. That is consistent with the second child inheriting the write end of the first child’s stdin pipe, which would hold that pipe open until the second hook exits. Whatever the exact cause, the effect on Git 2.56.0 is measurable: a parallel post-receive hook that reads all of stdin before doing its slow work gains nothing. Read the ref lines you need, then start the slow part, and measure on your own server before counting on the speed-up.

With jobs above 1, Git also merges hook stdout into stderr for pre-push so parallel output can be de-interleaved (git-config(1), hook.jobs). A pre-push hook that writes something meaningful to stdout behaves differently when run in parallel.

title: Config-based hooks: sharing hooks without copying files into .git/hooks
text:
The trap
Config-based hooks feel like policy, because they live in config next to everything else and can be set centrally in /etc/gitconfig or a tracked include. They are still courtesy. A teammate on Git 2.47 runs none of them and sees no warning (Case 4). --no-verify skips them all (Case 2). The event-wide off switch leaves a legacy hook file running (Case 2). An included hook runs whatever the last merge put into the working tree (Case 5). And jobs=4 on its own is a no-op until every hook declares parallel=true, and even then may not overlap (Case 6). If a rule must hold for every commit that reaches main, it belongs in a server-side check or a required CI job. The hook only gets it to the developer sooner.

title: Config-based hooks: sharing hooks without copying files into .git/hooks
text:
The boring rule

Define hooks as named hook.<name> blocks, one check per hook, and look at the result with git hook list --show-scope <event>. Share project hooks as a tracked .githooks/hooks.gitconfig that each clone includes on purpose, guarded by code-owner review. Opt a repository out with hook.<name>.enabled=false, and delete legacy .git/hooks files rather than relying on the event switch. Require Git 2.54+ and check it in setup. Run anything that must hold for everyone on the server, not in a hook.

title: Config-based hooks: sharing hooks without copying files into .git/hooks
text:
Try this

Move one hook you already use from .git/hooks/ into ~/.gitconfig as a hook.<name> block, and confirm with git hook list --show-scope <event> that it appears once, and not twice.
Give one hook two events (git config set --append hook.lint.event pre-push) and run git hook run pre-push -- origin https://example.invalid to see it fire without pushing.
In Case 3’s repository, set hook.check-subject.enabled=false in .git/config and confirm a long subject goes through, while .githooks/hooks.gitconfig stays unchanged.
Add a third post-receive hook to Case 6 without parallel=true. Predict the push time before you run it.
Write a scripts/setup.sh that fails with a clear message if git hook list commit-msg fails, and run it under the older Git on your machine if you have one.

title: Config-based hooks: sharing hooks without copying files into .git/hooks
text:
Sources

git-hook(1) (Git 2.56 manual, and the 2.54.0 version for what 2.54 already had: https://git-scm.com/docs/git-hook/2.54.0): config-defined hooks, list --show-scope, run -j, always-serial events, the WRAPPERS section: https://git-scm.com/docs/git-hook
git-config(1), hook.* keys (command, event, enabled, parallel, hook.jobs, hook.<event>.jobs): https://git-scm.com/docs/git-config
githooks(5): hook events, working directory, core.hooksPath: https://git-scm.com/docs/githooks
git-config(1), “Includes” (include.path, relative paths): https://git-scm.com/docs/git-config#_includes
Git 2.54.0 release notes (“Hook commands are now allowed to be defined (possibly centrally) in the configuration files”): https://github.com/git/git/blob/master/Documentation/RelNotes/2.54.0.adoc
Git 2.55.0 release notes (“Hook scripts defined via the configuration system can now be configured to run in parallel”): https://github.com/git/git/blob/master/Documentation/RelNotes/2.55.0.adoc
Git 2.56.0 source, hook.c (list_hooks(), list_hooks_add_configured(), get_hook_jobs()): https://github.com/git/git/blob/v2.56.0/hook.c

title: Theory
text:
Theory: Submodules Pin a Hash; Worktrees Share an Object Store
A submodule is a second repository whose current commit is recorded in the parent as a gitlink (mode 160000). A worktree is a second working directory for the same repository: one .git, several checkouts, one branch per worktree.

title: Theory
text:
Invariants

The superproject stores a URL (.gitmodules) and a gitlink hash, not the child’s files as blobs.
git clone of the parent does not fetch submodule objects unless --recurse-submodules / submodule update --init.
Two worktrees cannot check out the same branch (indexes would fight).
Worktree .git is a file pointing at the main repo’s worktrees/ metadata.

  submodule                         worktrees

  desk-api tree                     ~/desk-api        HEAD → main
    src/desk-lib → gitlink 9fce     ~/desk-api-hf     HEAD → hotfix
  desk-lib repo  A ← 9fce                 \              /
                                           shared objects/refs

title: Theory
text:
Why not always submodule
If two projects always change together, you are paying pin-and-update tax for a monorepo’s job. If they have separate release cycles, the pin is the feature.

title: Theory
text:
What can break

Committing in a submodule and forgetting to push it (parent points at a hash nobody has).
Detached HEAD in the submodule by default after update.
rm -rf a worktree directory without git worktree remove.

title: Theory
text:
How to read this chapter
Mechanics, worktrees, when to use which, lab; then foreach/sync, deinit, locks.

title: Submodules
text:
Submodule Mechanics: Add, Update, Clone
After this page you can attach another Git repository at a path and record which commit it should be.

title: Submodules
section: A submodule is a nested repository plus a gitlink
text:
A submodule is a nested repository plus a gitlink
desk-api might need a shared desk-lib history without merging the trees. A submodule stores a commit hash in the parent tree (a gitlink, mode 160000) and a URL in .gitmodules.
 desk-api  (superproject)
 ├── README.md
 ├── src/ping.py
 └── src/desk-lib/          gitlink 160000 → commit 9fceb02 of desk-lib
         └── (nested .git)

 desk-lib  (its own history)
 A ← B ← 9fceb02    ← the hash the parent pins
cd ~/desk/desk-api
git submodule add ~/desk/desk-lib src/desk-lib
git status
git commit -m "chore: add desk-lib submodule"
.gitmodules is a tracked file:
[submodule "src/desk-lib"]
    path = src/desk-lib
    url = /home/ada/desk/desk-lib
On Linux use an SSH URL for anything you will clone elsewhere (git@host:ada/desk-lib.git). A path only works on this machine.

title: Submodules
text:
Clone a superproject
git clone --recurse-submodules <url> desk-api
# or after a plain clone:
git submodule update --init --recursive
Without --recurse-submodules / update --init, the path exists as an empty directory.

title: Submodules
text:
Update the pin
cd src/desk-lib
git fetch
git switch main
git pull --ff-only
cd ../..
git add src/desk-lib
git commit -m "chore: bump desk-lib"
The parent records a new gitlink hash. Pulling the parent does not move the submodule until git submodule update.

title: Submodules
text:
Pitfalls

Committing in the submodule and forgetting to push it: the parent points at a hash nobody else can fetch.
Editing files in src/desk-lib while detached: git switch -c in the submodule first.
Nested submodules: --recursive on clone and update.

If the team is small and desk-lib changes with desk-api every day, a monorepo (chapter 15) or a copy may hurt less. Submodules shine when the nested project has its own release cycle.

title: Worktrees
text:
Git Worktrees: The Modern Alternative
After this page you can check out a second branch in a second directory that shares the same .git.

title: Worktrees
section: One object store, several working trees
text:
One object store, several working trees
cd ~/desk/desk-api
git worktree add ~/desk/desk-api-hotfix hotfix/timeout
Git creates ~/desk/desk-api-hotfix on a new branch hotfix/timeout (or an existing branch if you name one that is not already checked out). Both directories share objects and refs. git commit in the hotfix tree moves hotfix/timeout. main in the original tree is untouched.
 ~/desk/desk-api/                 ~/desk/desk-api-hotfix/
 working tree on main             working tree on hotfix/timeout
         \                           /
          \                         /
           └── shared .git ────────┘
               objects, refs, reflog, remotes
git worktree list

title: Worktrees
text:
Why not git clone again
A second clone duplicates objects. A worktree is cheap and sees the same remotes, stash, and reflog. You cannot check out the same branch in two worktrees; Git refuses so the two indexes cannot fight.

title: Worktrees
text:
Linux workflow
git fetch origin
git worktree add ~/desk/desk-api-pr origin/feat/ping-json
cd ~/desk/desk-api-pr
# review, run tests
cd ~/desk/desk-api
git worktree remove ~/desk/desk-api-pr
remove deletes the extra directory after the working tree is clean. git worktree prune cleans metadata if you rm -rf the directory by hand.

title: Worktrees
text:
Detached review
git worktree add --detach ~/desk/desk-api-tag v0.1.0
Inspect a tag without leaving your feature branch in the main directory.

title: Worktrees
text:
Hooks and GIT_DIR
Worktrees have .git as a file pointing at the main repo’s worktrees/… metadata. Hooks still run from core.hooksPath or the main .git/hooks. Scripts that assume .git/ is a directory should call git rev-parse --git-dir.

title: When to Use Which
text:
When to Use Which
After this page you can pick submodule, worktree, or neither for a desk problem.

title: When to Use Which
text:
Worktree
Use a worktree when one repository needs two checkouts: a hotfix while a feature is dirty, a PR review, a tag build. Same remotes, same hooks, cheap on Linux disk.

title: When to Use Which
text:
Submodule
Use a submodule when two repositories must stay separate histories, with the parent pinning a commit of the child: a shared library, a firmware blob, a docs site with its own release train.

title: When to Use Which
text:
Copy the files
If desk-lib is three Python files and only desk-api uses them, put them in desk-api. Submodule overhead is real.

title: When to Use Which
text:
Monorepo
If desk-web, desk-api, and desk-infra always change together, one repository with three directories may be simpler (chapter 15). Worktrees still apply (two branches of the monorepo). Submodules do not.

title: When to Use Which
text:
Extra clone
git clone to a second path is fine for a throwaway experiment you might delete with rm -rf. You duplicate objects until git gc. Worktree is cleaner for a second branch.

title: When to Use Which
text:
Extra remote
Two forges is remotes (chapter 11), not submodules. Push the same history twice.

title: When to Use Which
text:
Rule of thumb
Same project, two directories → worktree. Two projects, one pin → submodule. Two projects, always in lockstep → one repo.
 one repo, two checkouts     ──►  worktree
 two repos, pin a commit     ──►  submodule
 two repos, always together  ──►  one monorepo
 two forges, same history    ──►  extra remote

title: Hands-On: Submodule and Worktree
text:
Hands-On: A Repo with a Submodule and a Worktree
Two small Git repos on Linux, then a worktree of the parent.

title: Hands-On: Submodule and Worktree
text:
Child library
mkdir -p ~/desk/desk-lib
cd ~/desk/desk-lib
git init
echo "DESK_LIB=1" > version.txt
git add version.txt
git commit -m "chore: desk-lib version pin"

title: Hands-On: Submodule and Worktree
text:
Parent with submodule
cd ~/desk/desk-api
git submodule add ~/desk/desk-lib src/desk-lib
git status
git commit -m "chore: add desk-lib submodule"
ls src/desk-lib/version.txt

title: Hands-On: Submodule and Worktree
text:
Worktree of the parent
git worktree add ~/desk/desk-api-wt -b feat/wt-lab
cd ~/desk/desk-api-wt
git status
echo "worktree lab" >> README.md
git add README.md
git commit -m "docs: worktree lab"
cd ~/desk/desk-api
git log --oneline feat/wt-lab -1
main in ~/desk/desk-api does not have that commit until you merge.

title: Hands-On: Submodule and Worktree
text:
Cleanup
cd ~/desk/desk-api
git worktree remove ~/desk/desk-api-wt
git switch main
git merge --ff-only feat/wt-lab
git branch -d feat/wt-lab
Leave the submodule in place for later chapters, or remove it:
git rm src/desk-lib
git commit -m "chore: remove desk-lib submodule"
rm -rf ~/desk/desk-lib
Removing the submodule does not delete ~/desk/desk-lib unless you rm -rf it.

title: Hands-On: Submodule and Worktree
text:
Done when

git worktree list shows only the main tree
You know whether src/desk-lib is still a gitlink (git ls-files -s src/desk-lib shows mode 160000) or is gone
