title: Worktree Lifecycle for Parallel Work: add, prune, repair
text: Worktree Lifecycle for Parallel Work: add, prune, repair

title: Worktree Lifecycle for Parallel Work: add, prune, repair
text:
Thesis
A linked worktree is a second checkout of the same repository: one object database and one set of refs, but separate files, a separate index and a separate HEAD. That makes worktrees the cheapest way to run several lines of work side by side: a hotfix next to a feature, a throwaway build next to your editor, or several coding agents that must not overwrite each other’s files.
Creating worktrees is easy. What goes wrong is the end of their life. Delete the directory with rm -rf instead of git worktree remove and Git still thinks it exists. The branch stays “checked out” somewhere nobody can see, you cannot re-create the worktree at the same path, and you cannot delete the branch. Move the directory and Git loses track of it. Scripts that create one worktree per run pile up these dead entries until something fails.
This page walks the whole lifecycle on a real repository: create, inspect, break, prune, lock, move, repair. It ends with a throwaway-worktree script that cannot leak.
Everything below was run with git version 2.56.0. worktree list has shown prunable since Git 2.31, and --relative-paths needs 2.48 or later. Commit hashes in your run will differ.

title: Worktree Lifecycle for Parallel Work: add, prune, repair
text:
Mental model
 app/.git/                           ← the one repository
 ├── objects/, refs/                 ← shared by every worktree
 ├── HEAD, index                     ← main worktree's own
 └── worktrees/
     ├── app-auth/                   ← admin dir for ../app-auth
     │   ├── HEAD, index             ← that worktree's own
     │   ├── gitdir   ──────────────────►  /tmp/wt/app-auth/.git   (back-link)
     │   └── locked                  ← optional, holds the reason
     └── app-api/  ...

 app-auth/.git   (a file, not a directory)
     "gitdir: /tmp/wt/app/.git/worktrees/app-auth"   (forward link)







Fact
Consequence




Objects and refs are shared
A commit made in one worktree is immediately visible from all of them. No fetch or push between them


A branch can be checked out in only one worktree
git switch refuses with “already used by worktree”. Two agents can never share a branch by accident


Git links worktrees in both directions with absolute paths (by default)
Moving either the repository or the worktree breaks a link until git worktree repair


Deleting the directory does not delete the admin dir
The entry stays, marked prunable, until git worktree prune (or gc) removes it


gc prunes stale entries only after gc.worktreePruneExpire (default 3.months.ago)
Dead entries from scripts can linger for months


A locked worktree is never pruned
Use it for worktrees on removable or network storage

title: Worktree Lifecycle for Parallel Work: add, prune, repair
text:
Worked examples (Cases)
#!/bin/sh
# setup.sh — a tiny repository to practise worktrees on
set -eu
git init -q -b main app
cd app
git config user.name demo; git config user.email demo@example.com
echo "v1" > README; git add README; git commit -q -m "init"
mkdir -p /tmp/wt && cd /tmp/wt && sh setup.sh && cd app

Case 1: One worktree per line of work
git worktree add -b feat/auth ../app-auth
git worktree add -b feat/api ../app-api
git worktree list
git switch feat/auth
Preparing worktree (new branch 'feat/auth')
HEAD is now at 06fb4a0 init
Preparing worktree (new branch 'feat/api')
HEAD is now at 06fb4a0 init
/tmp/wt/app      06fb4a0 [main]
/tmp/wt/app-api  06fb4a0 [feat/api]
/tmp/wt/app-auth 06fb4a0 [feat/auth]
fatal: 'feat/auth' is already used by worktree at '/tmp/wt/app-auth'
The refusal is the feature. If you give each agent or terminal its own branch and its own worktree, they cannot write to each other’s files or move each other’s HEAD.
Work done in one worktree is visible in the main one straight away, because the refs are shared:
echo token > ../app-auth/auth.txt
git -C ../app-auth add auth.txt
git -C ../app-auth commit -q -m "auth: token"
git log --oneline feat/auth
ef29406 auth: token
06fb4a0 init


Case 2: rm -rf leaves a ghost
rm -rf ../app-api
git worktree list
git worktree add ../app-api feat/api
git branch -d feat/api
/tmp/wt/app      06fb4a0 [main]
/tmp/wt/app-api  06fb4a0 [feat/api] prunable
/tmp/wt/app-auth ef29406 [feat/auth]
Preparing worktree (checking out 'feat/api')
fatal: '../app-api' is a missing but already registered worktree;
use 'add -f' to override, or 'prune' or 'remove' to clear
error: cannot delete branch 'feat/api' used by worktree at '/tmp/wt/app-api'
Three symptoms with one cause: .git/worktrees/app-api/ still exists. prune removes it. Preview first:
git worktree prune -v --dry-run
git worktree prune -v
git worktree list
Removing worktrees/app-api: gitdir file points to non-existent location
Removing worktrees/app-api: gitdir file points to non-existent location
/tmp/wt/app      06fb4a0 [main]
/tmp/wt/app-auth ef29406 [feat/auth]
add -f would also “work”, but it re-registers over the ghost without telling you what the ghost was. Prune first, so you know what you are clearing.


Case 3: Lock what lives somewhere unreliable
A worktree on a USB disk or a network mount looks missing whenever that storage is unmounted, and prune would delete its entry. Lock it:
git worktree lock --reason "on USB disk" ../app-auth
git worktree list --porcelain
worktree /tmp/wt/app
HEAD 06fb4a058502ead9fe687ef46f0b713757558027
branch refs/heads/main

worktree /tmp/wt/app-auth
HEAD ef294063257176708420c85cab3c9f9655d74166
branch refs/heads/feat/auth
locked on USB disk

Use --porcelain in scripts: it is stable, one attribute per line, and includes the lock reason. A locked worktree survives prune even when its directory is gone:
git worktree add -q --lock --reason ci -b feat/l ../app-l
rm -rf ../app-l
git worktree prune -v
git worktree list
/tmp/wt/app     06fb4a0 [main]
/tmp/wt/app-l   06fb4a0 [feat/l] locked
/tmp/wt/app-rel 06fb4a0 [feat/rel]
/tmp/wt/moved   ef29406 [feat/auth]
(app-rel and moved come from the next two cases; this listing was taken at the end of the session.) Nothing was pruned. A lock is a promise that the directory will come back. Unlock it with git worktree unlock when that is no longer true.


Case 4: remove protects your work, mv breaks the link, repair fixes it
git worktree unlock ../app-auth
echo wip > ../app-auth/x
git worktree remove ../app-auth
fatal: '../app-auth' contains modified or untracked files, use --force to delete it
remove refuses to throw away uncommitted work. That safety check is exactly what rm -rf skips.
Now move the worktree with plain mv:
mv ../app-auth ../moved
git worktree list
git -C ../moved status --short
git worktree repair ../moved
git worktree list
cat ../moved/.git
cat .git/worktrees/app-auth/gitdir
/tmp/wt/app      06fb4a0 [main]
/tmp/wt/app-auth ef29406 [feat/auth] prunable
?? x
repair: gitdir incorrect: /tmp/wt/app/.git/worktrees/app-auth/gitdir
/tmp/wt/app   06fb4a0 [main]
/tmp/wt/moved ef29406 [feat/auth]
/tmp/wt/moved/.git
gitdir: /tmp/wt/app/.git/worktrees/app-auth
Inside ../moved, Git still works (the forward link is intact). From the main repository the worktree looks dead, and a prune at that moment would have deleted its entry. repair rewrote the back-link. Better still, move worktrees with git worktree move, which updates both links, and run repair from inside the main repository after moving the repository itself.


Case 5: Relative links for repositories that move
If the whole tree gets moved together (a container bind mount at a different path, a synced home directory), use relative links:
git worktree add --relative-paths -b feat/rel ../app-rel
cat ../app-rel/.git
cat .git/worktrees/app-rel/gitdir
git config --get extensions.relativeWorktrees
Preparing worktree (new branch 'feat/rel')
HEAD is now at 06fb4a0 init
gitdir: ../app/.git/worktrees/app-rel
../../../../app-rel/.git
true
Git turns on the repository extension extensions.relativeWorktrees, so Git versions older than 2.48 will refuse to open the repository. Set worktree.useRelativePaths=true to make it the default for new worktrees.


Case 6: A throwaway build that cannot leak
#!/bin/sh
# build-in-worktree.sh — build a ref in a throwaway worktree and always clean up
set -eu
ref=${1:-HEAD}
dir=$(mktemp -d)/build
git worktree add --detach --quiet "$dir" "$ref"
trap 'git worktree remove --force "$dir"; rmdir "$(dirname "$dir")"' EXIT
cd "$dir"
echo "building $(git rev-parse --short HEAD) in $dir"
cat README
for i in 1 2 3; do sh ../build-in-worktree.sh main; done
git worktree list
building 06fb4a0 in /tmp/tmp.7WzwdgzHCW/build
v1
building 06fb4a0 in /tmp/tmp.JUblBcUqaw/build
v1
building 06fb4a0 in /tmp/tmp.I9w49C4jYp/build
v1
/tmp/wt/app     06fb4a0 [main]
/tmp/wt/app-rel 06fb4a0 [feat/rel]
/tmp/wt/moved   ef29406 [feat/auth]
Three runs, zero leftovers. --detach avoids tying up a branch, and the EXIT trap removes the worktree through Git even when the build fails. Compare a script that cleans up with rm -rf:
d=$(mktemp -d)/b; git worktree add --detach -q "$d" main; rm -rf "$d"
git worktree list
git worktree prune -v
/tmp/wt/app           06fb4a0 [main]
/tmp/tmp.AkImVxMd26/b 06fb4a0 (detached HEAD) prunable
/tmp/wt/app-rel       06fb4a0 [feat/rel]
/tmp/wt/moved         ef29406 [feat/auth]
Removing worktrees/b: gitdir file points to non-existent location
Each such run leaves one more prunable entry, and gc will not clean them up for three months.

title: Worktree Lifecycle for Parallel Work: add, prune, repair
text:
The trap
A fixed worktree path plus one crash equals a script that never runs again. Many deploy scripts and agent harnesses use the same path every time (../build, ../agent-1). If one run is killed before its clean-up, the next run hits Case 2’s error at git worktree add (Git checks the path against registered entries) and stops. The usual “fix” is add -f, which hides the problem instead of finding out why the last run died.
With unique paths (mktemp) the failure is quieter but still there. Git names admin directories after the last path component, so the leftovers from Case 6’s rm -rf variant look like this:
for i in 1 2 3; do d=$(mktemp -d)/build; git worktree add --detach -q "$d" main; rm -rf "$d"; done
ls .git/worktrees
app-auth
app-l
app-rel
build
build1
build2
Nothing in those names tells you which run created them or whether anything still owns them. The fix is not a cleverer naming scheme. Remove worktrees with git worktree remove, and run git worktree prune at the start of any script or harness that creates worktrees, so each run begins from a known state.

title: Worktree Lifecycle for Parallel Work: add, prune, repair
text:
The boring rule

One task, one branch, one worktree. Create it with git worktree add, end it with git worktree remove (in a trap for scripts), move it with git worktree move, and lock anything on storage that comes and goes. Start every worktree-creating script with git worktree prune, and read state with git worktree list --porcelain, never by listing directories.

title: Worktree Lifecycle for Parallel Work: add, prune, repair
text:
Try this

Run Case 6 with the rm -rf variant ten times, then list .git/worktrees/. Run git worktree prune -v and count the lines.
Move the main repository (mv /tmp/wt/app /tmp/wt/app2), run git -C /tmp/wt/moved status, and then fix it with git worktree repair /tmp/wt/moved from inside app2.
Set gc.worktreePruneExpire=now, create and rm -rf a worktree, and confirm that git gc removes the entry.
Write a harness that starts three parallel jobs, each in its own --detach worktree, and prove with git worktree list --porcelain that none survive a kill of the harness (hint: trap INT and TERM as well as EXIT).

title: Worktree Lifecycle for Parallel Work: add, prune, repair
text:
Sources

git-worktree(1): add, list --porcelain, lock, move, prune, remove, repair, --relative-paths, worktree.useRelativePaths
git-config(1): gc.worktreePruneExpire, extensions.relativeWorktrees
git-gc(1): when gc prunes worktree metadata
Git release notes: 2.31 (prunable in worktree list), 2.48 (relative worktree paths)

title: Theory
text:
Theory: A Workflow is a Policy on Names, Not a Git Feature
Git Flow, GitHub Flow, and trunk-based development are agreements about which refs are long-lived, how long a feature name lives, and how main stays deployable. Git will merge whatever you ask. The workflow is which asks you allow.

title: Theory
text:
Invariants

Long-lived branches diverge; every extra one is a merge or rebase tax.
Short-lived feat/* off main (GitHub Flow topology) is independent of GitHub the product.
Trunk-based requires runtime flags or very small commits so main can take unfinished code.
Monorepo vs polyrepo is a repository boundary decision; worktrees still apply; submodules usually do not in a monorepo.

 Git Flow          main + develop + release/*     high ceremony
 GitHub Flow       main + short feat/*            this book’s desk default
 Trunk-based       main + flags                   high CI, tiny commits

title: Theory
text:
Why write it down
A strategy that exists only in chat is not enforceable. Chapter 31 (governance) is how a forge requires reviews and checks. This chapter is the graph you are asking Git to keep.

title: Theory
text:
What can break

Git Flow on a two-person desk-api (ceremony without versions in the wild).
Trunk-based without tests or flags.
A monorepo whose CI always builds everything.

title: Theory
text:
How to read this chapter
Git Flow, GitHub Flow/trunk, flags, mono/poly, choosing; then forking, stacked changes, release tags.

title: Git Flow
text:
Git Flow: The Classic Model
After this page you can name Git Flow’s long-lived branches and when the extra machinery is worth it.

title: Git Flow
text:
The picture
main          production; tagged releases
develop       next release; features merge here
feat/…        branched from develop, merged back (often --no-ff)
release/x.y   branched from develop, hotfixes, then merge to main *and* develop
hotfix/…      branched from main, merge to main *and* develop
main is always what is in production. develop is the integration line. Features never commit straight to main.
 main     A ─────────────── H1 ── v1.2
            \             ↗
 develop     B ← C ← D ← E ← F
                  \     ↗
 feat/invoices      X ← Y

title: Git Flow
text:
Commands (shape, not a plugin)
cd ~/desk/desk-api
git switch main
git switch -c develop
git switch -c feat/invoices develop
# … commits …
git switch develop
git merge --no-ff feat/invoices
git branch -d feat/invoices
--no-ff keeps a join node so git log --first-parent develop lists features.

title: Git Flow
text:
What it costs
Two long-lived branches that diverge. Every hotfix is merged twice. Release branches exist for weeks. For desk-api with one or two people, this is a lot of graph.

title: Git Flow
text:
What it buys
A support team that must ship 1.2.3 while develop already contains 2.0 work. Multiple versions in the wild. A release manager.
Use Git Flow when you actually have that. The original git-flow CLI is optional; the branch names are the model.
Chapter 31 is how a forge enforces this (protected main, required PRs). This page is the topology.

title: GitHub Flow and Trunk-Based
text:
GitHub Flow and Trunk-Based Development
After this page you can contrast a short-lived PR branch with committing to main behind flags.

title: GitHub Flow and Trunk-Based
text:
GitHub Flow (as a Git topology)
main          always deployable
feat/…        branched from main, opened as a PR, merged, deleted
There is no long-lived develop. Production is main (or a tag on it). CI on the PR is the gate.
 GitHub Flow

 main     A ← B ← C ← M          always deployable
               ↖     ↗
 feat/ping      D ← E            PR, then delete
git switch main
git pull --ff-only
git switch -c feat/ping-json
# commits, push, PR, merge on the forge
git switch main
git pull --ff-only
git branch -d feat/ping-json
The name “GitHub Flow” is a topology. You can do it on Forgejo or GitLab. The forge UI is a PR/MR; Git is short-lived branches off main.

title: GitHub Flow and Trunk-Based
text:
Trunk-based
Engineers commit to main (the trunk) at least daily, often several times a day. Features that are not ready stay dark behind a flag (next page). Release branches, if any, are cut from main and live days, not months.
 trunk-based

 main     A ← B ← C ← D ← E ← F     tiny commits, flags hide unfinished work
                     ╲
                      release/1.2   short-lived, if you even cut one
git switch main
# small commit
git pull --rebase
git push
Feature branches, when used, last hours. Rebase onto main before merge. --ff-only after a rebase is the usual integrate.

title: GitHub Flow and Trunk-Based
text:
Compare










Git Flow
GitHub Flow
Trunk-based




Long-lived lines
main + develop
main
main


Feature lifetime
Days–weeks
Hours–days
Hours or a flag


Release
release/* branch
Tag / deploy main
Tag / short release/*


Fits
Multi-version products
Web apps, desk tools
High-CI teams



desk-api in this book defaults to GitHub Flow topology: short feat/ branches, main deployable. Trunk-based is the same graph with even shorter branches.
Enforcement (required reviews, required checks) is chapter 31. The next page is flags, which make trunk-based possible.

title: Feature Flags
text:
Feature Flags and Deployment
After this page you can ship code to main that is not yet on for users.

title: Feature Flags
section: A flag is a runtime switch
text:
A flag is a runtime switch
The commit on main contains the new code. Production does not call it until a config value is true. That is how trunk-based teams merge daily without releasing half-built ping JSON.
 main     A ← B ← C ← flag-commit ← D     all on main

 production
   DESK_PING_JSON=0   →  old string path
   DESK_PING_JSON=1   →  JSON path

 Git shipped the code at flag-commit; the env var is the release.
Toy desk-api (Python, Linux):
# src/ping.py
import os

def ping():
    if os.environ.get("DESK_PING_JSON") == "1":
        return {"status": "ok"}
    return "ok"
export DESK_PING_JSON=1
python -c 'from src.ping import ping; print(ping())'
The flag lives in the environment, a file under /etc, or a later config service. Git holds the code; the flag holds the release.

title: Feature Flags
text:
What Git still does

Small commits on main (or short feat/ branches)
Revert the commit if the code is wrong (chapter 10)
The flag can stay off while you fix

A flag is not a substitute for git revert when the code crashes before the flag is read.

title: Feature Flags
text:
Cleanup
Every flag is debt. When DESK_PING_JSON is on everywhere, delete the old branch in the if and the env var. A follow-up commit: chore: remove ping JSON flag.

title: Feature Flags
text:
GitOps preview
Later parts deploy from Git. A flag in the application is still an env var on the cluster. A flag in Git (a value in desk-infra) is GitOps: changing the file and merging to main is the release. Same idea, different file.

title: Monorepos vs Polyrepos
text:
Monorepos vs Polyrepos
After this page you can place desk-web, desk-api, and desk-infra in one Git repository or three, on purpose.

title: Monorepos vs Polyrepos
text:
Polyrepo (this book’s default so far)
Three repositories, three histories, three remotes:
~/desk/desk-web
~/desk/desk-api
~/desk/desk-infra
Each clones, branches, and CI-runs on its own. A change that spans API and web is two pull requests. Versions of each other are documented (“web 1.2 needs api 1.4”) or ignored until something breaks.

title: Monorepos vs Polyrepos
text:
Monorepo
One repository:
~/desk/desk/
  web/
  api/
  infra/
One git clone, one main, one PR can touch all three. CI must learn to run only what changed, or it becomes slow. Sparse checkout and partial clone (chapter 19) exist because monorepos grow.

title: Monorepos vs Polyrepos
text:
Trade-offs









Monorepo
Polyrepo




Cross-project change
One PR
Several PRs, several versions


Access control
One repo (paths, CODEOWNERS)
Separate remotes, easier per-team ACLs


CI
Must be smart or it is slow
Simple per repo


Submodules
Rarely needed
Common for shared libs


Git scale
Packfiles, sparse, LFS
Each repo stays small

title: Monorepos vs Polyrepos
text:
Linux tooling
Path-based CI (git diff --name-only origin/main...HEAD | grep '^api/') is how a monorepo stays fast. CODEOWNERS (chapter 31) assigns api/ to one team. None of that requires GitHub; the files are in Git.

title: Monorepos vs Polyrepos
text:
This book
Labs keep three polyrepos so platform chapters can push desk-api to GitLab and Forgejo independently. If your real desk is a monorepo, the Git commands are the same; only the directory layout changes. Worktrees still apply. Submodules usually do not.

title: Choosing a Strategy
text:
Choosing a Strategy
After this page you can write a short default for desk-api and know where this book will enforce it later.

title: Choosing a Strategy
section: A default for this book’s desk
text:
A default for this book’s desk

Topology: GitHub Flow — short feat/ / fix/ branches off main, delete after integrate
Integrate: rebase the feature onto main, then --ff-only or a forge squash
main: always deployable; revert to undo (never rebase published main)
Repos: polyrepo (desk-web, desk-api, desk-infra) until a chapter says otherwise
Host: Linux; hooks and CI run there first

Write it in README.md or CONTRIBUTING.md in the repo. A strategy that exists only in someone’s head is not a strategy.

title: Choosing a Strategy
text:
When to change it

Multiple supported versions in production → Git Flow release branches
Several merges to main per engineer per day and strong tests → trunk-based plus flags
One PR always touches all three desks → consider a monorepo
A compliance officer needs a merge commit per change → --no-ff on main

title: Choosing a Strategy
text:
What Git will not decide
Git will merge whatever you ask. Forges add buttons (squash, rebase, merge). Chapter 31 is branch protection, code owners, required checks. This chapter is the agreement. The next part (power skills) is internals, reflog, bisect, and repair — the tools you want when the agreement meets a bad Tuesday.

title: The Forking Workflow
text:
The Forking Workflow
This page is a stub. Prose, labs, and diagrams come in a later writing pass.

title: The Forking Workflow
text:
Outline

Personal fork, upstream, PRs from forks.







Note



Core Git depth (Linux host). See content/_planning/SYLLABUS.md.

title: Stacked Changes: Stacked Pull Requests on GitHub
text: Stacked Changes: Stacked Pull Requests on GitHub

title: Stacked Changes: Stacked Pull Requests on GitHub
text:
Thesis
A large change is easier to review as a stack: a chain of small branches where each one builds on the one below it, and each one is reviewed as its own pull request. Git has always been able to build that chain. What used to be missing was the hosting side. Each pull request showed the whole chain’s diff, rules and CI ran against the wrong base, and merging the bottom PR left every PR above it pointing at a branch that no longer existed.
On 6 October 2026 GitHub made stacked pull requests generally available on every github.com plan, with support in GitHub Enterprise Server promised for a later release. A stack is now a first-class object on the server. GitHub knows the order, shows each layer’s diff against the layer below, evaluates rules as if every PR targeted the stack’s trunk, rebases the remaining layers when the bottom one merges, and lands any prefix of the stack in a single atomic operation. The local side is the gh stack extension for GitHub CLI.
The skill this page teaches is keeping three views of the stack in agreement: your branches, the stack metadata gh stack keeps beside them, and the stack object on GitHub. Most stack problems come from one of the three changing without the other two.
The transcripts use Git 2.47, GitHub CLI 2.46 and gh stack 0.2.1 (released 9 October 2026), on Linux. The gh stack documentation asks for GitHub CLI 2.0+ and Git 2.36+.

title: Stacked Changes: Stacked Pull Requests on GitHub
text:
Mental model
        trunk            layer 1              layer 2              layer 3
   main ◀───────── auth-model ◀──────── auth-route ◀──────── auth-tests
    │                 PR #41               PR #42               PR #43
    │              base: main         base: auth-model     base: auth-route
    │              diff: models.py    diff: routes.py      diff: test_routes.py
    │
    └── rules, required checks, CODEOWNERS, Actions: evaluated as if every PR targeted main

   merge PR #43  →  #41, #42, #43 land together (one atomic operation, bottom-up)
   merge PR #42  →  #41, #42 land; #43 stays open and is retargeted to main








Piece
Where it lives
What it knows




Branches
refs/heads/* in your clone and on GitHub
Commits only. Git has no idea they form a stack


Local stack metadata
.git/gh-stack (JSON)
Trunk, branch order, and the commit each layer was last based on


Stack object
GitHub
PR order, merge state, queue state. Drives the UI, merge box, webhooks and automatic rebases










Rule (GitHub docs)
Consequence




All branches in the same repository
No cross-fork stacks. Contributors without push access cannot stack


A stack must have a linear history between its branches to merge
After a lower layer or the trunk changes, run a cascading rebase (gh stack rebase, or Rebase stack in the merge box)


PRs merge bottom-up. Merging a PR merges every PR below it
“Merge” on the top PR lands the whole stack


Merge commit / squash / rebase all supported
Squash creates one commit per PR, so n PRs give n commits on the trunk


Merge queue
The stack enters as one merge group. Ejecting a PR also ejects every PR above it


Rebase without diff changes
Approvals are kept, even with “dismiss stale approvals” enabled


Bypass permissions
Only the lowest unmerged PR can be merged with a bypass

title: Stacked Changes: Stacked Pull Requests on GitHub
text:
Worked examples (Cases)
Install the extension once:
gh extension install github/gh-stack
gh stack --version
gh stack version 0.2.1
The lab below needs no GitHub repository and no network. A plain local repository called upstream stands in for GitHub: we commit to it directly to make “the trunk moved” or “a PR merged” happen, and desk-api is a clone of it. Nothing in the lab pushes. Source the setup file so your commit hashes match the transcripts:
# stack-setup.sh — source me: a local "GitHub" (upstream) and a clone of it (desk-api)
# upstream is an ordinary repository we commit to directly, so nothing in this lab pushes anywhere.
export GIT_AUTHOR_NAME=Ada GIT_AUTHOR_EMAIL=ada@example.com
export GIT_COMMITTER_NAME=Ada GIT_COMMITTER_EMAIL=ada@example.com
export GIT_AUTHOR_DATE="2026-10-13T08:00:00+05:30" GIT_COMMITTER_DATE="2026-10-13T08:00:00+05:30"
rm -rf /tmp/stack-lab && mkdir -p /tmp/stack-lab && cd /tmp/stack-lab
git init -q -b main upstream
printf 'def handler():\n    return 200\n' > upstream/app.py
git -C upstream add app.py && git -C upstream commit -qm "initial"
git clone -q upstream desk-api && cd desk-api
source stack-setup.sh

Case 1: Start a stack
gh stack init auth-model
printf 'class User:\n    def __init__(self, name):\n        self.name = name\n' > models.py
git add models.py && git commit -qm "Add User model"
✓ Created stack: main ← auth-model
  You're on auth-model (top of stack).

What's next:
  • commit your work as usual, then add a layer:  gh stack add
  • see your stack any time:                      gh stack view
  • when ready to open PRs:                       gh stack submit
gh stack init creates the first branch from the trunk and records the stack. From here on you commit with ordinary Git.


Case 2: One layer per reviewable idea
printf 'def login(user):\n    return 200\n' > routes.py
gh stack add -Am "Add /login route" auth-route
printf 'def test_login():\n    assert True\n' > test_routes.py
gh stack add -Am "Test /login" auth-tests
gh stack view --short
✓ Created branch auth-route (layer 2) with commit 576d4a2b6e114f9a1c8e322bd964323c6291278d
✓ Created branch auth-tests (layer 3) with commit 334abaf62c2030f3b831ac41c3a644cd2a0014d1
» auth-tests (current)
├ auth-route
├ auth-model
└ main
gh stack add -Am MSG NAME stages everything, commits, and creates the next layer in one step. The rule is in the docs and easy to miss: if the current branch has no commits yet, the commit lands on it. If it already has commits, a new branch is created on top. In Case 2 each current branch already had a commit, so each add created a new layer. Case 1 could have used gh stack add -Am "Add User model" instead of git commit. On a fresh auth-model the extension says so and commits in place:
⚠ Branch l1 has no prior commits — adding your commit here instead of creating a new branch
(That line comes from a separate one-layer scratch stack named l1.)


Case 3: Where the stack lives on your disk
jq . .git/gh-stack
{
  "schemaVersion": 1,
  "repository": "",
  "stacks": [
    {
      "trunk": {
        "branch": "main",
        "head": "c7ba999b678d838250f9f42aef4b8b3dcd9fe6a2"
      },
      "branches": [
        {
          "branch": "auth-model",
          "base": "c7ba999b678d838250f9f42aef4b8b3dcd9fe6a2"
        },
        {
          "branch": "auth-route",
          "base": "f789cde542e9cd2689a11b02cdc41b26b803950e"
        },
        {
          "branch": "auth-tests",
          "base": "576d4a2b6e114f9a1c8e322bd964323c6291278d"
        }
      ]
    }
  ]
}
This file is the second of the three views. It is plain JSON beside your refs. Note what it stores: for each layer, the commit it was based on, not the commit it currently points at. That is how gh stack notices that a lower layer has moved. repository is empty here because the lab’s remote is not on GitHub. In a real clone it names owner/repo.


Case 4: A review fix on the bottom layer
The reviewer of PR 1 wants a type annotation. Make the change in the layer it belongs to, not in the layer you happen to be on:
gh stack bottom
printf 'class User:\n    def __init__(self, name: str):\n        self.name = name\n' > models.py
git commit -qam "User: annotate name"
gh stack view --json | jq -r '.branches[] | "\(.name)\tneedsRebase=\(.needsRebase)"'
✓ Switched to auth-model
auth-model  needsRebase=false
auth-route  needsRebase=true
auth-tests  needsRebase=false
needsRebase=true on auth-route means “my recorded base is no longer the tip of the layer below”. On GitHub the merge box would show Rebase stack, and the stack cannot merge until its history is linear again.


Case 5: Trunk moves too; one cascading rebase fixes both
printf 'VERSION = "1.1"\n' > ../upstream/version.py                  # trunk moves on "GitHub"
git -C ../upstream add version.py && git -C ../upstream commit -qm "Bump version"
gh stack rebase
git log --oneline --graph --decorate --decorate-refs=refs/heads auth-tests
base=main   # what each PR's reviewer sees: the diff against the layer below
for b in auth-model auth-route auth-tests; do
  printf '%-11s vs %-11s %s\n' "$b" "$base" "$(git diff --shortstat "$base" "$b")"; base=$b
done
✓ Fetched latest main from origin
✓ Trunk main fast-forwarded to caee569
Stack detected: (main) <- auth-model <- auth-route <- auth-tests
Rebasing branches in order, starting from auth-model to auth-tests
✓ Rebased auth-model onto main
✓ Rebased auth-route onto auth-model
✓ Rebased auth-tests onto auth-route
All branches in stack rebased locally with main (caee569)
To push up your changes, run `gh stack push`
* cdf86eb (auth-tests) Test /login
* 4bfa7af (auth-route) Add /login route
* 9692066 (auth-model) User: annotate name
* 6459469 Add User model
* caee569 (main) Bump version
* c7ba999 initial
auth-model  vs main         1 file changed, 3 insertions(+)
auth-route  vs auth-model   1 file changed, 2 insertions(+)
auth-tests  vs auth-route   1 file changed, 2 insertions(+)
gh stack rebase fetched the trunk, fast-forwarded main, then rebased each layer onto the one below, bottom to top. The last loop prints what each PR’s reviewer sees. Every layer still shows only its own file, so nobody re-reviews models.py in PR 2.
To publish, gh stack push force-pushes each active branch with its own --force-with-lease. Its help text is explicit that this is not atomic:
Uses explicit per-branch --force-with-lease checks. Updates are not atomic: a
branch may update even if another branch is rejected. Fix the rejected branch
and run the command again; branches already updated will be unchanged.
gh stack sync (fetch, reconcile with GitHub, rebase, push, refresh PR state) pushes with --force-with-lease --atomic, so all branches move or none do. Prefer sync when reviewers are watching the stack.
gh stack submit is the step that creates things on GitHub. It pushes, creates one PR per layer with the right base branch, and links them into a stack object. The rest of this page stays local.


Case 6: What GitHub does that your clone cannot
These behaviours belong to the server. This lab cannot show them, so here they are as GitHub documents them:

Rules use the stack’s trunk. Required reviews, required checks, CODEOWNERS and code scanning are evaluated as if each PR targeted the trunk (usually main). A mid-stack PR is held to the same bar as the bottom one.
Actions see the trunk too. A workflow on pull_request for main runs for every PR in the stack, and github.event.pull_request.stack carries stack metadata to workflow expressions.
Merging the bottom PR rebases the rest automatically, and the next PR is retargeted to the trunk. If the trunk branch of a stack is deleted, GitHub now retargets the stack instead of closing its bottom PR.
Signed commits. The GA changelog and the stacked-PR reference say that a server-side Rebase stack creates signed replacement commits that keep the original authorship. The Managing stacked pull requests how-to still carried an older note saying server-side rebase commits are not signed. If your branch rules require signatures, test once on your repository, or rebase locally with gh stack rebase so your own signing configuration applies.
Webhooks. pull_request events include a stacked action when a PR joins a stack.
Other tools. Branches pushed by Jujutsu, Sapling or plain Git can be linked into a stack with gh stack link or on the website. The extension is a convenience, not a requirement.

title: Stacked Changes: Stacked Pull Requests on GitHub
text:
The trap
A layer lands outside the stack, and the stack still believes it is open.
A colleague merges auth-model into main some other way: from a non-stacked PR, a squash merge done by hand, or a cherry-pick to main. GitHub never saw a stack merge, so neither your metadata nor the stack object knows that layer 1 has landed. The next cascading rebase tries to replay layer 1 onto a trunk that already contains it in squashed form:
# someone lands layer 1 on "GitHub" as a plain squash merge, outside the stack
git -C ../upstream fetch -q "$PWD" auth-model
git -C ../upstream merge -q --squash FETCH_HEAD >/dev/null
git -C ../upstream commit -qm "Add User model (#41)"
gh stack rebase; echo "exit=$?"
git status --short
gh stack rebase --abort
✓ Fetched latest main from origin
✓ Trunk main fast-forwarded to aae8b37
Stack detected: (main) <- auth-model <- auth-route <- auth-tests
Rebasing branches in order, starting from auth-model to auth-tests
⚠ Rebasing auth-model onto main — conflict
Conflict worktree: /tmp/stack-lab/desk-api
Resolve and stage files in that worktree; continuation may be run from any worktree.

Conflicted files:
  C models.py (lines 2–6)

To resolve:
  1. Open each conflicted file and look for conflict markers:
     <<<<<<< HEAD  (incoming changes from main)
     =======
     >>>>>>>  (changes being rebased)
  2. Edit the file to keep the desired changes and remove the markers
  3. Stage resolved files: `git add <file>`
  4. Continue:  `gh stack rebase --continue`

Resolve conflicts on auth-model, then run `gh stack rebase --continue`
Or abort this operation with `gh stack rebase --abort`
exit=3
AA models.py
✓ Rebase aborted and branches restored
Exit code 3 is the documented “rebase conflict” code. The conflict is not a real disagreement between two changes. It is the same change arriving twice under different hashes. Resolving it by hand (“keep both”, “keep ours”) is how stacks end up with duplicated or half-reverted code. --abort puts every branch back, which is why the last line is safe.
Fix the branches first, then fix the metadata, and only then let anything talk to GitHub:
git rebase --onto origin/main auth-model auth-tests --update-refs
git log --oneline --graph --decorate --decorate-refs=refs/heads auth-tests
gh stack unstack --local
gh stack init auth-route auth-tests
gh stack view --json | jq -r '.branches[] | "\(.name)\tneedsRebase=\(.needsRebase)"'
Rebasing (1/3)
Rebasing (2/3)
Rebasing (3/3)
Successfully rebased and updated refs/heads/auth-tests.
Updated the following refs with --update-refs:
    refs/heads/auth-route
* 6ef7b7a (auth-tests) Test /login
* 5dd7caa (auth-route) Add /login route
* aae8b37 (main) Add User model (#41)
* caee569 Bump version
* c7ba999 initial
✓ Stack removed from local tracking
✓ Adopted 2 branches: main ← auth-route ← auth-tests
  You're on auth-tests (top of stack).

What's next:
  • see the full stack:                          gh stack view
  • move between branches:                       gh stack switch
  • link these PRs into a Stack on GitHub:       gh stack submit
auth-route  needsRebase=false
auth-tests  needsRebase=false
--onto origin/main auth-model auth-tests replays only the commits above the landed layer (the third “Rebasing” step is the update-ref instruction), and --update-refs carries auth-route along. The mechanics are the same as for a squash-merged bottom branch with plain Git. See update-refs and keep-base in the rebasing chapter. gh stack unstack --local forgets the stale tracking without calling GitHub. Plain gh stack unstack would also dissolve the stack on the server. gh stack init with existing branch names adopts them in order. Then run gh stack submit. Its documented steps include updating the base branch of existing PRs, here moving the auth-route PR onto main, and creating or updating the stack object on GitHub so that it holds only the two remaining PRs.
Prevention is cheaper than cure. Land stacked work only through the stack, from the merge box or with gh stack merge. Then GitHub records the merge, rebases the layers above, and gh stack sync brings that state back into your clone: push skips merged and queued branches, and view marks them isMerged. No tool can recognise a change that landed some other way. When a cascading rebase conflicts on code you know is already on the trunk, abort and cut the layer off as shown above. Do not resolve the conflict.

title: Stacked Changes: Stacked Pull Requests on GitHub
text:
The boring rule

One reviewable idea per layer, all branches in one repository. Make fixes in the layer they belong to, then gh stack rebase (or sync) and never hand-merge a layer out of order. Publish with gh stack sync (atomic) or submit, and land through the stack, bottom-up, never around it. When the three views disagree, fix the branches, then the local metadata (unstack --local + init), then GitHub.

title: Stacked Changes: Stacked Pull Requests on GitHub
text:
Try this

Run the lab, then add a fourth layer with gh stack add -Am "Document /login" auth-docs. Use gh stack down, up, top and bottom, and check with gh stack view --short which branch is current after each one.
Repeat Case 4 with gh stack rebase --upstack from auth-model instead of a full rebase, and compare the output with Case 5.
Reproduce the trap, but this time resolve the conflict with git checkout --theirs models.py, git add and gh stack rebase --continue. Inspect git log -p main..auth-tests and decide whether the result is what a reviewer approved.
In a scratch repository on GitHub that you own, gh stack submit --auto --open a three-layer stack (without --open, --auto creates drafts). Merge the middle PR from the website and confirm that the bottom PR merged with it and the top PR was retargeted to main.
In the same scratch repository, enable “Require signed commits” on main, click Rebase stack after moving main, and check git log --show-signature on the rewritten commits. Record which of the two documented behaviours you get.

title: Theory
text:
Theory: Content Addressing is the Whole Trick
Git is a content-addressed filesystem plus names. Internals are not trivia; they are why hosting, LFS, and fsck look the way they do.

title: Theory
text:
Invariants

Object name = hash of type + size + payload (SHA-1 historically, SHA-256 optional).
Blobs have no filename; trees bind names to hashes.
Packfiles are compression (deltas) of that object set, not the data model.
A server is constrained by quarantine, receive.denyCurrentBranch, and hook timing around these objects.

commit → tree → blob
   \→ parent commit
packfile = many objects + delta chains  (disk, not mental model)

Editing files under .git/objects by hand.
Assuming SHA-1 collision is a daily concern (it is a research/hosting concern).

title: Content Addressing — SHA-1, SHA-256, and the Git 3.0 Switch
text:
Content Addressing — SHA-1, SHA-256, and the Git 3.0 switch
Every Git object is named by a hash of its own bytes. That one decision is why history is tamper-evident, why two clones agree on what “commit 7c77260” means without talking to each other, and why deduplication is free. It is also why changing the hash function is the hardest migration Git has ever planned: the hash is the name, so a new function renames every object in every repository.
Git has supported SHA-256 repositories since 2.29. The project’s BreakingChanges document now commits to making SHA-256 the default for new repositories in Git 3.0 (no release date yet), alongside main as the initial branch and reftable as the ref backend. This chapter shows what content addressing actually hashes, what a SHA-256 repository looks like, what does not cross between the two formats, and how to get ready without breaking anything today.

title: Content Addressing — SHA-1, SHA-256, and the Git 3.0 Switch
text:
Mental model
object bytes  =  "<type> <size>\0" + payload
object name   =  H(object bytes)          H = SHA-1  (40 hex, 20 bytes)
                                          H = SHA-256 (64 hex, 32 bytes)

blob ──┐
blob ──┼── tree ── commit ── commit ── …     every arrow is a hash
blob ──┘                                     → change one byte, every name above it changes

one repository = ONE object format (extensions.objectFormat)
two formats    = two different names for the same content → no shared history on the wire




SHA-1 repository
SHA-256 repository




Object name length
40 hex
64 hex


core.repositoryformatversion
0 (or 1)
1


extensions.objectFormat
unset (or sha1)
sha256


Empty tree
4b825dc…
6ef19b4…


Push/fetch with the other format
refused
refused


Default today (2.56)
yes
--object-format=sha256


Default in Git 3.0 (planned)
no
yes, for new repositories



SHA-1 is not being removed: BreakingChanges states there is no plan to deprecate the sha1 format. Existing repositories keep working. What changes is what git init creates when you do not say.

title: Content Addressing — SHA-1, SHA-256, and the Git 3.0 Switch
text:
Worked examples
All cases were run on Debian 13 with Git 2.56.0 built from the release tarball, plus two extra builds of the same source: one with WITH_BREAKING_CHANGES=YesPlease (a preview of Git 3.0 defaults) and one with Rust enabled (needed for Case 6). Commands assume git is 2.56; the other two builds are called by full path.
git --version
git version 2.56.0
To make the object names below reproducible on your machine, fix identity and dates first:
export GIT_AUTHOR_NAME=Ada GIT_AUTHOR_EMAIL=ada@example.com
export GIT_COMMITTER_NAME=Ada GIT_COMMITTER_EMAIL=ada@example.com
export GIT_AUTHOR_DATE='2026-10-08T09:00:00+05:30' GIT_COMMITTER_DATE='2026-10-08T09:00:00+05:30'

Case 1: hash an object by hand
A blob is "blob <size>\0" followed by the file contents. Hash those bytes with the ordinary coreutils tools and compare with what Git computes in a repository of each format:
printf 'hello\n' > hello.txt
printf 'blob 6\0hello\n' | sha1sum
printf 'blob 6\0hello\n' | sha256sum

git init -q s1
git init -q --object-format=sha256 s256
for r in s1 s256; do (cd $r && cp ../hello.txt . && echo "$r: $(git hash-object hello.txt)"); done
ce013625030ba8dba906f756967f9e9ca394464a  -
2cf8d83d9ee29543b34a87727421fdecb7e3f3a183d337639025de576db9ebb4  -
s1: ce013625030ba8dba906f756967f9e9ca394464a
s256: 2cf8d83d9ee29543b34a87727421fdecb7e3f3a183d337639025de576db9ebb4
Same bytes, same algorithm, same name, with no Git involved. That is the whole trick, and it is also the whole problem: the SHA-256 name of hello shares nothing with its SHA-1 name.


Case 2: what a SHA-256 repository is
for r in s1 s256; do
  (cd $r && echo "== $r" &&
   git rev-parse --show-object-format --show-ref-format &&
   git config --get core.repositoryformatversion; git config --get extensions.objectformat)
done
== s1
sha1
files
0
== s256
sha256
files
1
sha256
The format is one line of repository config plus a format-version bump to 1, which makes Git versions that predate repository extensions refuse to open the repository rather than misread it. Never edit extensions.objectFormat by hand on a repository with objects in it: the existing objects keep their old names, and Git will not find them.
Commits look the same, just with longer names:
git init -q -b main --object-format=sha256 app256 && cd app256
echo 'hello' > README && git add README && git commit -q -m 'first commit'
git log --format='%H %s'
git rev-parse --short HEAD
git cat-file -p HEAD
git log --format=%H | awk '{print length($0)}'
cd ..
7c77260fad0cad11b0ae2ca24098d6d36ee56d96ad221d0d6f485f0911ac3c33 first commit
7c77260
tree cacbd5aeac8aafd15f1acb153e9a189e0b607b7ee7d874aee3534d1babdfcb21
author Ada <ada@example.com> 1791430200 +0530
committer Ada <ada@example.com> 1791430200 +0530

first commit
64
Abbreviated names stay seven characters by default, so everyday output barely changes. Scripts that consume full names are a different story (Case 4).


Case 3: what does not cross between formats
git init -q --bare -b main remote-sha1.git
(cd app256 && git push ../remote-sha1.git main)

git init -q -b main app1 && (cd app1 && echo x > f && git add f && git commit -q -m one)
(cd app256 && git fetch ../app1 main)

git clone -q app256 clone256 && git -C clone256 rev-parse --show-object-format
fatal: the receiving end does not support this repository's hash algorithm
fatal: the remote end hung up unexpectedly
fatal: mismatched algorithms: client sha256; server sha1
sha256

Push and fetch across formats are refused, in both directions. No silent conversion happens.

Clone adopts the remote’s format. A SHA-256 server produces SHA-256 clones; you do not choose.

The consequence for teams: a repository’s format is a property of the project, decided once at creation, and every mirror, fork, CI cache, and forge that touches it must speak that format. BreakingChanges makes the Git 3.0 default switch conditional on exactly that ecosystem readiness: libraries, applications, and forges. Check your hosting platform, CI runners, and Git libraries before you create SHA-256 repositories that others must use.



Case 4: tooling that hard-codes SHA-1
Two assumptions break first: “an object name is 40 hex characters” and magic constants like the empty-tree ID.
for r in app1 app256; do
  echo "== $r ($(git -C $r rev-parse --show-object-format))"
  git -C $r hash-object -t tree /dev/null
  git -C $r rev-parse HEAD | grep -Exq '[0-9a-f]{40}' && echo "40-hex check: pass" || echo "40-hex check: FAIL"
  git -C $r rev-parse HEAD | grep -Exq '[0-9a-f]{40}([0-9a-f]{24})?' && echo "40-or-64 check: pass"
done
== app1 (sha1)
4b825dc642cb6eb9a060e54bf8d69288fbee4904
40-hex check: pass
40-or-64 check: pass
== app256 (sha256)
6ef19b41225c5369f1c104d45d8d85efa9b057b53b14b4b9b939dd74decc5321
40-hex check: FAIL
40-or-64 check: pass
Audit hooks, CI scripts, and database columns for:








Assumption
Where it hides
Replace with




[0-9a-f]{40}
Hook validation, log parsers, webhook handlers
Accept 40 or 64, or ask git rev-parse --show-object-format


CHAR(40) / fixed-width columns
Deploy trackers, review tools
Width 64


4b825dc… empty tree
“diff against nothing” scripts
git hash-object -t tree /dev/null


0000…0000 (40 zeros) for created/deleted refs
pre-receive / update hooks
Compare against a string of zeros of the received length


“short SHA is unique enough” in URLs
Dashboards
Unchanged; abbreviation rules are the same





Case 5: previewing Git 3.0 defaults, and pinning yours
Git’s source can be built with the planned Git 3.0 behaviour switched on:
make prefix=/opt/git-3preview NO_TCLTK=1 NO_RUST=1 WITH_BREAKING_CHANGES=YesPlease all
sudo make prefix=/opt/git-3preview NO_TCLTK=1 NO_RUST=1 WITH_BREAKING_CHANGES=YesPlease install
/opt/git-3preview/bin/git version --build-options | grep default
default-ref-format: reftable
default-hash: sha256
/opt/git-3preview/bin/git init g3
cd g3 && /opt/git-3preview/bin/git rev-parse --show-object-format --show-ref-format && /opt/git-3preview/bin/git symbolic-ref HEAD
hint: Using 'main' as the name for the initial branch since Git 3.0.
hint: If you expected Git to create 'master', the just-created
hint: branch can be renamed via this command:
hint:
hint:   git branch -m master
hint:
hint: Disable this message with "git config set advice.defaultBranchName false"
Initialized empty Git repository in /tmp/vcs/g3/.git/
sha1
reftable
refs/heads/main
main and reftable flipped as documented. The object format did not: this 2.56.0 preview build reports default-hash: sha256 in its build options, but in our runs git init without other settings (also tried with an empty environment) still created a SHA-1 repository. The --object-format flag, init.defaultObjectFormat, and GIT_DEFAULT_HASH all produced SHA-256 as expected. Reading the source shows why tests may not notice: t/test-lib.sh exports GIT_DEFAULT_HASH from the build’s default-hash. The lesson is the boring one: a preview build is a preview. Do not infer the future default from it; state the format you want.
Stating it is cheap and works on today’s Git, on the preview, and on Git 3.0:
git -c init.defaultObjectFormat=sha256 init -q -b main k1 && git -C k1 rev-parse --show-object-format
GIT_DEFAULT_HASH=sha256 git init -q -b main k2 && git -C k2 rev-parse --show-object-format
/opt/git-3preview/bin/git -c init.defaultRefFormat=files -c init.defaultBranch=master init -q k3
/opt/git-3preview/bin/git -C k3 rev-parse --show-object-format --show-ref-format
/opt/git-3preview/bin/git -C k3 symbolic-ref HEAD
sha256
sha256
sha1
files
refs/heads/master
For a fleet, put the choices in system or global config (or your provisioning tooling) so the Git 3.0 upgrade changes nothing you did not decide:
# /etc/gitconfig (or ~/.gitconfig) — make today's defaults explicit
[init]
    defaultObjectFormat = sha1     # or sha256, once your forge and tools are ready
    defaultRefFormat = files
    defaultBranch = main


Case 6: the interoperability work (compatObjectFormat)
Git 2.52’s release notes mark “the beginning of SHA1-SHA256 interoperability work”: a SHA-256 repository that also maintains a SHA-1 name for every object, so that it can one day talk to SHA-1 peers. In 2.56 the switch exists but needs a Rust-enabled build. The default NO_RUST=1 build refuses:
git init -q -b main --object-format=sha256 compat && cd compat
git config extensions.compatObjectFormat sha1
echo hi > a && git add a
fatal: compatibility hash algorithm support requires Rust
With Git 2.56.0 built with Rust enabled (rust: enabled in --build-options, rustc 1.99), the same steps work. Then build the same content in a plain SHA-1 repository and compare:
G=/opt/git-2.56-rust/bin/git
$G init -q -b main --object-format=sha256 compat && cd compat
$G config extensions.compatObjectFormat sha1
echo hi > a && $G add a && $G commit -q -m c1
$G rev-parse HEAD
$G rev-parse --output-object-format=sha1 HEAD
ls .git/objects
cd .. && $G init -q -b main plain1 && cd plain1
echo hi > a && $G add a && $G commit -q -m c1 && $G rev-parse HEAD
cd ../compat
$G rev-parse --output-object-format=sha1 'HEAD^{tree}'
$G -C ../plain1 rev-parse 'HEAD^{tree}'
$G cat-file -t 15307cff4ea19f61d3bb0b98bc73102e2454352c
$G push ../r1.git main      # r1.git: a bare SHA-1 repository
13c18aac72ade018e9d88a6f80239f88397fdf997c3437bce30b870bf87e720a
15307cff4ea19f61d3bb0b98bc73102e2454352c
00
13
96
info
loose-object-idx
pack
15307cff4ea19f61d3bb0b98bc73102e2454352c
c49897f29f9819a0ab6850d7e22443508a1a29d5
c49897f29f9819a0ab6850d7e22443508a1a29d5
commit
fatal: the receiving end does not support this repository's hash algorithm
fatal: the remote end hung up unexpectedly
The SHA-256 repository computed the same SHA-1 commit and tree names as the native SHA-1 repository: it re-serialises each object the way a SHA-1 repository would and hashes that, recording the pairs in loose-object-idx. cat-file can already look objects up by their SHA-1 name. The network protocol cannot use them yet, so the push is still refused. This is the foundation for a future where a project migrates to SHA-256 while contributors on SHA-1 keep pushing. It is groundwork, not something to deploy.


Case 7: migrating an existing repository today
There is no in-place conversion. The supported route is to replay history into a new repository, which gives every commit a new name:
git init -q -b main --object-format=sha256 conv256
(cd app1 && git fast-export --all) | (cd conv256 && git fast-import --quiet)
git -C app1 log --format='%H %s'
git -C conv256 log --format='%H %s'
aaec54ba980d0b7c3e8f4afe2fd0e72e8fa15d5d one
9e2c3721012ae0d829ab2717b83446230a71ab4fc873830ae5c98b7ee39aa75b one
Everything that refers to old names breaks: commit hashes quoted in messages and issues, signed commits and tags (the signature covered the old bytes), submodule pointers, CI caches, and every clone. Treat it like a history rewrite of the whole project: announce it, freeze pushes, convert, re-sign tags if you rely on signatures, and have everyone re-clone.

Cheat sheet

title: Content Addressing — SHA-1, SHA-256, and the Git 3.0 Switch
text:
Safety

Changing extensions.objectFormat in an existing repository does not convert anything. It just makes the repository unreadable.
Push and fetch refuse to cross formats, so you cannot corrupt a remote by accident. You can strand yourself by creating SHA-256 repositories your forge or CI cannot host.
A converted repository is a different project as far as names go. Keep the SHA-1 original read-only for as long as anything references its commit IDs.
compatObjectFormat is experimental and Rust-only in 2.56. Do not enable it on repositories other people depend on.

title: Content Addressing — SHA-1, SHA-256, and the Git 3.0 Switch
text:
Hands-on checklist

Reproduce Case 1 and confirm sha256sum of "blob 6\0hello\n" matches git hash-object in a SHA-256 repository.
Run git version --build-options on your workstation, CI image, and server. Write down default-hash and default-ref-format for each.
Grep your hooks and CI for {40}, CHAR(40), and 4b825dc. Fix what you find.
Add init.defaultObjectFormat, init.defaultRefFormat, and init.defaultBranch to the config you provision, set to what you use today.
Create a throwaway SHA-256 repository on your forge (if it allows that) and push to it from CI. That is the real readiness test.

title: git maintenance
text:
git maintenance
Git commands that add data (add, commit, fetch) optimize for a snappy UI. They do not spend time reshaping the whole object database. git maintenance is the operator tool that runs background (or manual) optimization tasks: commit-graph, prefetch, loose-object packing, multi-pack-index repacks, and more — without turning every git status into a full gc.

title: git maintenance
text:
Mental model
foreground Git  ──► writes packs / loose objects / refs  (fast path)
        │
        ▼
git maintenance run / start
        │
        ├── commit-graph      (faster reachability / log)
        ├── prefetch          (objects ready before real fetch)
        ├── loose-objects     (loose → pack, carefully)
        ├── incremental-repack (multi-pack-index dance)
        └── pack-refs, …      (ref iteration speed)
git maintenance start registers the repo and installs a scheduler (systemd user timers on modern Linux, else cron; launchctl / schtasks on macOS / Windows). register alone updates config; start = register + schedule.

title: git maintenance
text:
Tasks that matter at scale








Task
What it does
Default under incremental strategy




commit-graph
Incremental commit-graph write + verify; safe beside concurrent Git
hourly


prefetch
git fetch into refs/prefetch/ (no tag update; does not move remote-tracking branches)
hourly


loose-objects
Delete loose objects already packed; pack a batch of remaining loose objects
daily


incremental-repack
multi-pack-index expire then repack small packs into a larger one
daily


pack-refs
Pack loose refs into a single file
weekly (when enabled by strategy)


gc
Full garbage collection / aggressive repack — expensive; not on the incremental schedule
manual / other strategies



Prefetch makes the next interactive git fetch mostly a tip update when objects were already downloaded. Exclude a remote with remote.<name>.skipFetchAll if that remote should not be prefetched.
incremental-repack uses the multi-pack-index (MIDX): expire unreferenced packs, then repack a batch of small packs and retarget MIDX entries. Default batch size 0 means “try to fold into one pack.”

title: git maintenance
text:
Worked examples

Case 1: One-shot tasks on a lab clone
cd /path/to/large-repo

# Inspect whether auto thresholds say work is due
git maintenance is-needed --auto; echo "exit=$?"

# Run specific safe tasks explicitly
git maintenance run --task=commit-graph
git maintenance run --task=loose-objects
git maintenance run --task=incremental-repack

# Optional: see commit-graph files appear
ls -la .git/objects/info/commit-graph 2>/dev/null || ls -la .git/objects/info/commit-graphs/ 2>/dev/null || true
Use --task when you want a known order. Without --task, Git runs tasks with maintenance.<task>.enabled=true (by default that is mainly gc unless you set a strategy).


Case 2: Enable incremental strategy and register
cd /path/to/large-repo

git maintenance register
# Sets maintenance.strategy=incremental if unset, adds repo to global maintenance.repo,
# enables recommended schedules, sets maintenance.auto=false in this repo

git config --get maintenance.strategy
git config --get-all --global maintenance.repo | tail -n 5
git config --get maintenance.auto
Expected shape: incremental, a path entry under maintenance.repo, and maintenance.auto=false so foreground commands do not also kick auto-maintenance while the scheduler owns the job.


Case 3: git maintenance start on Linux
cd /path/to/large-repo
git maintenance start --scheduler=auto
# On Linux with user systemd: systemd-timer; otherwise crontab

systemctl --user list-timers 'git-maintenance*' 2>/dev/null || true
# Or: crontab -l | sed -n '/GIT MAINTENANCE/,/END GIT MAINTENANCE/p'
Timers run git for-each-repo --config=maintenance.repo maintenance run --schedule=hourly|daily|weekly. Stop with git maintenance stop (leaves the repo registered). unregister removes the repo from the global list (--force if unsure).


Case 4: Prefetch vs a normal fetch
# After maintenance has run prefetch on a registered remote:
git show-ref | grep prefetch | head
git fetch origin
# Ideal case: tips move with little or no object transfer
Prefetch refs live under refs/prefetch/ so your origin/main does not jump until you fetch.


Case 5: Manual vs scheduled, and locks
# Manual full gc via maintenance (preferred over bare git gc when using the framework)
git maintenance run --task=gc

# Auto mode: only if thresholds say so (loose object count, pack count, …)
git maintenance run --auto
Each git maintenance run takes an object database lock. Overlapping hourly runs on huge multi-repo schedules can skip a cycle — shrink task cost or stagger repos if windows exceed an hour. Do not mix bare git gc with concurrent git maintenance run; prefer git maintenance run --task=gc.

title: git maintenance
text:
Strategy cheat sheet







maintenance.strategy
Intent




none
Scheduled maintenance runs nothing by default


gc
Run the gc task


geometric
Geometric pack repack + auxiliary cleanup; strong default for manual maintenance on large repos (Git 2.50+ docs)


incremental
Small non-deleting tasks on a schedule; manual path still uses gc



Tune with maintenance.<task>.enabled and maintenance.<task>.schedule (hourly / daily / weekly). Threshold knobs include maintenance.commit-graph.auto, maintenance.loose-objects.auto, maintenance.incremental-repack.auto.

title: git maintenance
text:
Safety

Prefetch contacts remotes on a timer — ensure credentials/agents work non-interactively or exclude remotes.
gc deletes stale data; incremental tasks prefer not to. Know which strategy you enabled before leaving a laptop on a huge monorepo overnight.
Customizing systemd units: use drop-ins under ~/.config/systemd/user/git-maintenance@.service.d/; start overwrites the main unit files.
maintenance.auto=false after register is intentional; re-enable only if you understand double scheduling.

title: git maintenance
text:
Hands-on checklist

On a disposable clone, run commit-graph and incremental-repack with --task.
git maintenance register and confirm maintenance.strategy / maintenance.repo.
git maintenance start; list timers or crontab region.
Trigger prefetch; inspect refs/prefetch/; run a normal git fetch and note transfer size.
git maintenance stop and unregister when the lab is done.

title: git maintenance
text:
Pitfalls








Symptom
Likely cause
Fix




Hourly tasks sometimes skip
Overlap on object DB lock
Fewer repos per user, cheaper tasks, or longer spacing


Remote-tracking branches “randomly” move
Not prefetch — something else fetching
Prefetch should only touch refs/prefetch/


Disk grows after incremental mode
No full gc; MIDX keeps more packs briefly
Periodic manual gc / geometric strategy if policy allows


Scheduler missing on Linux
No user systemd / lingering
loginctl enable-linger $USER or use --scheduler=crontab


unregister errors
Repo not in list
git maintenance unregister --force
